      "description": "Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest.     {
      "name": "mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_start",
      "description": "Open the Browser pane: pass `url` to open a browser tab at a URL (no dev server needed — use this for external sites, staging, docs, or your deployed app), OR pass `name` to start a dev server from .claude/launch.json.\n\nStart a dev server by name from .claude/launch.json. If .claude/launch.json doesn't exist, create it first with this format:\n{\n  \"version\": \"0.0.1\",\n  \"configurations\": [\n    {\n      \"name\": \"<unique-name>\",\n      \"runtimeExecutable\": \"<command>\",\n      \"runtimeArgs\": [\"<args>\"],\n      \"port\": <port>\n    }\n  ]\n}\nSet \"runtimeExecutable\" to the command (e.g. \"npm\"), \"runtimeArgs\" to the arguments (e.g. [\"run\", \"dev\"]), and \"port\" to the server port. An optional \"url\" (http/https) opens the preview there instead of http://localhost:<port>. A localhost \"url\" must be just the server's origin — no path or query, matching the entry's port — for example \"https://localhost:8443\" or \"http://app.localhost:3000\"; to show a specific page, navigate after the preview opens. Non-localhost URLs may carry paths and are subject to the user's permission and the organization's browsing policy. A configuration with \"url\" and no command attaches to an already-running server. Only include servers you actually need to preview. Reuses the server if already running. ALWAYS use this instead of Bash for running servers. If the deliverable is already published as an Artifact, update the Artifact instead of starting a server to show it.",

    {
      "name": "mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window",
      "description": "Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset \"desktop\" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset \"desktop\" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.",
      "schema": {
        "name": "mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window",
        "description": "Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab.       "name": "mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control",
      "description": "Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac.               "description": "What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'inspect' returns the accessibility tree of the front app (what a screen reader reads, which can differ from what is drawn) as JSON — per element: type, label, value, frame [x,y,width,height] in device points from the top-left, traits the type does not imply, enabled only when false, children. Call 'inspect' before a 'tap' on anything you have not located in this screen's tree, before answering what text a screen shows, and before reporting a control's state (a switch's value, whether a button is enabled, which tab is selected) or whether a sheet, alert or other modal is in front (the result says so) — never guess coordinates from memory of similar apps, and do not 'screenshot' for these. Go straight to 'screenshot' for color, images, and layout. Three reads: no marker and no x/y = the whole visible tree (the safe default when you do not know the exact label); marker = the first element, in tree order, whose label contains that CASE-SENSITIVE substring — a title can match before the button with the same text, so check the matched element's type; x/y = the element drawn on top at that point, as a tap would find it, with its descendants (a point between controls hits their container). If a marker misses or returns the wrong element, read the whole tree instead of guessing or screenshotting. Then tap the center of the target's frame. Hidden, off-screen, and illegibly small elements are omitted and counted; text longer than its area shows is cut (it ends with ...). Only the x/y read resolves occlusion, and only by bars and containers it can recognize: a frame from the whole-tree or marker read that overlaps a later sibling (a tab bar, a sheet) may be covered, so before tapping it read x/y at its center; a point on a sheet's blank area can still read the content behind it, so when the result reports a modal, stay inside it. A tree over the size cap loses its deepest levels first and says so — narrow with marker, or with x/y on the target itself: a point in a gap answers the container around it, which is no smaller; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Firecrawl provides web search, page retrieval, site URL discovery, multi-page collection, structured page data, monitoring, and multi-source research that returns structured data. Match the requested operation to the tool boundary: firecrawl_scrape retrieves one supplied page and can return JSON matching a supplied schema, firecrawl_map enumerates URLs under a site without retrieving their content, and firecrawl_agent runs multi-source research and returns structured data when the URLs are not known or the answer spans several sites (an entity plus its fields, a list, a dataset); its result is read with firecrawl_agent_status. For biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature, the firecrawl_research_* tools search a paper index of abstracts and full text; firecrawl_search with categories: [\"research\"] is a website filter over ordinary web results and reaches different sources. For a programming question — code behaviour, a library or framework, an API contract, an error message, or a known bug — firecrawl_developer_search (or firecrawl_search with categories: [\"developer\"]) searches an index of repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and curated documentation sites. Authenticated firecrawl_search returns web results together with matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. Alexandria is Firecrawl's catalogue of data providers and workflows across companies, people, jobs, finance and filings, public records and government spending, real estate, places and restaurants, retail and prices, package registries and developer data, news, research, and more; providers return typed, sourced records through published contracts. #43 ASSISTANT · claude-opus-5 · 2026-09-22T11:43:23.886Z · session 362d46b6 · uuid 17419f45
**T+0 ≈ now. Phase 1 (read-only) running. No code written.**

## Uncomfortable truth first

Your list is 100% **schema** defects. Every one of them is real, and every one of them is the cheap kind — a type system, a normaliser and an afternoon fix them. Not one of them would actually hurt a traveller, because a schema defect makes the agent *fail loudly or return nothing*.

The defects that burn a real person are **semantic**: the record parses perfectly, looks clean, and is confidently wrong. You found zero of those, and this file has at least four. The worst one is in a field you didn't mention.

---

## Ranked by traveller harm

### 1. `City Lodge Berlin` has Munich's coordinates — [Certain]
`{"lat": 48.1351, "lng": 11.5820}` is the canonical centroid of **Munich**. Berlin is `52.5200, 13.4050`. That's 585 km. Nothing inside the record contradicts itself — `city: "Berlin"`, `country: "DE"`, coords parse, coords are in Germany, coords are on land. A validator checking "is this a valid lat/lng" passes it. An agent that says "your hotel is here" and hands off to maps sends someone to the wrong federal state.

Likely mechanism, worth saying out loud: record 3 (Innsbruck) is `47.2692, 11.4041` — *correct*. The two lng values are 15 km apart. This smells like a copy-paste or a default-fill along one axis, which means the defect class is "coords silently inherited from a neighbouring record", not "one typo". **Only a cross-field consistency check (city ↔ coords) catches this.** This is the planted defect.

### 2. `Sunset Bay Resort & Spa` is adults-only **and** has a kids club — [Certain]
`description: "An adults-only sanctuary of tranquility"` vs `features: [..., "kids club"]`. Both fields are well-formed. Whichever the agent believes, somebody books wrong: a family denied at check-in on a non-refundable rate, or a couple paying a premium for a resort full of children. Structured field contradicts free text — and free text is where the *binding policy* lives.

### 3. Records 1 and 2 are the same hotel, with conflicting star ratings — [Certain]
"Hotel Mare Azzurro" / "Mare Azzu**r**o Hotel", both Rimini. `stars: 4` vs `rating: "3 stars"`. No shared ID, no matching key — name differs by one character, one calls it `hotel_name`, the other `name`, one has `city`+`country`, the other a joined string. Two failure modes, both bad: **no dedup** → the traveller sees two hotels and thinks they have a choice, or **naive dedup** → last-write-wins silently picks a star rating. There is no principled winner here; the honest answer is "conflict, surfaced, not resolved".

### 4. Advertised amenity contradicted by the review in the same file — [Certain]
Record 1: `amenities: "pool,wifi,parking"`. Record 2 (same hotel): `"pool was closed for the whole of August"`. Someone books a beach hotel in August for the pool. The data *contains* the counter-evidence and any merge that just unions amenities destroys it.

### 5. `null` ≠ `false` ≠ missing — you flagged the nullability, not the semantics — [Certain]
`Alpenhof Garni` has `amenities: null`. Its German description says `"Frühstück inklusive"` (breakfast included) and `"Kein Restaurant"` (**no** restaurant). So:
- Unknown amenities get rendered as "no amenities" → the hotel is wrongly filtered out of "must have breakfast".
- The one *negative* fact in the dataset lives only in prose, in German. An agent that summarises amenities will happily let someone plan dinner at a hotel with no kitchen.
- `Garni` in the name is itself a classification term meaning "no restaurant" — the data says it three times and the schema captures it zero times.

Three distinct states (`null`, key absent, `""` on City Lodge's description) all collapse to "empty" in most parsers. **Unknown must survive as unknown, not be flattened to false.**

### 6. Prices are not comparable — [Certain]
`price_from_eur: 89` (number, EUR, in the field name) vs `price_from: "180 USD"` (string, USD, in the value). Sort by price and 89 beats 180 in a unit mix that means nothing. Worse: no date, no occupancy, no board basis, no tax/fee treatment. A "from" price with no stay date is a number no traveller can ever transact at.

### 7. Everything is stale, and only one record admits it — [Certain]
`last_seen: "2023-11-02"` — 2 years 10 months old today. The other four records carry **no timestamp at all**, so the agent cannot even distinguish "fresh" from "unknown age". "Newly renovated in 2019" is being presented as a selling point in 2026. Hotels close, rebrand and double their prices on that timescale.

### 8. `stars` and `rating` are different quantities — [Likely]
You spotted these as a naming inconsistency. It's worse: `stars` is an **official government classification** (1–5, regulated in IT/AT/DE). `rating` on a scraped record could be that, or a guest score (out of 5, or out of 10 on Booking). Here it's the string `"3 stars"` which *looks* like a classification — but it came from a scrape, so it might be a rounded guest score. Merging them into one number is a category error that is invisible once merged.

### 9. Language and locale leakage — you had this, plus the bit that bites
Descriptions in EN and DE. But the sharper one: `location: "Rimini, Italien"` — the **country is in German**. So it matches neither `"IT"` nor `"Italy"`. A country filter drops this record, and the deduped Rimini hotel silently vanishes from an "Italy" search.

### 10. Free text is unvalidated and un-sanitised — [Certain, harm Likely]
`"<b>WELCOME TO PARADISE!!!</b>"` — raw HTML in a description, from a partner feed. Two problems: it renders as markup or leaks tags, and more importantly, **scraped free-text fields are a prompt-injection surface**. This file's descriptions go into an LLM context verbatim; a scraped field is attacker-controllable by the scraped site.

### 11. Marketing superlatives repeated as fact — [Certain]
`"Best hotel in Rimini!"`, `"luxury at unbeatable prices"`, `"paradise"`. If the agent restates these in its own voice, it is making an unverifiable comparative advertising claim on the hotel's behalf. Distinct from #10: this one parses fine and reads fine. It's a *trust* defect.

### 12. `review_snippets` is two cherry-picked strings — [Certain]
No count, no dates, no distribution, no rating. One negative, one positive. Any summary of "what reviewers say" from n=2 is sampling bias presented as evidence.

### 13. Structural, low harm (your list, mostly)
`name`/`hotel_name`; `amenities` CSV-string vs `features` array; `city`+`country` vs joined `location` vs nothing; `country` as ISO-2 vs free text (`"Mexico"`); **no stable ID on any record** (can't dedup, can't update, can't cite a source row); uncontrolled amenity vocabulary (`"pool"` / `"swimming pool"` / `"3 pools"` — a `pool` filter misses two of three; `"free WiFi"` smuggles a *price* claim into an amenity; `"pets allowed"` is a policy, not a facility); `"3 pools"` has a quantity trapped in a string; record 4 has no country and no rating at all; `source` exists but there's no **trust tier** — a scrape and a contracted partner feed are weighted identically.

---

## Scorecard vs your list

| You found | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Different field names | ✅ real, low harm — #13 |
| Description in different languages | ✅ — and the *country* is too (#9); the German record is where the only negative fact hides (#5) |
| Location missing in some records | ✅ — but the dangerous case isn't missing, it's **present and wrong** (#1) |
| `rating` vs `stars` | ✅ — and they're different *quantities*, not just different names (#8) |
| amenities CSV vs features array | ✅ — plus uncontrolled vocabulary makes filters silently under-return (#13) |
| Nullable vs non-nullable | ✅ — the real bug is `null` being read as `false` (#5) |

**Missed entirely:** wrong coordinates, the internal contradiction (adults-only/kids club), the cross-record duplicate with conflicting stars, the review that contradicts the amenity, currency/price incomparability, staleness, marketing claims, injection surface, no stable ID.

---

## The line I'd take into Phase 2

A normaliser that unifies field names and types makes this data **look** clean while leaving all six harmful defects intact — arguably worse, because the output now has the authority of a schema. The valuable feature is not the normaliser. It's whichever thing **detects conflict and refuses to collapse it**.

My pick if you want one: **#1 + #2 as one feature** — a validator that cross-checks fields against each other (city↔coords, structured↔prose, amenity↔review) and emits typed conflicts rather than a merged record. It's the only feature here where the hard part is genuinely hard, so it earns a real failure-mode test suite.

Second choice: **#3, the dedup + conflict-surfacing merge** — more code, more obviously "a feature", and forces you to defend a matching strategy.

Tell me which and I'll go. Clock says you have ~8 min of Phase 1 budget left if you want to push back on the ranking first.

#55 ASSISTANT · claude-opus-5 · 2026-09-22T11:52:20.672Z · session 362d46b6 · uuid 591ff0c6
**Three disagreements before the file. All three change what gets built, so read them.**

**1. Your case 1 will silently pass unless we add derived claims.** Only *one* source asserts anything about City Lodge Berlin's location — `partner-feed-a` says `city: "Berlin"` and `coords: Munich`. A claim check that compares sources against each other sees one source, no disagreement, and stamps it `supported`. The planted defect survives the tool built to catch it. Fix: coords produce a **derived claim** (`derived:coords` → nearest known city) which then conflicts with the stated city. Same shape for case 2 — adults-only and kids club are both from record 4, one source. So claims must be keyed by **(source, field-path)**, not by source. Two claims from the same record must be able to conflict.

**2. `stale` is not a fourth status, it's a second axis.** Your case 4 asks for pool-vs-review *and* the 2023 staleness on the same property. If status is one enum, marking it `stale` erases the `conflict` — you'd lose the pool finding to report the age. I'd emit `status` (supported | conflict | absent) and `staleness` (fresh | stale | unknown) side by side. Note `unknown`: four of five records have no timestamp at all, and "we don't know how old this is" is not the same as fresh.

**3. `absent` is doing two jobs and that's defect #5 reappearing.** `Alpenhof Garni` has `amenities: null` but its German description says `"Frühstück inklusive"` and `"Kein Restaurant"`. If "nobody mentioned a restaurant" and "a source affirmatively says there is no restaurant" both print as `absent`, the tool that exists to stop null-means-false has done exactly that. A negative assertion is a claim with value `false` → prints `supported (false)`. `absent` means no source spoke.

**What you missed:** two of the six.
- **#5, unknown-vs-false** — Alpenhof, above. Costs almost nothing given you already specified `absent`, and it's the case that proves the status vocabulary is honest. **I'd add it as case 5.**
- **#6, currency** — `89` EUR vs `"180 USD"`. A claim check structurally *cannot* catch this: the two prices are on different properties, so there's no conflict to detect. It's a cross-property comparability defect. **I'd drop it and name it in Known gaps** rather than bend the model around it.

And one correction to your framing: this doesn't **fix** the six defects, it **surfaces** them. Your own "don't pick a winner" instruction is what makes it valuable — a normaliser that repaired these would just be confidently wrong in a cleaner schema. I'm building detection, not repair.

Writing DECISIONS.md with those three deltas in. Say the word if you want any reverted.

Two things about that\nshape carry most of the weight:\n\n- **The source key is `(feed, field-path)`, not just `feed`.** The worst errors in\n  this data are a single record disagreeing with *itself*: one partner record says\n  `city: \"Berlin\"` and `coords: 48.1351, 11.5820`, which is Munich; one scrape says\n  `description: \"adults-only\"` and `features: [... \"kids club\"]`. If claims were\n  attributed per-feed, both would read as a single uncontested source and pass.\n- **Coordinates emit a derived claim.** `coords` are resolved to a nearest known\n  city and asserted as a `city` claim from `derived:coords`, so a location that is\n  internally inconsistent becomes an ordinary conflict between two claims rather\n  than a thing no comparison can see.\n\nStatus is two independent axes, because one property is routinely both things at\nonce:\n\n| `status` | meaning |\n|---|---|\n| `supported` | one or more sources assert it, and they agree (the value may be `false` — an affirmative *no*) |\n| `conflict` | two or more sources assert incompatible values |\n| `absent` | no source asserts anything about this field |\n\n| `staleness` | meaning |\n|---|---|\n| `fresh` | newest supporting observation is within the freshness window |\n| `stale` | newest supporting observation is older than the window |\n| `unknown` | no source carries a timestamp at all |\n\n`absent` and `supported (false)` are kept apart deliberately. `Alpenhof Garni` has\n`amenities: null` and a German description reading `\"Kein Restaurant\"` — \"nobody\nsaid\" and \"a source said no\" are different facts, and collapsing them is how a\nnormaliser tells a traveller a hotel has no breakfast when the feed simply never\nmentioned breakfast.\n\n**On conflict the tool prints both values and both sources and stops.** It does not\nrank feeds, take the newest, or take the majority. # The Go loop

Style is not this skill's job. `evolve-skills:code-standards` owns Go style and
autoloads on `.go` files. This skill owns the **order of work** and the
**verification gate**, because that is what distinguishes a Go change that holds
in production from one that compiles.

Two hard rules that override convenience:

1. **Maker is not checker.** The thing that proves the change works is a test or
   a tool, never your own reading of the diff.
2. **Never claim a gate passed without pasting its output.** "Tests pass" with no
   output is worth nothing. `ok pkg 0.412s` is worth something.

---

## Phase -1 — Is there a clock?

If the task named a time limit, a practice or mock interview, a technical test,
a take-home or a case study, **stop and load `hour-build` first**. It owns the
clock, the phase budget, the `DECISIONS.md` deliverable and the commit cadence,
and it owns how MUCH you attempt.

**There is no sprint mode.** It existed, it was used twice, and both times it
was read as permission to skip verification — once dropping RED, once dropping
Phase 5b mutation, which is the highest-yield step in the loop. Its only sound
rule ("cover fewer things, cover them properly") already lives in `hour-build`
as *"test one thing properly, smoke-test the rest"*. Two skills stating the same
rule, one of them as a permission to skip, is how the rule got lost.

So: `hour-build` owns BREADTH — it decides how much to attempt. This skill owns
DEPTH and does not negotiate it. Whatever you do attempt gets the taxonomy, RED
before green, mutation on every guard, and the gate. If the clock is tight, the
answer is to attempt less, never to verify less.

Observed failure (ygo-monorepo, 2026-09): sprint mode was read as licence to
drop RED. Three services shipped in one commit with no test files; the first
test arrived a commit later and passed on its first run. Two guards were later
found unverified by mutation, and one bug (`ParseFloat` accepting `NaN`)
survived to review. The rule was in this file the whole time.



Observed failure: "this is an hour practice interview session" routed here on
the word Go alone, `hour-build` never fired, and the build finished with no git
history at all — the artefact that was supposed to prove the work happened
inside the window.

## Phase 0 — State the target before touching a file

Three lines, no more. Skip only for a one-line fix.

```
Goal:      what the caller can do afterwards that it cannot do now
Done when: the named test(s) green, vet clean, race clean
Not doing: the adjacent thing you are deliberately leaving alone
```

If you cannot write the "Done when" without guessing, the task is underspecified.
Say so and ask. Do not start a loop with no way to terminate it.

## Phase 1 — Failure taxonomy, before any test

Write the list of ways this code can be wrong, **before** the happy path exists
in your head. This is the step that separates a Go engineer from someone who
writes Go, and in a transcript it is the most visible signal of how you think.

For each input and each dependency, ask what happens when it is: absent, zero,
nil, empty, negative, enormous, malformed, duplicated, out of order, slow,
cancelled, or arriving twice.

Read [references/failure-taxonomy.md](references/failure-taxonomy.md) for the
Go-specific catalogue — nil map writes, slice aliasing, typed nil, at-least-once
delivery, goroutine leaks, context propagation, partial writes. Pull the five to
ten entries that apply and write them down as a list. Discard the rest.

If the code calls a model, turns a sentence into a query, ranks, bundles from
model output, or exposes a tool or action, also read
[references/llm-boundary.md](references/llm-boundary.md) and pull the rows that
apply. The Go catalogue will not name them. A schema-valid result can still be
the wrong trip.

Output of this phase is a plain list, not prose:

```
F1  empty input slice          -> return empty, no error, no panic
F2  ctx cancelled mid-flight   -> stop within one poll, return ctx.Err()
F3  duplicate delivery         -> second call is a no-op, same result
F4  upstream 429               -> honour Retry-After, do not hammer
F5  nil receiver on the store  -> programmer error, panic is correct
```

## Phase 2 — RED. The failure cases become failing tests first

Write the table test with the failure rows first and the happy path **last**.
A table whose rows are four failures and one success is the shape to aim for.

```go
func TestParsePrice(t *testing.T) {
	tests := []struct {
		name    string
		in      string
		want    Cents
		wantErr error
	}{
		{"empty", "", 0, ErrEmptyPrice},
		{"not a number", "abc", 0, ErrMalformedPrice},
		{"negative", "-1.00", 0, ErrNegativePrice},
		{"overflow", "99999999999999999999", 0, ErrPriceRange},
		{"comma decimal", "199,00", 19900, nil},
		{"plain", "199.00", 19900, nil},
	}
	for _, tt := range tests {
		t.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {
			t.Parallel()
			got, err := ParsePrice(tt.in)
			if !errors.Is(err, tt.wantErr) {
				t.Fatalf("err = %v, want %v", err, tt.wantErr)
			}
			if got != tt.want {
				t.Errorf("got %d, want %d", got, tt.want)
			}
		})
	}
}
```

Run it and **show the failure**. A test suite that was never seen red is not
known to test anything.

**The checkable form of this rule: the first `go test` of the session must
FAIL, and it must fail for the architectural reason you named — not on a
syntax error, an unresolved import, or an undefined symbol.** A red that says
`undefined: Calculate` proves only that you have not written the function yet.
Read the failure output and confirm it names the behaviour: a wrong value, a
missing error, a deadline that was not honoured. If the compiler is what is
failing, stub the signature to return a zero value and run again — *that* red
is the one that counts. If your first test run is green, you wrote the implementation first —
which is the rule people break while believing they followed it, because the
tests do eventually get written and do eventually go red. Do not retrofit the
order. Say it plainly in Phase 6: "tests were written after the implementation",
and treat every guard in the diff as unverified until Phase 5b mutates it. The `go-checks.sh` hook reports this automatically on
every `.go` edit, so the red state lands in the transcript without you narrating it.

Assertion rules:
- `errors.Is` / `errors.As` for error identity, never string comparison.
- `cmp.Diff(want, got)` for structs, with the diff in the failure message.
- One behaviour per subtest, named for the behaviour, not `case1`.
- `t.Parallel()` only when the subtest touches no process-global state. `t.Setenv`
  and `t.Chdir` are incompatible with it.

If a model produced the output, there is no single wanted value, and a table of
`cmp.Diff` against one completion does not test the behaviour. The first red
test is a property, or a contract against a fake provider: the ranking is a
permutation of the candidates, a budget is never exceeded, every returned id is
in the filtered set, an out-of-scope tool call is refused. Golden files are for
the deterministic shell only — the prompt you assembled, the schema parse, the
id-existence check — not for the model's text. A property that holds for the
zero value (an empty ranking has no out-of-stock id) is not red. The fake must
return a candidate the guard has to reject, and the first run must accept it.
The rows are in [references/llm-boundary.md](references/llm-boundary.md).

## Phase 3 — GREEN. Minimal implementation, nothing speculative

Write the least code that turns the tests green. No extra configuration knob, no
interface with one implementation, no abstraction for a second caller that does
not exist. If you notice something worth doing that is out of scope, note it and
keep going.

## Phase 4 — Instrument what can go wrong

Every branch identified in Phase 1 gets one of three treatments, and you should be
able to say which and why:

| Treatment | When | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| Return a wrapped error | The caller can decide | `fmt.Errorf("enrich %s: %w", id, err)` |
| Log and continue | Degradation the caller must not see as failure | `slog.WarnContext(ctx, "cache unavailable, falling through", "err", err)` |
| Count it | Silent degradation that must not stay silent | a counter plus an alert on the rate |

The third is the one people forget, and it is the one that matters in an AI or
network-facing service: a fallback nobody counts is indistinguishable from being
broken.

Read [references/observability.md](references/observability.md) for the `log/slog`
error-path idioms: where to log versus where to wrap, what never goes in a log
line, `LogValuer` for redaction, and how a span and a log line divide the work.

## Phase 5 — The gate

Run these in order. Paste the real output. Stop at the first failure and fix it.

```bash
gofmt -l .                                   # must print nothing
go vet ./...
go test ./... -count=1 -shuffle=on
go test ./... -race -count=1                 # the one people skip
golangci-lint run ./...                      # if the repo configures it
govulncheck ./...                            # on dependency changes
```

`-race` is not optional. A data race is invisible until it corrupts data in
production, and the detector is the only thing that finds it. `-shuffle=on`
catches tests that pass only in declaration order.

### Phase 5b — Mutate the guard. A green suite is not evidence yet.

Every tool above answers "does the code pass the tests". None answers "would
the tests notice if the code were wrong". So for each guard you wrote in
Phase 4 — a `case <-ctx.Done()` in a select, a channel's buffer size, a mutex,
a bounds check, a deadline — **delete it, run the suite, and name the test that
goes red.**

```bash
cp pkg/thing.go "$TMPDIR/thing.bak"   # session scratch, not /tmp
# delete exactly one guard
go test ./... -count=1 -run TheTestThatMustFail
cp "$TMPDIR/thing.bak" pkg/thing.go   # always restore before moving on
```

**A mutation run that produced no output did not run.** It is never a pass.
The two states look identical through a `grep`, and the wrong reading is the
one that reassures you. Before recording any mutant as uncaught, confirm the
suite actually executed — a `--- FAIL` or an `ok` line, not an empty filter.
*Observed (ygo-core, 2026-09): a mutation deleting `ctx.Done()` from a fetch
loop was wrapped in `timeout 60 go test`. `timeout` is GNU coreutils and is not
on macOS, so the shell printed `command not found`, the grep matched nothing,
and the mutant was one keystroke from being recorded as "no test catches this".
Re-run with `go test -timeout`, it failed loudly in two places.* If a mutant
genuinely needs a wall-clock bound, use `go test -timeout`, which is in the
toolchain you already have.

If nothing fails, you have a test that cannot fail. That is worse than no test,
because its green tick will be cited as evidence — by you, in the next message.

An invariant is a guard too. "Never recommend out-of-stock inventory", "never
exceed the budget", "never return an id that is not in the set" — delete the
check, run the suite, and name the test that goes red. That test is the
property test, not one hand-picked example. A single example stays green when
the check is gone and the example happened to be safe. See
[references/llm-boundary.md](references/llm-boundary.md).

This is not optional on concurrency work, and it is cheap: one edit, one run.
Observed cost of skipping it: a goroutine-leak test that polled for two seconds
passed with the cancellation case deleted, because an uncancelled worker still
exits when its own timer fires. `vet`, `golangci-lint`, `govulncheck`,
`-shuffle=on` and `-race -count=10` all passed against that hole. Only the
mutation found it. Rebuild the test so the mutant is still misbehaving at the
moment you measure — a latency far longer than the test, and a short window.

Say in Phase 6 which guards you mutated and which you did not.

Read [references/verify.md](references/verify.md) for the full gate, the
`golangci-lint` v2 linter set worth enabling, `testing/synctest` for deterministic
concurrency tests, native fuzzing, `rapid` for property tests, and testcontainers
for integration tests.

## Phase 6 — Say what you did not do

Close with the honest remainder: what is untested, what you assumed, what you
deliberately left out, and what would change your mind. One or two lines.

---

## Transcript discipline

This skill is often running where someone other than you will read the log later.
That changes nothing about the work and two things about the output:

- **Show tool output, do not summarise it.** The value of a log is that the reader
  can check you. A pasted `--- FAIL` block is worth a paragraph of prose.
- **Tag confidence on judgment, not on mechanics.** The global rule stands and is
  worth showing a reader: a claim that rests on inference or a gap gets
  `[Certain]` / `[Likely]` / `[Guessing]`. What it does not need is a tag on
  something the terminal just proved. "`[Certain]` the tests pass" above a pasted
  `ok example.com/x 0.3s` is noise, and a log full of it reads as theatre rather
  than calibration.

  The split that works: **tag a recommendation, a reading of someone else's
  system, an estimate, or an unverified assumption. Do not tag a tool result, a
  file you just read, or a step you are about to take.** Roughly one tag per
  decision, none per action.

Terse and decided beats thorough-sounding. If a phase produced nothing worth
saying, say nothing about it.

**Phase 0**

```
Goal:      `go run ./cmd/claimcheck testdata/hotels.json` groups the two Rimini
           records into one property and prints every claim with its sources,
           a status (supported | conflict | absent) and a staleness axis.
Done when: case 1 green — City Lodge Berlin's `city` reports conflict between
           partner-feed-a/city ("Berlin") and derived:coords ("Munich");
           gofmt/vet/test -race clean.
Not doing: cases 2-5 in this module; any conflict resolution; currency.
```

**Phase 1 — failure taxonomy** (the ones I'm pulling from the catalogue for this module)

```
F1  name absent on a record          -> record kept, grouped under its own key, never dropped silently
F2  amenities null vs key-absent vs "" -> zero claims, never a false claim
F3  coords present, city absent      -> derived claim stands alone -> supported, NOT conflict
F4  coords match no known city       -> emit NO derived claim; must not assert a wrong city
F5  no timestamp on any source       -> staleness unknown, NOT fresh
F6  same value from two sources      -> supported; dedupe on value, not on source count
F7  grouping too loose               -> two different hotels merged into one property
F8  grouping too tight               -> Azzurro/Azzuro stay separate, case 3 becomes undetectable
F9  nil map write building the index -> panic
```

F3/F4/F6/F7 are the ones that make case 1 either work or silently pass, so they're rows in the first table.

  "content": "// Package claimcheck groups hotel records from mixed feeds into properties and\n// reports what each feed claims about them, without resolving disagreements.\npackage claimcheck\n\nimport (\n\t\"encoding/json\"\n\t\"io\"\n\t\"time\"\n)\n\n// Status is what the set of claims for one field looks like taken together.\ntype Status string\n\nconst (\n\t// Supported means at least one source asserts a value and all agree. The\n\t// value may be \"false\": an affirmative denial is support, not absence.\n\tSupported Status = \"supported\"\n\t// Conflict means two or more sources assert incompatible values.\n\tConflict Status = \"conflict\"\n\t// Absent means no source asserts anything about the field.\n\tAbsent Status = \"absent\"\n)\n\n// Staleness is independent of Status: a field is routinely both in conflict and\n// out of date, and collapsing the two into one enum loses whichever is reported\n// second.\ntype Staleness string\n\nconst (\n\tFresh   Staleness = \"fresh\"\n\tStale   Staleness = \"stale\"\n\tUnknown Staleness = \"unknown\"\n)\n\n// FreshWindow is how old an observation may be before it is reported stale.\nconst FreshWindow = 365 * 24 * time.Hour\n\n// Claim is one source asserting one value for one field.\n//\n// Source is a feed name joined to the field path it came from, not the feed\n// alone, because the sharpest errors in this data are a single record\n// disagreeing with itself.\ntype Claim struct {\n\tField      string\n\tValue      string\n\tSource     string\n\tObservedAt time.Time // zero value means the feed carried no timestamp\n}\n\n// Finding is every claim about one field of one property, plus what they add up\n// to.\ntype Finding struct {\n\tField     string\n\tStatus    Status\n\tStaleness Staleness\n\tClaims    []Claim\n}\n\n// Property is a real-world hotel, which may be described by several records.\ntype Property struct {\n\tKey      string\n\tName     string\n\tSources  []string\n\tFindings []Finding\n}\n\n// Coords is a decimal lat/lng pair as it appears in the partner feeds.\ntype Coords struct {\n\tLat float64 `json:\"lat\"`\n\tLng float64 `json:\"lng\"`\n}\n\n// Record is the union of every field shape seen across the feeds. Pointer and\n// slice fields distinguish \"the feed said null or nothing\" from \"the feed said\n// an empty value\", which is a distinction the report depends on.\ntype Record struct {\n\tSource         string   `json:\"source\"`\n\tHotelName      string   `json:\"hotel_name\"`\n\tName           string   `json:\"name\"`\n\tCity           string   `json:\"city\"`\n\tCountry        string   `json:\"country\"`\n\tLocation       string   `json:\"location\"`\n\tStars          *int     `json:\"stars\"`\n\tRating         string   `json:\"rating\"`\n\tDescription    string   `json:\"description\"`\n\tAmenities      *string  `json:\"amenities\"`\n\tFeatures       []string `json:\"features\"`\n\tReviewSnippets []string `json:\"review_snippets\"`\n\tCoords         *Coords  `json:\"coords\"`\n\tPriceFromEUR   *int     `json:\"price_from_eur\"`\n\tPriceFrom      string   `json:\"price_from\"`\n\tLastSeen       string   `json:\"last_seen\"`\n}\n\n// LoadRecords decodes a feed dump.\nfunc LoadRecords(r io.Reader) ([]Record, error) {\n\tvar recs []Record\n\tif err := json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(&recs); err != nil {\n\t\treturn nil, err\n\t}\n\treturn recs, nil\n}\n\n// Group collects records that describe the same property.\nfunc Group(recs []Record) []Property {\n\treturn nil\n}\n\n// Check groups records and reports the claim status of every known field.\nfunc Check(recs []Record, now time.Time) []Property {\n\treturn nil\n}\n\n// FindingFor returns the finding for a field, and whether one was reported.\nfunc (p Property) FindingFor(field string) (Finding, bool) {\n\tfor _, f := range p.Findings {\n\t\tif f.Field == field {\n\t\t\treturn f, true\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn Finding{}, false\n}\n"
}

The diff contains only what the change needed.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 1. Types are the cheapest documentation we have\\n\\n**Type it as strongly as the language allows.** Not for the compiler — for the reader, human or agent, landing cold: the signature should say what a function takes and returns without reading the body or chasing call sites.\\n\\n- **Push types outward to the boundary.** Parse and validate untrusted input (HTTP body, device payload, env var, file) *once*, at the edge, into a typed value. Inside the boundary, trust the types. \\\"Parse, don't validate.\\\"\\n- **Name the domain, don't reuse the primitive.** Three `string` parameters in a row will be called in the wrong order. A `DeviceId`/`SessionId` newtype or branded type costs a line and removes the class of error — especially for what we pass everywhere: device serials, session ids, timestamps, units.\\n- **Make illegal states unrepresentable.** A discriminated union or sealed class beats a struct with four nullable fields and an implied rule.\\n- **A type that lies is worse than no type.** A cast that makes the build pass converts a compile-time failure into a runtime one.\\n\\n## 2. Functional by default\\n\\n**In every language that supports it:** declarative over imperative, values over mutation, composition over inheritance, and the language's own algorithm library over a loop you wrote. The imperative version is always available; it carries the burden of justification.\\n\\n- **Say what, not how.** `filter → map → fold` over an index loop with an accumulator.\\n- **Reuse the built-in algorithm** — it is already correct and already optimised; a hand-rolled one is a fresh bug surface. Each language file names the library.\\n- **Pure by default.** Inputs to outputs; no hidden reads, no mutated arguments, no I/O. Effects go to the edges (§7).\\n- **Name a non-trivial lambda.** A fifteen-line anonymous closure is worse than the loop it replaced.\\n- **Use the language's own monadic vocabulary** for the failure path (`Option`/`Result`, `?.`/`??`, `optional`/`expected`, narrowed `T | None`) instead of nested null checks and try/catch pyramids — and **do not smuggle in what the language does not have.** A hand-built monad library is a private dialect nobody else can review.\\n\\n**Where the paradigm stops:**\\n\\n- **Known allocation-sensitive contexts — Unity `Update`/`FixedUpdate`/`LateUpdate`, per-sample DSP callbacks, ISRs, the kernel data path, a render loop.** There, preallocated imperative code is the default and needs no measurement. Everywhere else, an imperative rewrite for performance needs a profile, stated in the commit.\\n- **A language that does not idiomatically support it** — C, Bash, kernel code, Go. The residue still pays: pure helpers, no hidden global state, the standard library over hand-rolling.\\n\\n## 3. Names\\n\\nEvery fact in a name never goes stale, never costs a separate read, and cannot contradict the code.\\n\\n- Name after **what it means in the domain**, not what it is technically. `sessionsAwaitingUpload`, not `list2` or `sessionArray`.\\n- **Omit needless words.** Strip what the type already says (`sensorList`, `configObject`), the empty role-nouns (`Manager`, `Helper`, `Utils`, `Handler`, `Info`, `Impl`), and verbs that do no work (`doCalculate`). Error types keep the ecosystem's suffix (`Error`, `Exception`); spend the words before it on what went wrong — `SessionAlreadyClosedError`, not `SessionError`.\\n- **Don't stack words like bricks.** A name needing five words is usually a thing doing five things.\\n- **Strongly avoid single-letter names.** Three carve-outs: a loop index or coordinate in a small scope; a mathematical or signal-processing symbol where the surrounding code is written in that vocabulary (`n`, `fs`, `x[n]`); Go method receivers.\\n- **No code names or metaphors in identifiers.** A module called `Poseidon` costs every reader a lookup forever.\\n- **Booleans read as assertions** — `isConnected`, `hasConsent`. Never negated (`notReady`).\\n- **Same concept, same word, everywhere.** Pick `device` or `headset` and hold the line; the domain's settled terms live in [`domain-modeling`](../../../vendor/mattpocock/skills/skills/engineering/domain-modeling/SKILL.md).\\n- **Don't stutter.** `Condition.isTrue()`, not `Condition.checkCondition()`; `session.New()`, not `session.NewSession()`.\\n- **Accessors are nouns where the language leaves it open** — `count()` not `getCount()` in Rust, Go (Effective Go mandates it) and C++ (Google's guide: accessors are named like variables). Keep the binding convention where one exists: JavaBean accessors, C# properties, Kotlin `val`.\\n- **Units in the name or the type** — `timeout_s`, `window_ms`, `sample_rate_hz`, `amplitude_uv`. A bare `duration` in signal code is a defect.\\n\\n### Arguments: fewer first, then named\\n\\n- **Reduce the count before improving the names.** Three parameters that always travel together are a type.\\n- **A boolean parameter is usually two functions.** `render(data, true)` means the function does two things and the caller picks. Modules and boundaries\\n\\nThe highest-leverage quality property, and the one AI-generated code most often gets wrong — it produces *many shallow* modules where a few deep ones belong.\\n\\n- **Deep over shallow.** A module worth having hides substantially more complexity than its interface exposes. A wrapper as wide as its implementation bought nothing. Vocabulary: the vendored [`codebase-design`](../../../vendor/mattpocock/skills/skills/engineering/codebase-design/SKILL.md) skill.\\n- **Put the seam where the change will come** — a second transport, a second storage backend. New code does not add to an existing bucket.\\n\\n### Small outside, free to be larger inside\\n\\n**Prefer small** — files, types, functions, interfaces — because a reader holds a handful of ideas at once, and at every level a component should be understandable in terms of a small number of well-named parts. **Prefer deep** because a module's value is hidden complexity over exposed interface. These agree about interfaces and contest only implementations, so: **a deep module is small on the outside and free to be larger on the inside.** Split a function that is a sequence of named steps; do not split a coherent implementation into ten files to make each short. Ten one-line wrappers are worse than one clear twenty-line function — that is shallow-module proliferation wearing smallness as a disguise, and it is the failure AI-generated code falls into.\\n\\n**Start simple.** Complexity arrives in answer to a real requirement or a measured problem, never in anticipation of one.\\n\\n## 5. Errors and failure\\n\\n- **Fail fast at the boundary, degrade gracefully at the top.** Reject bad input where it arrives, naming what was wrong. Decide how to survive it once, at a level that can decide.\\n- **Errors carry context** — which device, session, file, upstream call. Never `throw new Error('failed')`.\\n- **Distinguish expected from exceptional.** \\\"Device not connected\\\" is a normal state and belongs in the return type. \\\"Disk is corrupt\\\" is exceptional.\\n- **Retries need a bound and a backoff**, and only wrap idempotent operations.\\n- **Bound every queue, buffer and batch**, and decide what happens when it fills — block, drop oldest, drop newest, fail. For a sensor stream, drop with a counter and a metric; never drop silently.\\n\\n## 6. Output: the data plane and the control plane\\n\\n- **stdout is the data plane** — the output a caller consumes or parses, with a stable documented shape, and *nothing else on it*. One stray progress line silently corrupts whatever is downstream.\\n- **stderr is the control plane** — logs, progress, warnings, everything *about* the run. Also where all output goes when the program has no data plane, which is the common case: services, daemons, device tools that only perform an action.\\n- **Print is not a logger.** `print`, `console.log`, `println!`, `fmt.Println`, `echo` all default to stdout. Diagnostics go through the language's logging facility, which goes to stderr and can be turned off.\\n- **Configure the log format once, centrally** — timestamp, level, source, message, plus ambient context (request/device/session id) bound to the logger or scope, never pasted into every message. A per-module logger gives the source for free.\\n- **Levels mean what the reader must do.** `error`: someone must act. `warn`: someone should look. `info`: normal operation worth narrating. `debug`: only when diagnosing. A line nobody will act on hides the one that matters.\\n- **Structured (key/value or JSON) where anything will aggregate the logs**; human-readable for a local CLI or device script.\\n\\nAndroid, Unity, the kernel and the browser have no usable stdout; the principle holds — data out through the API, diagnostics through the platform's log channel — and the language files name the channel.\\n\\n## 7. State, mutation and time\\n\\n- **Immutable by default.** `const`/`val`/`final`/frozen. Relax only where mutation is the point (a hot loop, a buffer).\\n- **Never hand back a mutable internal.** Returning the live `List` or array is a private field with extra syntax. Return a read-only view, a copy, or a method that does what the caller wanted.\\n- **No hidden global state.** Module-level mutable singletons make tests order-dependent. Pass dependencies in.\\n- **Pure core, effectful shell.** Inject the clock, the filesystem, randomness and the network. `now: datetime` as a parameter is the difference between a test and a flake.\\n\\n**Time bites us harder than most** — timestamped biometric samples cross headset → gateway → time-series store:\\n\\n- **Monotonic clock for durations, wall clock for timestamps.** `time.monotonic()`, `Instant`, `steady_clock`, `SystemClock.elapsedRealtime()`, `performance.now()`.\\n- **Store and transmit UTC** with an explicit offset or `Z`; convert to local only for display.\\n- **Device time is not cloud time.** Record which clock a timestamp came from; never join two clocks without reconciling. Silent mixing surfaces as an unexplained gap in a session months later.\\n\\n## 8. Testability and tests\\n\\n- **Hard to test is information about the design.** Reach for a better seam before a heavier mock.\\n- **Test behaviour, not implementation.** A test that breaks on every refactor is a tax; one that passes while behaviour breaks is a lie.\\n- **Failure modes first** — empty, malformed, timeout, disconnection, concurrent second call. The happy path is the one manual use finds anyway.\\n- **Deterministic or delete it.** No sleeps as synchronisation, no real network or hardware, no test-order or wall-clock dependence.\\n- **Name the test after the claim** — `rejects_a_session_with_no_consent`, not `test3`.\\n- **Prefer a real implementation or an in-memory fake over a mock with five expectations.**\\n- **Signal processing gets a synthetic input with a known answer** — a pure sine at a known frequency, a known artefact — never golden-output pinning.\\n\\n## 9. Concision and clarity\\n\\nConcise means *less to read*, not fewer characters.\\n\\n- **Delete rather than comment out.** Git remembers.\\n- **Guard clauses over nested conditionals.** Keep the main path at the left margin.\\n- **Keep cognitive complexity low, and let the linter measure it** (`C901`, `readability-function-cognitive-complexity`, detekt, ESLint `complexity`).\\n- **Extract a function when you would otherwise write a comment explaining the next ten lines** — the name is the comment and stays true. Apply the §4 test: extract a *sequence of named steps*; do not shatter a coherent implementation into one-line wrappers.\\n- **Kill the cleverness.** A dense one-liner that takes three reads is not concise.\\n- **Do not build what you were not asked for.** Speculative options, flags and extension points are the commonest form of AI over-delivery.\\n\\n## 10. Comments and documentation\\n\\nA comment is a cost to justify: nothing checks it, so a stale one misinforms; a correct one is still attention spent; and the further a description sits from the code, the faster it rots unnoticed. Express a fact as far up this list as you can:\\n\\n| Form | Checked by | How it fails |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| Types and signatures | the compiler, every build | cannot go stale |\\n| Tests | every CI run | goes red |\\n| Names | every reader | drifts, in plain sight |\\n| Inline and doc comments | nothing | quietly |\\n| Repo docs and diagrams | nothing | fastest, least visibly |\\n\\nSo the first three moves are **rename**, **extract**, or **introduce a type**. Comments that survive explain **why**, never what. They earn their place for: a **workaround** (what is broken, whose bug, **link the ticket**); a **regex** (intent plus a matching and a non-matching example); a **gap in the language** (`/* blocking= */ true` in C++); a **non-local invariant**; a **hardware or platform quirk** (\\\"one bind per boot — a second call crashes the HAL\\\"); a **measured performance decision**, with the number; a **deliberate omission** — an ignored error, a suppressed lint, an empty branch.\\n\\n**Public API doc comments are a different artefact** — the contract for someone who will never open the body (the Pegasus SDK `API` surface, `evt-demo-core`, shared `libs/`): what it does, assumes, throws, and its units and ranges. **High-level architecture docs earn their place** because the alternative is reading the whole codebase; keeping them current is real work an agent is good at. **A stale comment is a bug** — fix it in the same diff, and keep `README`/`CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` true, since that is the first thing the next agent reads.\\n\\n## 11. Efficiency, honestly\\n\\n- **Correct, clear, then fast — and fast only when measured**, outside the known hot paths named in §2.\\n- **Know the order of magnitude.** An accidental O(n²) over a session's samples, or a query in a loop, is a design defect regardless of profiling.\\n- **Costs live at the boundaries** — I/O, serialisation, allocation in a loop, round-trips. Batch, stream, do not load a whole recording to read its header.\\n- **State the measurement in the commit** when a change is made for performance, or the next reader will \\\"simplify\\\" it back.\\n\\n## 12. Dependencies, security and participant data\\n\\n- **Reuse what exists here first** — search the repo and the sibling repos before writing a helper.\\n- **A new dependency is a decision with a cost** — supply chain, licence, upgrade burden, bundle size. Small, maintained, pinned; anything load-bearing gets an ADR.\\n- **Validate at every trust boundary** — HTTP handlers, device payloads, file parsers, CLI arguments, IPC, and **query text**: a request value never enters a Flux/SQL string by interpolation.\\n- **Configuration is injected and validated at startup.** No hardcoded endpoints, ARNs, buckets, ports. Parse config once into a typed object and **fail at boot**, not on the first request that needs the missing value.\\n\\n**Participant data.** We hold biometric signals and metadata from human research participants.\\n\\n- **The identifier that travels is the pseudonymous session/device id.** Names, contact details and anything that re-identifies a participant live only in the consent/enrolment store, never in signal payloads, file names, logs, metrics labels, bug reports or test fixtures.\\n- **Signal data is sensitive by default** — EEG/ECG/PPG payloads are treated as identifying even when no name is attached. Encrypted at rest on device and in the cloud; never copied to a laptop or a shared drive outside the documented data path.\\n- **Retention outlives code.** Before a migration drops, renames or reinterprets a field that holds study data, check the study's retention and consent constraints — §13 — and get it confirmed, not assumed.\\n- **Real recordings are not test fixtures.** Tests use synthetic signals or an approved de-identified dataset.\\n\\n## 13. Contracts and compatibility\\n\\nA **contract** is any interface you cannot change unilaterally because the two sides deploy separately — a headset in the field runs firmware from months ago while the cloud ships weekly: a published API, a wire format, a persisted schema, a file layout, a CLI's stdout.\\n\\n**No change may require both sides to deploy together.** Every change is expand → migrate → contract: add the new thing tolerated-but-not-required; move writers then readers (or the reverse, whichever is safe); remove the old thing once nothing uses it.\\n\\n- **Protobuf** (`sensor.proto`, device ↔ cloud): never reuse or renumber a tag (mark removed ones `reserved`); additive only, readers ignore unknown fields; never change a field's type or meaning; never promote optional to required or tighten validation on a field in the wild. The `.proto` is the contract; generated code is not (§0.6).\\n- **Persisted schemas** (DynamoDB, Influx, S3 layouts, on-device files): migrations are re-runnable and forward-compatible; the old shape stays readable until every writer has moved.\\n- **Published API surfaces** (Pegasus SDK `API`, `evt-demo-core`, shared `libs/`): semver meant literally; deprecate before removing, with the language's marker **and the replacement named in the message**; never change a public signature or behaviour silently.\\n\\n## 14. Before you call it done\\n\\n- The formatter and linter for the language have run and pass; where none is configured, the PR says so.\\n- The tests you added fail without your change.\\n- The unhappy paths have somewhere to go.\\n- No `TODO` without a ticket key, no debug print, no commented-out block, no unused import or dead branch.\\n- The diff contains only what the change needed.\\n\\n---\\n\\n*Sources worth reading whole:* Kevlin Henney, *Seven Ineffective Coding Habits of Many Programmers* (§3, §10); John Ousterhout, *A Philosophy of Software Design* (§4, via `codebase-design`); Martin Fowler, *Refactoring* ch. 3 (the smell baseline `code-review` applies on top of this).\\n\\n===== /Users/yuratestdev/.claude/plugins/cache/evolve/evolve-skills/0.1.0/skills/code-standards/languages/go.md =====\\n# Go\\n\\n**There is no Go in these repos today.** This file exists so the first Go service does not invent its conventions under deadline; it stays short until then.\\n\\n**Canonical standard:** [Effective Go](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go), the [Go Code Review Comments](https://go.dev/wiki/CodeReviewComments) wiki, and the [Google Go Style Guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/go/). Go has the least room for a house style of any language we use — that is the point of the language.\\n\\n**Tooling:** `gofmt`/`goimports`, `go vet`, `golangci-lint` (which bundles `staticcheck`), `go test -race ./...` in CI. `gofmt` is non-configurable, which is why Go never has a formatting argument.\\n\\n**House rules beyond the canonical guides, when Go lands:**\\n\\n- **`log/slog` to stderr for diagnostics, `fmt.Print*` only for the data plane** (§6 of [universal.md](../reference/universal.md)); `slog.With(\\\"device\\\", id)` binds context once; never `log.Fatal` in a library.\\n- **`context.Context` first parameter on anything that does I/O, honoured; every goroutine has an owner and a way to stop.**\\n- **Errors wrapped with `%w` and context at the call site**; `panic` for programmer error only.\\n- **Accept interfaces, return structs; define the interface where it is consumed; keep it to one or two methods.**\\n- **Do not build a `Map`/`Filter`/`Option` library.** Go's idiom is the explicit loop and the explicit `if err != nil`; `slices`/`maps`/`cmp` cover the generic algorithms. This is where \\\"do not smuggle in what the language does not have\\\" bites hardest.\\n- **Layout:** `cmd/<binary>/main.go`, `internal/` by default, `main` tiny.\\n\\nWhen the first Go module exists, add its repo and layout here and expand only what the code shows is needed.\"}}\n",

fields present: %v\", fields(props[0]))\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\tif diff := cmp.Diff(tt.want, got); diff != \"\" {\n\t\t\t\tt.Errorf(\"finding mismatch (-want +got):\\n%s\", diff)\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t})\n\t}\n}\n\nfunc TestGroup(t *testing.T) {\n\tt.Parallel()\n\n\ttests := []struct {\n\t\tname string\n\t\trecs []Record\n\t\twant int\n\t}{\n\t\t{\n\t\t\t// Grouping too tight: the two Rimini records stay apart, and the\n\t\t\t// 4-vs-3 star conflict becomes undetectable because there is\n\t\t\t// nothing to compare against.\n\t\t\tname: \"same hotel spelled differently is one property\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{\n\t\t\t\t{Source: \"partner-feed-a\", HotelName: \"Hotel Mare Azzurro\", City: \"Rimini\"},\n\t\t\t\t{Source: \"scrape-booking-sites\", Name: \"Mare Azzuro Hotel\", Location: \"Rimini, Italien\"},\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t\twant: 1,\n\t\t},\n\t\t{\n\t\t\t// Grouping too loose: two real hotels merge and every field between\n\t\t\t// them is reported as a conflict that does not exist.\n\t\t\tname: \"different hotels in one city stay separate\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{\n\t\t\t\t{Source: \"partner-feed-a\", HotelName: \"Hotel Mare Azzurro\", City: \"Rimini\"},\n\t\t\t\t{Source: \"partner-feed-a\", HotelName: \"Grand Hotel Rimini\", City: \"Rimini\"},\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t\twant: 2,\n\t\t},\n\t\t{\n\t\t\t// A chain name in two cities is two properties. Name alone is not a\n\t\t\t// key.\n\t\t\tname: \"same name in different cities stays separate\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{\n\t\t\t\t{Source: \"partner-feed-a\", HotelName: \"City Lodge\", City: \"Berlin\"},\n\t\t\t\t{Source: \"partner-feed-a\", HotelName: \"City Lodge\", City: \"Hamburg\"},\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t\twant: 2,\n\t\t},\n\t\t{\n\t\t\t// An unnamed record is still a record. Dropping it loses whatever it\n\t\t\t// claims without saying so.\n\t\t\tname: \"record with no name is kept\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{\n\t\t\t\t{Source: \"scrape-booking-sites\", Location: \"Rimini, Italien\"},\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t\twant: 1,\n\t\t},\n\t\t{\n\t\t\tname: \"no records is no properties\",\n\t\t\trecs: nil,\n\t\t\twant: 0,\n\t\t},\n\t}\n\n\tfor _, tt := range tests {\n\t\tt.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {\n\t\t\tt.Parallel()\n\n\t\t\tgot := Group(tt.recs)\n\t\t\tif len(got) != tt.want {\n\t\t\t\tnames := make([]string, 0, len(got))\n\t\t\t\tfor _, p := range got {\n\t\t\t\t\tnames = append(names, p.Name)\n\t\t\t\t}\n\t\t\t\tt.Errorf(\"got %d properties %v, want %d\", len(got), names, tt.want)\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t})\n\t}\n}\n\nfunc fields(p Property) []string {\n\tout := make([]string, 0, len(p.Findings))\n\tfor _, f := range p.Findings {\n\t\tout = append(out, f.Field)\n\t}\n\treturn out\n}\n"
}

  "content": "package claimcheck\n\nimport \"math\"\n\n// knownCities is a fixed lookup, not a geocoder. It is enough to turn a\n// coordinate pair into a claim that can be compared against a stated city,\n// which is the whole job here; a feed naming a city outside this table gets no\n// derived claim rather than a wrong one.\nvar knownCities = []struct {\n\tName string\n\tLat  float64\n\tLng  float64\n}{\n\t{\"Berlin\", 52.5200, 13.4050},\n\t{\"Hamburg\", 53.5511, 9.9937},\n\t{\"Munich\", 48.1351, 11.5820},\n\t{\"Innsbruck\", 47.2692, 11.4041},\n\t{\"Rimini\", 44.0678, 12.5695},\n\t{\"Playa del Carmen\", 20.6296, -87.0739},\n}\n\n// derivedCityRadiusKM is how close a coordinate must be to a known city before\n// we are willing to assert that city. A hotel is not always in the centre, but\n// it is not 50km outside it either.\nconst derivedCityRadiusKM = 50\n\n// nearestCity returns the known city containing these coordinates, or false if\n// none is close enough to assert honestly.\nfunc nearestCity(c Coords) (string, bool) {\n\tbest, bestKM := \"\", math.Inf(1)\n\tfor _, city := range knownCities {\n\t\tkm := haversineKM(c.Lat, c.Lng, city.Lat, city.Lng)\n\t\tif km < bestKM {\n\t\t\tbest, bestKM = city.Name, km\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\tif bestKM > derivedCityRadiusKM {\n\t\treturn \"\", false\n\t}\n\treturn best, true\n}\n\n// haversineKM is great-circle distance in kilometres.\nfunc haversineKM(lat1, lng1, lat2, lng2 float64) float64 {\n\tconst earthRadiusKM = 6371\n\tdLat := (lat2 - lat1) * math.Pi / 180\n\tdLng := (lng2 - lng1) * math.Pi / 180\n\ta := math.Sin(dLat/2)*math.Sin(dLat/2) +\n\t\tmath.Cos(lat1*math.Pi/180)*math.Cos(lat2*math.Pi/180)*\n\t\t\tmath.Sin(dLng/2)*math.Sin(dLng/2)\n\treturn earthRadiusKM * 2 * math.Atan2(math.Sqrt(a), math.Sqrt(1-a))\n}\n"
}

{
  "file_path": "/Users/yuratestdev/Desktop/GOLAND/ygo-task/internal/claimcheck/group.go",
  "content": "package claimcheck\n\nimport (\n\t\"strings\"\n\t\"unicode\"\n)\n\n// nameNoise are words that describe a category of hotel rather than identify\n// one, so they must not decide whether two records are the same property.\nvar nameNoise = map[string]bool{\n\t\"hotel\": true, \"hotels\": true, \"resort\": true, \"spa\": true,\n\t\"garni\": true, \"the\": true, \"and\": true,\n}\n\n// group is a property under construction.\ntype group struct {\n\tkey     string\n\tname    string\n\trecords []Record\n}\n\n// Group collects records that describe the same property, keyed on a collapsed\n// name plus the stated city.\n//\n// The city half of the key is deliberately the city the record states, never\n// the one its coordinates imply: grouping has to work before the location has\n// been checked, or a record with bad coordinates would be filed under the wrong\n// property and its other claims would vanish from the report.\nfunc Group(recs []Record) []Property {\n\tvar order []*group\n\tindex := map[string]*group{}\n\n\tfor _, rec := range recs {\n\t\tkey := groupKey(rec)\n\t\tg, ok := index[key]\n\t\tif !ok {\n\t\t\tg = &group{key: key, name: displayName(rec)}\n\t\t\tindex[key] = g\n\t\t\torder = append(order, g)\n\t\t}\n\t\tg.records = append(g.records, rec)\n\t}\n\n\tprops := make([]Property, 0, len(order))\n\tfor _, g := range order {\n\t\tprops = append(props, Property{\n\t\t\tKey:     g.key,\n\t\t\tName:    g.name,\n\t\t\tSources: distinctSources(g.records),\n\t\t})\n\t}\n\treturn props\n}\n\n// groupKey is the collapsed name and stated city joined.\nfunc groupKey(rec Record) string {\n\treturn collapseName(recordName(rec)) + \"|\" + strings.ToLower(statedCity(rec))\n}\n\n// collapseName reduces a hotel name to an identity that survives the spelling\n// drift between feeds: case, punctuation, word order, category words, and\n// doubled letters (\"Mare Azzurro\" against \"Mare Azzuro\").\n//\n// Collapsing repeated letters is a blunt instrument. It merges the one\n// duplicate this data contains and it would merge genuinely different names\n// that differ only by a doubled letter; it is a heuristic standing in for\n// entity resolution, not a substitute for it.\nfunc collapseName(name string) string {\n\tvar words []string\n\tfor _, w := range strings.FieldsFunc(strings.ToLower(name), func(r rune) bool {\n\t\treturn !unicode.IsLetter(r) && !unicode.IsDigit(r)\n\t}) {\n\t\tif !nameNoise[w] {\n\t\t\twords = append(words, w)\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\n\tvar b strings.Builder\n\tvar prev rune\n\tfor _, r := range strings.Join(words, \"\") {\n\t\tif r != prev {\n\t\t\tb.WriteRune(r)\n\t\t}\n\t\tprev = r\n\t}\n\treturn b.String()\n}\n\n// recordName is whichever name field this feed shape uses.\nfunc recordName(rec Record) string {\n\tif rec.HotelName != \"\" {\n\t\treturn rec.HotelName\n\t}\n\treturn rec.Name\n}\n\n// displayName is what to call the property in the report.\nfunc displayName(rec Record) string {\n\tif n := recordName(rec); n != \"\" {\n\t\treturn n\n\t}\n\tif rec.Location != \"\" {\n\t\treturn \"(unnamed, \" + rec.Location + \")\"\n\t}\n\treturn \"(unnamed)\"\n}\n\n// statedCity is the city the record itself asserts, from whichever field shape\n// it uses. It does not consult coordinates.\nfunc statedCity(rec Record) string {\n\tif rec.City != \"\" {\n\t\treturn rec.City\n\t}\n\tif rec.Location != \"\" {\n\t\treturn strings.TrimSpace(strings.SplitN(rec.Location, \",\", 2)[0])\n\t}\n\treturn \"\"\n}\n\n// distinctSources lists each feed once, in first-seen order.\nfunc distinctSources(recs []Record) []string {\n\tseen := map[string]bool{}\n\tvar out []string\n\tfor _, rec := range recs {\n\t\tif rec.Source != \"\" && !seen[rec.Source] {\n\t\t\tseen[rec.Source] = true\n\t\t\tout = append(out, rec.Source)\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn out\n}\n"
}

  "new_string": "func Group(recs []Record) []Property {\n\tgroups := groupRecords(recs)\n\tprops := make([]Property, 0, len(groups))\n\tfor _, g := range groups {\n\t\tprops = append(props, g.property())\n\t}\n\treturn props\n}\n\n// groupRecords buckets records by group key, preserving first-seen order so the\n// report is stable across runs.\nfunc groupRecords(recs []Record) []*group {\n\tvar order []*group\n\tindex := map[string]*group{}\n\n\tfor _, rec := range recs {\n\t\tkey := groupKey(rec)\n\t\tg, ok := index[key]\n\t\tif !ok {\n\t\t\tg = &group{key: key, name: displayName(rec)}\n\t\t\tindex[key] = g\n\t\t\torder = append(order, g)\n\t\t}\n\t\tg.records = append(g.records, rec)\n\t}\n\treturn order\n}\n\n// property is the group without its claims filled in.\nfunc (g *group) property() Property {\n\treturn Property{\n\t\tKey:     g.key,\n\t\tName:    g.name,\n\t\tSources: distinctSources(g.records),\n\t}\n}"
}

  "content": "package claimcheck\n\nimport (\n\t\"cmp\"\n\t\"slices\"\n\t\"time\"\n)\n\n// knownFields is the set of fields the report always speaks about. A field is\n// only ever \"absent\" relative to a list like this one — without it, a field\n// nobody claimed is indistinguishable from a field nobody thought to ask about.\nvar knownFields = []string{\"city\"}\n\n// lastSeenLayout is the date format the scrape feed uses.\nconst lastSeenLayout = \"2006-01-02\"\n\n// Check groups records and reports the claim status of every known field.\nfunc Check(recs []Record, now time.Time) []Property {\n\tgroups := groupRecords(recs)\n\tprops := make([]Property, 0, len(groups))\n\tfor _, g := range groups {\n\t\tp := g.property()\n\t\tp.Findings = findings(claimsFor(g.records), now)\n\t\tprops = append(props, p)\n\t}\n\treturn props\n}\n\n// claimsFor extracts every claim each record makes.\nfunc claimsFor(recs []Record) []Claim {\n\tvar out []Claim\n\tfor _, rec := range recs {\n\t\tout = append(out, cityClaims(rec)...)\n\t}\n\treturn out\n}\n\n// cityClaims are what a record says, and what its coordinates imply, about\n// which city the property is in.\n//\n// The coordinate claim is attributed to \"derived:coords\" rather than to the\n// feed, so that a record contradicting itself produces two comparable claims.\n// Attributing both to the feed would make the contradiction invisible: one\n// source, no disagreement, reported as supported.\nfunc cityClaims(rec Record) []Claim {\n\tobserved := observedAt(rec)\n\tvar out []Claim\n\n\tif rec.City != \"\" {\n\t\tout = append(out, Claim{\n\t\t\tField: \"city\", Value: rec.City,\n\t\t\tSource: rec.Source + \"/city\", ObservedAt: observed,\n\t\t})\n\t}\n\tif city := locationCity(rec); city != \"\" {\n\t\tout = append(out, Claim{\n\t\t\tField: \"city\", Value: city,\n\t\t\tSource: rec.Source + \"/location\", ObservedAt: observed,\n\t\t})\n\t}\n\tif rec.Coords != nil {\n\t\t// A coordinate outside the lookup asserts nothing. Naming the nearest\n\t\t// entry regardless of distance would manufacture a conflict.\n\t\tif city, ok := nearestCity(*rec.Coords); ok {\n\t\t\tout = append(out, Claim{\n\t\t\t\tField: \"city\", Value: city,\n\t\t\t\tSource: \"derived:coords\", ObservedAt: observed,\n\t\t\t})\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn out\n}\n\n// locationCity is the city half of a joined \"City, Country\" location string.\nfunc locationCity(rec Record) string {\n\tif rec.City != \"\" || rec.Location == \"\" {\n\t\treturn \"\"\n\t}\n\treturn statedCity(rec)\n}\n\n// observedAt is when the feed says it saw this, or the zero time when it does\n// not say. Zero is \"unknown\", never \"now\": treating an undated record as fresh\n// is how three-year-old data gets presented as current.\nfunc observedAt(rec Record) time.Time {\n\tif rec.LastSeen == \"\" {\n\t\treturn time.Time{}\n\t}\n\tt, err := time.Parse(lastSeenLayout, rec.LastSeen)\n\tif err != nil {\n\t\t// An unparseable date is not a reason to drop the record's claims, and\n\t\t// it is not a reason to call them fresh. It is unknown, like no date.\n\t\treturn time.Time{}\n\t}\n\treturn t\n}\n\n// findings reports every known field, including the ones nobody claimed.\nfunc findings(claims []Claim, now time.Time) []Finding {\n\tbyField := map[string][]Claim{}\n\tfor _, c := range claims {\n\t\tbyField[c.Field] = append(byField[c.Field], c)\n\t}\n\n\tout := make([]Finding, 0, len(knownFields))\n\tfor _, field := range knownFields {\n\t\tfieldClaims := byField[field]\n\t\tslices.SortFunc(fieldClaims, func(a, b Claim) int {\n\t\t\treturn cmp.Or(cmp.Compare(a.Source, b.Source), cmp.Compare(a.Value, b.Value))\n\t\t})\n\t\tout = append(out, Finding{\n\t\t\tField:     field,\n\t\t\tStatus:    statusOf(fieldClaims),\n\t\t\tStaleness: stalenessOf(fieldClaims, now),\n\t\t\tClaims:    fieldClaims,\n\t\t})\n\t}\n\treturn out\n}\n\n// statusOf counts distinct values, not claims: two feeds agreeing is stronger\n// support, never a conflict.\nfunc statusOf(claims []Claim) Status {\n\tif len(claims) == 0 {\n\t\treturn Absent\n\t}\n\tvalues := map[string]bool{}\n\tfor _, c := range claims {\n\t\tvalues[c.Value] = true\n\t}\n\tif len(values) > 1 {\n\t\treturn Conflict\n\t}\n\treturn Supported\n}\n\n// stalenessOf reports on the freshest observation behind the claims, and\n// distinguishes \"we know it is old\" from \"no feed told us how old it is\".\nfunc stalenessOf(claims []Claim, now time.Time) Staleness {\n\tvar newest time.Time\n\tfor _, c := range claims {\n\t\tif c.ObservedAt.After(newest) {\n\t\t\tnewest = c.ObservedAt\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\tif newest.IsZero() {\n\t\treturn Unknown\n\t}\n\tif now.Sub(newest) > FreshWindow {\n\t\treturn Stale\n\t}\n\treturn Fresh\n}\n"
}

{
  "file_path": "/Users/yuratestdev/Desktop/GOLAND/ygo-task/internal/claimcheck/report.go",
  "content": "package claimcheck\n\nimport (\n\t\"fmt\"\n\t\"io\"\n\t\"strings\"\n)\n\n// Report writes every property with every claim, its source, and what the\n// claims add up to.\n//\n// A conflict prints every competing value side by side and stops there. No feed\n// outranks another, the newest does not win, and the majority does not win:\n// nothing in this data justifies any of those rules, and a single merged value\n// would carry the authority of a schema while being a guess.\nfunc Report(w io.Writer, props []Property) error {\n\tfor i, p := range props {\n\t\tif i > 0 {\n\t\t\tif _, err := fmt.Fprintln(w); err != nil {\n\t\t\t\treturn err\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t}\n\t\tif err := reportProperty(w, p); err != nil {\n\t\t\treturn err\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn nil\n}\n\nfunc reportProperty(w io.Writer, p Property) error {\n\tif _, err := fmt.Fprintf(w, \"%s\\n  sources: %s\\n\", p.Name, strings.Join(p.Sources, \", \")); err != nil {\n\t\treturn err\n\t}\n\tfor _, f := range p.Findings {\n\t\tif _, err := fmt.Fprintf(w, \"  %-14s %-10s %s\\n\",\n\t\t\tf.Field, strings.ToUpper(string(f.Status)), f.Staleness); err != nil {\n\t\t\treturn err\n\t\t}\n\t\tfor _, c := range f.Claims {\n\t\t\tif _, err := fmt.Fprintf(w, \"      %-22s %-28s %s\\n\",\n\t\t\t\tstrconvQuote(c.Value), c.Source, observedLabel(c)); err != nil {\n\t\t\t\treturn err\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn nil\n}\n\n// observedLabel keeps \"the feed carried no date\" visually distinct from a date,\n// so an undated claim is never read as a current one.\nfunc observedLabel(c Claim) string {\n\tif c.ObservedAt.IsZero() {\n\t\treturn \"no date\"\n\t}\n\treturn c.ObservedAt.Format(lastSeenLayout)\n}\n\n// strconvQuote wraps a value so an empty string is visible in the report rather\n// than printing as blank space.\nfunc strconvQuote(s string) string { return `\"` + s + `\"` }\n"
}

  "content": "// Command claimcheck reports what each feed claims about each hotel property,\n// and where those claims disagree.\npackage main\n\nimport (\n\t\"fmt\"\n\t\"log/slog\"\n\t\"os\"\n\t\"time\"\n\n\t\"github.com/yuratestdev/ygo-task/internal/claimcheck\"\n)\n\nfunc main() {\n\tif err := run(os.Args[1:], os.Stdout); err != nil {\n\t\tslog.Error(\"claimcheck failed\", \"err\", err)\n\t\tos.Exit(1)\n\t}\n}\n\nfunc run(args []string, out *os.File) error {\n\tif len(args) != 1 {\n\t\treturn fmt.Errorf(\"usage: claimcheck <hotels.json>\")\n\t}\n\n\tf, err := os.Open(args[0])\n\tif err != nil {\n\t\treturn fmt.Errorf(\"open feed: %w\", err)\n\t}\n\tdefer f.Close()\n\n\trecs, err := claimcheck.LoadRecords(f)\n\tif err != nil {\n\t\treturn fmt.Errorf(\"decode feed: %w\", err)\n\t}\n\n\tprops := claimcheck.Check(recs, time.Now())\n\tif err := claimcheck.Report(out, props); err != nil {\n\t\treturn fmt.Errorf(\"write report: %w\", err)\n\t}\n\n\tif n := claimcheck.UnresolvedCoords(); n > 0 {\n\t\tslog.Warn(\"some coordinates were never cross-checked\", \"count\", n)\n\t}\n\treturn nil\n}\n"
}
