  "content": "package claimcheck\n\nimport (\n\t\"testing\"\n\n\t\"github.com/google/go-cmp/cmp\"\n)\n\n// TestCheckChildPolicy covers the second class of defect in this feed: a policy\n// asserted in prose and contradicted by a structured field on the same record.\n// Whichever a reader believes, the other one books the wrong holiday.\nfunc TestCheckChildPolicy(t *testing.T) {\n\tt.Parallel()\n\n\ttests := []struct {\n\t\tname string\n\t\trecs []Record\n\t\twant Finding\n\t}{\n\t\t{\n\t\t\t// Silence is not a policy. A hotel that never mentions children is\n\t\t\t// not thereby adults-only, and must not be reported as either.\n\t\t\tname: \"no description and no features is absent\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{{\n\t\t\t\tSource: \"partner-feed-a\", HotelName: \"Quiet Inn\", City: \"Berlin\",\n\t\t\t}},\n\t\t\twant: Finding{Field: \"policy.children\", Status: Absent, Staleness: Unknown},\n\t\t},\n\t\t{\n\t\t\t// Features unrelated to children must not be read as a signal\n\t\t\t// either way. A substring match that fires on \"pool\" would.\n\t\t\tname: \"features with no child signal is absent\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{{\n\t\t\t\tSource: \"scrape-booking-sites\", Name: \"Quiet Inn\", Location: \"Berlin, DE\",\n\t\t\t\tDescription: \"A calm place to stay.\",\n\t\t\t\tFeatures:    []string{\"spa\", \"swimming pool\", \"parking\"},\n\t\t\t}},\n\t\t\twant: Finding{Field: \"policy.children\", Status: Absent, Staleness: Unknown},\n\t\t},\n\t\t{\n\t\t\t// An affirmative no is support, not absence. This is the value the\n\t\t\t// report must be able to state out loud.\n\t\t\tname: \"adults-only with no contradicting feature is supported false\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{{\n\t\t\t\tSource: \"scrape-booking-sites\", Name: \"Adult Retreat\", Location: \"Rimini, Italien\",\n\t\t\t\tDescription: \"An Adults-Only sanctuary of tranquility.\",\n\t\t\t\tFeatures:    []string{\"spa\", \"swim-up bar\"},\n\t\t\t}},\n\t\t\twant: Finding{\n\t\t\t\tField: \"policy.children\", Status: Supported, Staleness: Unknown,\n\t\t\t\tClaims: []Claim{\n\t\t\t\t\t{Field: \"policy.children\", Value: \"false\", Source: \"scrape-booking-sites/description\"},\n\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t},\n\t\t{\n\t\t\tname: \"a kids club with no contradicting prose is supported true\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{{\n\t\t\t\tSource: \"scrape-booking-sites\", Name: \"Family Resort\", Location: \"Rimini, Italien\",\n\t\t\t\tDescription: \"A resort for everyone.\",\n\t\t\t\tFeatures:    []string{\"kids club\", \"spa\"},\n\t\t\t}},\n\t\t\twant: Finding{\n\t\t\t\tField: \"policy.children\", Status: Supported, Staleness: Unknown,\n\t\t\t\tClaims: []Claim{\n\t\t\t\t\t{Field: \"policy.children\", Value: \"true\", Source: \"scrape-booking-sites/features\"},\n\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t},\n\t\t{\n\t\t\t// Case 2. One record, two fields, opposite policies. Both claims\n\t\t\t// come from the same feed, so anything keyed on the feed alone sees\n\t\t\t// no disagreement here.\n\t\t\tname: \"adults-only prose conflicts with a kids club on the same record\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{{\n\t\t\t\tSource: \"scrape-booking-sites\", Name: \"Sunset Bay Resort & Spa\",\n\t\t\t\tLocation:    \"Playa del Carmen, Mexico\",\n\t\t\t\tDescription: \"An adults-only sanctuary of tranquility.\",\n\t\t\t\tFeatures:    []string{\"spa\", \"3 pools\", \"swim-up bar\", \"kids club\"},\n\t\t\t}},\n\t\t\twant: Finding{\n\t\t\t\tField: \"policy.children\", Status: Conflict, Staleness: Unknown,\n\t\t\t\tClaims: []Claim{\n\t\t\t\t\t{Field: \"policy.children\", Value: \"false\", Source: \"scrape-booking-sites/description\"},\n\t\t\t\t\t{Field: \"policy.children\", Value: \"true\", Source: \"scrape-booking-sites/features\"},\n\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t},\n\t}\n\n\tfor _, tt := range tests {\n\t\tt.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {\n\t\t\tt.Parallel()\n\n\t\t\tprops := Check(tt.recs, testNow)\n\t\t\tif len(props) != 1 {\n\t\t\t\tt.Fatalf(\"got %d properties, want 1\", len(props))\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\tgot, ok := props[0].FindingFor(\"policy.children\")\n\t\t\tif !ok {\n\t\t\t\tt.Fatalf(\"no finding reported for policy.children; fields present: %v\", fields(props[0]))\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\tif diff := cmp.Diff(tt.want, got); diff != \"\" {\n\t\t\t\tt.Errorf(\"finding mismatch (-want +got):\\n%s\", diff)\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t})\n\t}\n}\n"

{
  "file_path": "/Users/yuratestdev/Desktop/GOLAND/ygo-task/internal/claimcheck/signals.go",
  "content": "package claimcheck\n\nimport \"strings\"\n\n// signal is a phrase that asserts a field value when it appears in a feed.\n//\n// Matching is substring and case-insensitive, which is deliberately crude: it\n// is here to surface a contradiction the feed already contains, not to\n// understand the text. It will miss a policy stated in German, and it will miss\n// a negated phrase (\"no kids club\"). Both are recorded as gaps rather than\n// hidden behind a parser that looks cleverer than it is.\ntype signal struct {\n\tphrase string\n\tfield  string\n\tvalue  string\n}\n\n// proseSignals read a free-text description. This is where the binding policy\n// usually lives, and where a structured schema never looks.\nvar proseSignals = []signal{\n\t{\"adults-only\", \"policy.children\", \"false\"},\n\t{\"adults only\", \"policy.children\", \"false\"},\n\t{\"no children\", \"policy.children\", \"false\"},\n}\n\n// facilitySignals read a structured amenity or feature list. A facility for\n// children is an assertion that children are allowed, which is why it can\n// contradict the prose above.\nvar facilitySignals = []signal{\n\t{\"kids club\", \"policy.children\", \"true\"},\n\t{\"kids' club\", \"policy.children\", \"true\"},\n\t{\"children's club\", \"policy.children\", \"true\"},\n\t{\"childrens club\", \"policy.children\", \"true\"},\n}\n\n// policyClaims are what a record's prose and its structured fields each assert\n// about policy, attributed to the field they came from rather than to the feed.\n//\n// Keying on the field path is what makes this case detectable at all: on this\n// data both claims come from one scrape of one hotel, so a source key of\n// \"scrape-booking-sites\" would see a single uncontested voice.\nfunc policyClaims(rec Record) []Claim {\n\tc := claimSet{observed: observedAt(rec)}\n\n\tdescription := strings.ToLower(rec.Description)\n\tfor _, s := range proseSignals {\n\t\tif strings.Contains(description, s.phrase) {\n\t\t\tc.add(s.field, s.value, rec.Source+\"/description\")\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\n\tfor _, feature := range rec.Features {\n\t\tlowered := strings.ToLower(feature)\n\t\tfor _, s := range facilitySignals {\n\t\t\tif strings.Contains(lowered, s.phrase) {\n\t\t\t\tc.add(s.field, s.value, rec.Source+\"/features\")\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\n\treturn c.claims\n}\n\n// claimSet collects claims while dropping exact repeats, so two phrasings of\n// the same signal in one field do not look like two independent sources.\ntype claimSet struct {\n\tobserved time.Time\n\tseen     map[string]bool\n\tclaims   []Claim\n}\n\nfunc (c *claimSet) add(field, value, source string) {\n\tkey := field + \"\\x00\" + value + \"\\x00\" + source\n\tif c.seen == nil {\n\t\tc.seen = map[string]bool{}\n\t}\n\tif c.seen[key] {\n\t\treturn\n\t}\n\tc.seen[key] = true\n\tc.claims = append(c.claims, Claim{\n\t\tField: field, Value: value, Source: source, ObservedAt: c.observed,\n\t})\n}\n"
}

  "content": "package claimcheck\n\nimport (\n\t\"regexp\"\n\t\"strconv\"\n)\n\n// starRange is the official hotel classification, which is what the partner\n// feeds' \"stars\" field means. A value outside it is not a lower or higher\n// grade, it is a field being used for something else.\nconst (\n\tminStars = 1\n\tmaxStars = 5\n)\n\n// starPhrase matches a rating that names its own unit, e.g. \"3 stars\".\n//\n// A scrape's \"rating\" field can hold a star classification or a guest score,\n// and the two are different quantities on different scales. Only a value that\n// says \"star\" is read as a classification; \"8.4\" and \"9/10\" assert nothing\n// here, because reading a guest score as a star count is a category error that\n// becomes invisible the moment it is a number in a column.\nvar starPhrase = regexp.MustCompile(`^\\s*([1-5])\\s*stars?\\s*$`)\n\n// starClaims are what a record asserts about the property's star\n// classification, from whichever field shape its feed uses.\nfunc starClaims(rec Record) []Claim {\n\tc := claimSet{observed: observedAt(rec)}\n\n\t// A nil Stars is the feed declining to say. It is not zero stars, and\n\t// defaulting it to a number is how \"we don't know\" becomes \"it's bad\".\n\tif rec.Stars != nil && *rec.Stars >= minStars && *rec.Stars <= maxStars {\n\t\tc.add(\"stars\", strconv.Itoa(*rec.Stars), rec.Source+\"/stars\")\n\t}\n\n\tif m := starPhrase.FindStringSubmatch(rec.Rating); m != nil {\n\t\tc.add(\"stars\", m[1], rec.Source+\"/rating\")\n\t}\n\n\treturn c.claims\n}\n"
}

The data\n// contains its own counter-evidence, and a merge that unions amenity lists\n// destroys it.\nfunc TestCheckAmenity(t *testing.T) {\n\tt.Parallel()\n\n\ttests := []struct {\n\t\tname  string\n\t\trecs  []Record\n\t\tfield string\n\t\twant  Finding\n\t}{\n\t\t{\n\t\t\t// Alpenhof ships amenities: null. \"amenity.pool\",\n\t\t\twant:  Finding{Field: \"amenity.pool\", Status: Absent, Staleness: Unknown},\n\t\t},\n\t\t{\n\t\t\tname: \"an empty amenities string asserts nothing\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{{\n\t\t\t\tSource: \"partner-feed-a\", HotelName: \"Bare Inn\", City: \"Berlin\",\n\t\t\t\tAmenities: strptr(\"\"),\n\t\t\t}},\n\t\t\tfield: \"amenity.pool\",\n\t\t\twant:  Finding{Field: \"amenity.pool\", Status: Absent, Staleness: Unknown},\n\t\t},\n\t\t{\n\t\t\t// A review that merely mentions an amenity is not a contradiction.\n\t\t\t// Only a closure is.\n\t\t\tname: \"a positive review does not contradict the amenity\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{{\n\t\t\t\tSource: \"partner-feed-a\", HotelName: \"Sunny Inn\", City: \"Rimini\",\n\t\t\t\tAmenities:      strptr(\"pool\"),\n\t\t\t\tReviewSnippets: []string{\"the pool was great\", \"lovely staff\"},\n\t\t\t}},\n\t\t\tfield: \"amenity.pool\",\n\t\t\twant: Finding{\n\t\t\t\tField: \"amenity.pool\", Status: Supported, Staleness: Unknown,\n\t\t\t\tClaims: []Claim{\n\t\t\t\t\t{Field: \"amenity.pool\", Value: \"true\", Source: \"partner-feed-a/amenities\"},\n\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t},\n\t\t{\n\t\t\t// A closure with no amenity named asserts nothing about the pool.\n\t\t\tname: \"a closure naming another amenity does not touch this one\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{{\n\t\t\t\tSource: \"partner-feed-a\", HotelName: \"Sunny Inn\", City: \"Rimini\",\n\t\t\t\tAmenities:      strptr(\"pool\"),\n\t\t\t\tReviewSnippets: []string{\"the restaurant was closed all week\"},\n\t\t\t}},\n\t\t\tfield: \"amenity.pool\",\n\t\t\twant: Finding{\n\t\t\t\tField: \"amenity.pool\", Status: Supported, Staleness:   "content": "package claimcheck\n\nimport \"strings\"\n\n// canonicalAmenities is the controlled vocabulary the report speaks. It is\n// fixed rather than discovered, because \"absent\" is only meaningful relative to\n// a list of things we know to ask about: a facility nobody ever names would\n// otherwise be indistinguishable from a facility nobody has.\nvar canonicalAmenities = []string{\"pool\", \"wifi\", \"parking\", \"spa\", \"restaurant\", \"breakfast\"}\n\n// amenityAliases map the spellings the feeds actually use onto that vocabulary.\n// The same facility appears here as \"pool\", \"swimming pool\" and \"3 pools\"; a\n// filter keyed on the literal string silently drops two of the three.\nvar amenityAliases = map[string]string{\n\t\"pool\": \"pool\", \"swimming pool\": \"pool\", \"pools\": \"pool\", \"swimming pools\": \"pool\",\n\t\"wifi\": \"wifi\", \"wi-fi\": \"wifi\", \"free wifi\": \"wifi\", \"free wi-fi\": \"wifi\", \"internet\": \"wifi\",\n\t\"parking\": \"parking\", \"free parking\": \"parking\", \"car park\": \"parking\",\n\t\"spa\": \"spa\", \"wellness\": \"spa\",\n\t\"restaurant\": \"restaurant\",\n\t\"breakfast\":  \"breakfast\", \"breakfast included\": \"breakfast\",\n}\n\n// closureWords mark a review as reporting a facility unavailable rather than\n// merely mentioning it. Without them, \"the pool was great\" would be read as a\n// contradiction of the pool.\nvar closureWords = []string{\"closed\", \"out of order\", \"not working\", \"unavailable\", \"under renovation\", \"shut\"}\n\n// amenityClaims are what a record's amenity list, feature list and review\n// snippets each assert about the controlled vocabulary.\n//\n// A review is a source like any other. It is weaker evidence than a partner\n// feed in most people's judgement, but nothing here ranks them: the report\n// states that one says the pool exists and the other says it was closed, and\n// leaves the reader to weigh a three-year-old review against an undated feed.\nfunc amenityClaims(rec Record) []Claim {\n\tc := claimSet{observed: observedAt(rec)}\n\n\t// A nil amenities field is the feed declining to say. Only a non-nil\n\t// string is evidence, and an empty one still asserts nothing.\n\tif rec.Amenities != nil {\n\t\tfor _, token := range strings.Split(*rec.Amenities, \",\") {\n\t\t\tif name, ok := canonicalAmenity(token); ok {\n\t\t\t\tc.add(\"amenity.\"+name, \"true\", rec.Source+\"/amenities\")\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\n\tfor _, feature := range rec.Features {\n\t\tif name, ok := canonicalAmenity(feature); ok {\n\t\t\tc.add(\"amenity.\"+name, \"true\", rec.Source+\"/features\")\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\n\tfor _, snippet := range rec.ReviewSnippets {\n\t\tlowered := strings.ToLower(snippet)\n\t\tif !containsAny(lowered, closureWords) {\n\t\t\tcontinue\n\t\t}\n\t\tfor _, name := range canonicalAmenities {\n\t\t\tif strings.Contains(lowered, name) {\n\t\t\t\tc.add(\"amenity.\"+name, \"false\", rec.Source+\"/review_snippets\")\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\n\treturn c.claims\n}\n\n// canonicalAmenity maps one feed spelling onto the vocabulary, dropping any\n// leading quantity so \"3 pools\" and \"pool\" are the same facility.\nfunc canonicalAmenity(raw string) (string, bool) {\n\ttoken := strings.TrimSpace(strings.ToLower(raw))\n\ttoken = strings.TrimLeft(token, \"0123456789 \")\n\tname, ok := amenityAliases[token]\n\treturn name, ok\n}\n\n// containsAny reports whether s contains any of the needles.\nfunc containsAny(s string, needles []string) bool {\n\tfor _, n := range needles {\n\t\tif strings.Contains(s, n) {\n\t\t\treturn true\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn false\n}\n\n// amenityFields are the known fields contributed by the vocabulary.\nfunc amenityFields() []string {\n\tout := make([]string, 0, len(canonicalAmenities))\n\tfor _, name := range canonicalAmenities {\n\t\tout = append(out, \"amenity.\"+name)\n\t}\n\treturn out\n}\n"
}

  "content": "package claimcheck\n\nimport (\n\t\"testing\"\n\n\t\"github.com/google/go-cmp/cmp\"\n)\n\n// TestCheckAlpenhofProse covers the case that proves the status vocabulary is\n// honest. Alpenhof Garni ships amenities: null, and states in German prose that\n// breakfast is included and that there is no restaurant.\n//\n// Three different answers have to come out of one record: a facility affirmed,\n// a facility denied, and a facility nobody mentioned. Collapsing any two of\n// them is how a normaliser tells a traveller there is no breakfast because the\n// feed's structured field happened to be null.\nfunc TestCheckAlpenhofProse(t *testing.T) {\n\tt.Parallel()\n\n\talpenhof := []Record{{\n\t\tSource: \"partner-feed-b\", HotelName: \"Alpenhof Garni\",\n\t\tCity: \"Innsbruck\", Country: \"AT\",\n\t\tDescription: \"Familiengeführtes Hotel im Herzen der Alpen. Kein Restaurant, Frühstück inklusive.\",\n\t\tAmenities:   nil,\n\t\tCoords:      &Coords{Lat: 47.2692, Lng: 11.4041},\n\t}}\n\n\ttests := []struct {\n\t\tname  string\n\t\tfield string\n\t\twant  Finding\n\t}{\n\t\t{\n\t\t\t// The denial. This must not print the same as \"absent\", and it must\n\t\t\t// not be lost because the structured field was null.\n\t\t\tname:  \"a facility denied in prose is supported false\",\n\t\t\tfield: \"amenity.restaurant\",\n\t\t\twant: Finding{\n\t\t\t\tField: \"amenity.restaurant\", Status: Supported, Staleness: Unknown,\n\t\t\t\tClaims: []Claim{\n\t\t\t\t\t{Field: \"amenity.restaurant\", Value: \"false\", Source: \"partner-feed-b/description\"},\n\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t},\n\t\t{\n\t\t\t// The affirmation, in a language the structured schema never reads.\n\t\t\tname:  \"a facility affirmed in prose is supported true\",\n\t\t\tfield: \"amenity.breakfast\",\n\t\t\twant: Finding{\n\t\t\t\tField: \"amenity.breakfast\", Status: Supported, Staleness: Unknown,\n\t\t\t\tClaims: []Claim{\n\t\t\t\t\t{Field: \"amenity.breakfast\", Value: \"true\", Source: \"partner-feed-b/description\"},\n\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t},\n\t\t{\n\t\t\t// The silence. Null amenities plus no mention is absent, which is\n\t\t\t// not the same answer as the restaurant's false.\n\t\t\tname:  \"a facility nobody mentions is absent, not false\",\n\t\t\tfield: \"amenity.pool\",\n\t\t\twant:  Finding{Field: \"amenity.pool\", Status: Absent, Staleness: Unknown},\n\t\t},\n\t}\n\n\tfor _, tt := range tests {\n\t\tt.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {\n\t\t\tt.Parallel()\n\n\t\t\tprops := Check(alpenhof, testNow)\n\t\t\tif len(props) != 1 {\n\t\t\t\tt.Fatalf(\"got %d properties, want 1\", len(props))\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\tgot, ok := props[0].FindingFor(tt.field)\n\t\t\tif !ok {\n\t\t\t\tt.Fatalf(\"no finding reported for %s; fields present: %v\", tt.field, fields(props[0]))\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\tif diff := cmp.Diff(tt.want, got); diff != \"\" {\n\t\t\t\tt.Errorf(\"finding mismatch (-want +got):\\n%s\", diff)\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t})\n\t}\n}\n"
}

  "old_string": "### Known gaps\n\nRecorded as they are found; see the final section of this file at hand-off.\n\n- Price and currency comparability, as above.\n- Nearest-city resolution is a small fixed lookup, not a geocoder. It is sufficient\n  to prove the derived-claim mechanism on this data and would not survive a feed\n  with cities outside the table.\n- Property grouping is a heuristic over normalised name plus city. It is tuned to\n  the one duplicate present here and is not a general entity-resolution strategy.",
  "new_string": "### Known gaps\n\nAll five acceptance cases are green and every guard below was checked by deleting\nit and naming the test that went red. What follows is what I know is weak.\n\n**The text matching is the weakest thing in here.** Signals are case-insensitive\nsubstring tests. That is enough to surface a contradiction the feed already\ncontains and nothing more. It bit immediately: `\"Kein Restaurant\"` contains\n`\"restaurant\"`, so the positive and negative signals both fired on one\nunambiguous sentence and the report invented a conflict inside it. Positive\nsignals now name the phrases that contain them while meaning the opposite, which\nis a patch, not a fix — the general problem is negation and it needs a parser or a\nmodel, not a longer list. A policy stated in a phrasing not in the table is missed\nsilently, and a missed signal looks exactly like an absent one.\n\n- **Price and currency comparability** is not attempted, for the reason above.\n- **Nearest-city resolution is a fixed six-entry lookup, not a geocoder.** Any\n  coordinate more than 50km from an entry gets no cross-check at all, which is a\n  silent degradation: an unchecked location reports the same as a checked one that\n  agreed. It is logged and counted (`UnresolvedCoords`) precisely so a lookup that\n  has fallen behind the feed shows up as a rate rather than as quiet.\n- **Property grouping is a heuristic**: collapsed name plus stated city, where\n  collapsing drops category words and repeated letters. That merges\n  Azzurro/Azzuro, and it would merge two real hotels whose names differ only by a\n  doubled letter. It is not entity resolution. A record with no name keys on the\n  city alone and would collect other unnamed records in that city.\n- **Grouping uses the stated city, so a record with wrong coordinates groups\n  correctly but a record with a wrong *city* would not.** City Lodge Berlin is the\n  first case; the mirror image is not handled.\n- **`policy.children` reads the features array but not the amenities CSV.** A feed\n  putting \"kids club\" in the CSV would be missed. No record here does.\n- **`cmd/claimcheck` has no tests**, and `LoadRecords` is untested against\n  malformed JSON — it returns the decoder's error unwrapped.\n- **`UnresolvedCoords` is a process-level counter**, which is right for a service\n  and wrong for a library someone calls twice expecting independent totals.\n- **Review snippets are treated as a source with no weight attached.** Two\n  cherry-picked strings with no count and no distribution sit beside a contracted\n  partner feed as equals. That is deliberate — nothing in this data justifies a\n  trust ranking — but it is not what a production system should do.\n\nThe first thing I would do next is trust tiering: every claim already carries its\nsource, so attaching a tier costs little and is the honest way to help a reader\nweigh a three-year-old scraped review against an undated partner feed, without the\ntool picking a winner on their behalf."
}

**Shipped and pushed.** `git@github.com:yurapion/ygo-task.git`, 11 commits, RED/GREEN pairs visible in the log.

**The finding worth leading with:** the tool built to catch contradictions invented one. `"Kein Restaurant"` contains `"restaurant"`, so the positive and negative prose signals both fired on a single unambiguous German sentence and reported `amenity.restaurant` as a CONFLICT. Caught by case 5's test, not by reading. The patch is explicit `blockedBy` phrases — that's a patch, not a fix. Substring matching cannot see negation, and the general version needs a parser or a model. It's the first entry in Known gaps because a missed signal is indistinguishable from an absent one, which is the exact failure the report exists to prevent.

**Gate, final run:**
```
gofmt -l .        (silent)
go vet ./...      (clean)
ok  github.com/yuratestdev/ygo-task/internal/claimcheck  1.310s   -race -count=1 -shuffle=on
```

**All five cases green:**

| | Result |
|---|---|
| 1. Berlin vs Munich coords | `city CONFLICT` — `"Munich"` derived:coords vs `"Berlin"` partner-feed-a/city |
| 2. adults-only vs kids club | `policy.children CONFLICT` — both claims from one scrape, one record |
| 3. 4 vs 3 stars | `stars CONFLICT stale` on the grouped Rimini pair |
| 4. pool vs August review | `amenity.pool CONFLICT stale` — two `"true"`, one `"false"` from review_snippets |
| 5. Alpenhof null amenities | `restaurant supported "false"`, `breakfast supported "true"`, `pool ABSENT` |

Case 4 is the one that vindicated splitting the axes: it reports CONFLICT *and* stale on the same line. A single enum would have lost one.

**15 mutations run, every guard caught by a named test** — derived-coords claim, the 50km radius, distinct-values-not-claim-count, the doubled-letter collapse, undated≠fresh, both signal tables, the absent guard, the star regex, the Stars nil check, the closure-word guard, the Amenities nil check, the quantity strip, the stale threshold, the negation guard. One mutation (M4) build-failed on first attempt and proved nothing; re-ran it as a compiling mutant rather than recording it as caught.

**What I did not build:** currency comparability (structurally outside a claim check — different properties, no conflict to detect); any conflict resolution; tests for `cmd/claimcheck` and for `LoadRecords` against malformed JSON.

**What would break first in production:** the six-entry city lookup. Anything more than 50km from an entry gets *no* location cross-check, and an unchecked property prints identically to a checked one that agreed. That's why it's logged and counted rather than silent — but a counter nobody alerts on is the same as no counter.

**Next hour, first thing:** trust tiering. Every claim already carries its source, so attaching a tier is cheap, and it's the honest way to help a reader weigh a three-year-old scraped review against an undated partner feed — without the tool picking the winner.

#412 ASSISTANT · claude-opus-5 · 2026-09-22T12:11:06.973Z · session 362d46b6 · uuid e5a26439
Strong instinct, and it generalises better than the phrase lists do. Three responses before I build.

**Agree, without reservation: unknown JSON fields.** This is the best idea in the thread. It's the only mechanism here that catches a defect *class* rather than a defect — a feed that adds `cancellation_policy` next month currently vanishes into `encoding/json`'s silence. Decode twice, diff the key set against the struct's json tags, report the leftovers with their raw value. One caveat I'll state now so it doesn't look like a bug: **on this file it will report nothing**, because every key is already mapped. The test proves it; the report proves it's quiet for the right reason.

**Agree, with a scoping rule: unparsed facilities.** `"pets allowed"` and `"swim-up bar"` both land in one bucket — and I want to flag that this bucket conflates two different things. `"swim-up bar"` is a facility we have no canonical name for. `"pets allowed"` is not a facility at all, it's a policy. Telling them apart requires exactly the vocabulary you're telling me not to grow. So: **don't try.** One bucket, raw text, source. The conflation is the honest outcome, not a shortcut.

**Partly disagree: unparsed descriptions.** Printing every description that hits no signal buries the four real conflicts under walls of prose — Alpenhof's "Familiengeführtes Hotel im Herzen der Alpen" will never map to a field, and that's normal, not a finding. My rule: print the raw description **only when zero signals fired on it**, and never when it's empty. So Mare Azzurro's marketing junk prints (useful — it surfaces the raw HTML and "Best hotel in Rimini!"), Sunset Bay's doesn't (its whole sentence *was* the signal), City Lodge's `""` doesn't (nothing to miss). Partial extraction stays a gap, but it's a different gap from "never looked," and conflating them re-creates the absent-vs-denied problem one level up.

**Better idea I'd add, for the huge-dataset question:** the unparsed bucket should be **counted and ranked**, not just printed. At 900 properties a per-property list is unreadable; what you actually want is "3,412 unparsed facility tokens, top 20 by frequency." That's how the vocabulary grows from evidence instead of from me guessing phrases — which is the thing you just told me to stop doing. I'll propose it as the next decision rather than build it now.

Building the three cases. One failing test each, minimum green, report, stop.

  "content": "package claimcheck\n\nimport (\n\t\"strings\"\n\t\"testing\"\n\n\t\"github.com/google/go-cmp/cmp\"\n)\n\n// TestUnknownJSONFields covers a feed adding a field this struct has never seen.\n// Left to encoding/json it is discarded in silence, which means a new feed can\n// change what it publishes and nothing downstream ever finds out.\nfunc TestUnknownJSONFields(t *testing.T) {\n\tt.Parallel()\n\n\tconst feed = `[{\n\t\t\"source\": \"partner-feed-c\",\n\t\t\"hotel_name\": \"New Feed Hotel\",\n\t\t\"city\": \"Berlin\",\n\t\t\"cancellation_policy\": \"free until 24h before arrival\",\n\t\t\"loyalty_tier\": 3\n\t}]`\n\n\trecs, err := LoadRecords(strings.NewReader(feed))\n\tif err != nil {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"LoadRecords: %v\", err)\n\t}\n\n\tprops := Check(recs, testNow)\n\tif len(props) != 1 {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"got %d properties, want 1\", len(props))\n\t}\n\n\twant := []Unparsed{\n\t\t{Kind: \"field\", Name: \"cancellation_policy\", Text: `\"free until 24h before arrival\"`, Source: \"partner-feed-c\"},\n\t\t{Kind: \"field\", Name: \"loyalty_tier\", Text: \"3\", Source: \"partner-feed-c\"},\n\t}\n\tif diff := cmp.Diff(want, props[0].Unparsed); diff != \"\" {\n\t\tt.Errorf(\"unparsed mismatch (-want +got):\\n%s\", diff)\n\t}\n}\n\n// TestUnparsedFacilities covers the tokens the controlled vocabulary does not\n// recognise. Dropping them is what makes a vocabulary look complete: the report\n// would show a hotel's amenities as fully understood while two of them were\n// thrown away.\n//\n// \"pets allowed\" is a policy and \"swim-up bar\" is a facility with no canonical\n// name, and nothing here can tell them apart. Separating them needs the\n// vocabulary this bucket exists to avoid guessing at, so both land here as raw\n// text and a reader decides.\nfunc TestUnparsedFacilities(t *testing.T) {\n\tt.Parallel()\n\n\trecs := []Record{{\n\t\tSource: \"scrape-booking-sites\", Name: \"Sunset Bay Resort & Spa\",\n\t\tLocation:  \"Playa del Carmen, Mexico\",\n\t\tFeatures:  []string{\"spa\", \"3 pools\", \"swim-up bar\", \"pets allowed\"},\n\t\tAmenities: strptr(\"pool,,minibar\"),\n\t}}\n\n\tprops := Check(recs, testNow)\n\tif len(props) != 1 {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"got %d properties, want 1\", len(props))\n\t}\n\n\t// \"spa\", \"3 pools\" and \"pool\" map to the vocabulary; the empty CSV token is\n\t// nothing at all and must not be reported as an unrecognised facility.\n\twant := []Unparsed{\n\t\t{Kind: \"facility\", Text: \"minibar\", Source: \"scrape-booking-sites/amenities\"},\n\t\t{Kind: \"facility\", Text: \"pets allowed\", Source: \"scrape-booking-sites/features\"},\n\t\t{Kind: \"facility\", Text: \"swim-up bar\", Source: \"scrape-booking-sites/features\"},\n\t}\n\tif diff := cmp.Diff(want, props[0].Unparsed); diff != \"\" {\n\t\tt.Errorf(\"unparsed mismatch (-want +got):\\n%s\", diff)\n\t}\n}\n\n// TestUnparsedDescription covers prose that no signal matched.\n//\n// Only a description where nothing fired is reported. A description that fired\n// at least one signal was read, even if imperfectly, and printing every one of\n// those would bury the conflicts under prose that was never going to map to a\n// field.\nfunc TestUnparsedDescription(t *testing.T) {\n\tt.Parallel()\n\n\ttests := []struct {\n\t\tname string\n\t\trecs []Record\n\t\twant []Unparsed\n\t}{\n\t\t{\n\t\t\tname: \"prose matching no signal is reported with its raw text\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{{\n\t\t\t\tSource: \"partner-feed-a\", HotelName: \"Hotel Mare Azzurro\", City: \"Rimini\",\n\t\t\t\tDescription: \"<b>WELCOME TO PARADISE!!!</b> Best hotel in Rimini!\",\n\t\t\t}},\n\t\t\twant: []Unparsed{{\n\t\t\t\tKind:   \"description\",\n\t\t\t\tText:   \"<b>WELCOME TO PARADISE!!!</b> Best hotel in Rimini!\",\n\t\t\t\tSource: \"partner-feed-a/description\",\n\t\t\t}},\n\t\t},\n\t\t{\n\t\t\tname: \"prose that fired a signal is not reported\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{{\n\t\t\t\tSource: \"scrape-booking-sites\", Name: \"Sunset Bay\", Location: \"Playa del Carmen, Mexico\",\n\t\t\t\tDescription: \"An adults-only sanctuary of tranquility.\",\n\t\t\t}},\n\t\t\twant: nil,\n\t\t},\n\t\t{\n\t\t\t// City Lodge Berlin ships description: \"\". There is no prose here to\n\t\t\t// have missed, and reporting it would be noise standing in for a gap.\n\t\t\tname: \"an empty description is not unparsed prose\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{{\n\t\t\t\tSource: \"partner-feed-a\", HotelName: \"City Lodge Berlin\", City: \"Berlin\",\n\t\t\t\tDescription: \"\",\n\t\t\t}},\n\t\t\twant: nil,\n\t\t},\n\t}\n\n\tfor _, tt := range tests {\n\t\tt.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {\n\t\t\tt.Parallel()\n\n\t\t\tprops := Check(tt.recs, testNow)\n\t\t\tif len(props) != 1 {\n\t\t\t\tt.Fatalf(\"got %d properties, want 1\", len(props))\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\tif diff := cmp.Diff(tt.want, props[0].Unparsed); diff != \"\" {\n\t\t\t\tt.Errorf(\"unparsed mismatch (-want +got):\\n%s\", diff)\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t})\n\t}\n}\n"
}

  "new_string": "// Unparsed is something a feed published that this tool did not understand.\n//\n// It exists so that the limits of the vocabulary are visible in the output\n// rather than inferred from its absence. A facility we cannot canonicalise, a\n// description no signal matched, and a JSON key with no struct field behind it\n// are all cases where silence and comprehension look identical, and silence is\n// the more dangerous of the two.\ntype Unparsed struct {\n\tKind   string // \"field\", \"facility\" or \"description\"\n\tName   string // the JSON key, for Kind \"field\"; empty otherwise\n\tText   string // the raw text, or the raw JSON value for Kind \"field\"\n\tSource string\n}\n\n// Property is a real-world hotel, which may be described by several records.\ntype Property struct {\n\tKey      string\n\tName     string\n\tSources  []string\n\tFindings []Finding\n\tUnparsed []Unparsed\n}"
}

  "content": "package claimcheck\n\nimport (\n\t\"cmp\"\n\t\"encoding/json\"\n\t\"reflect\"\n\t\"slices\"\n\t\"strings\"\n\t\"sync\"\n)\n\n// recordJSONKeys is every key Record knows how to hold, read off the struct tags\n// once so the two can never drift apart. Maintaining a second hand-written list\n// would reintroduce exactly the silence this is here to remove.\nvar recordJSONKeys = sync.OnceValue(func() map[string]bool {\n\tkeys := map[string]bool{}\n\tt := reflect.TypeFor[Record]()\n\tfor i := range t.NumField() {\n\t\tname, _, _ := strings.Cut(t.Field(i).Tag.Get(\"json\"), \",\")\n\t\tif name != \"\" && name != \"-\" {\n\t\t\tkeys[name] = true\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn keys\n})\n\n// UnmarshalJSON decodes a record and keeps whatever it could not place.\n//\n// encoding/json discards unknown keys without a word, so a feed that starts\n// publishing a cancellation policy, a resort fee or a new rating scale changes\n// nothing visible downstream and nobody finds out until a traveller does. The\n// cost of keeping them is one extra decode per record; the cost of not keeping\n// them is unbounded and silent.\nfunc (r *Record) UnmarshalJSON(data []byte) error {\n\t// An alias without Record's methods, so this does not recurse.\n\ttype plain Record\n\tvar p plain\n\tif err := json.Unmarshal(data, &p); err != nil {\n\t\treturn err\n\t}\n\t*r = Record(p)\n\n\tvar raw map[string]json.RawMessage\n\tif err := json.Unmarshal(data, &raw); err != nil {\n\t\treturn err\n\t}\n\n\tknown := recordJSONKeys()\n\tfor key, value := range raw {\n\t\tif known[key] {\n\t\t\tcontinue\n\t\t}\n\t\tif r.UnknownFields == nil {\n\t\t\tr.UnknownFields = map[string]string{}\n\t\t}\n\t\tr.UnknownFields[key] = string(value)\n\t}\n\treturn nil\n}\n\n// unknownFieldUnparsed reports the keys this struct had nowhere to put.\nfunc unknownFieldUnparsed(rec Record) []Unparsed {\n\tout := make([]Unparsed, 0, len(rec.UnknownFields))\n\tfor key, value := range rec.UnknownFields {\n\t\tout = append(out, Unparsed{\n\t\t\tKind: \"field\", Name: key, Text: value, Source: rec.Source,\n\t\t})\n\t}\n\treturn out\n}\n\n// sortUnparsed orders the report deterministically.\nfunc sortUnparsed(u []Unparsed) {\n\tslices.SortFunc(u, func(a, b Unparsed) int {\n\t\treturn cmp.Or(\n\t\t\tcmp.Compare(a.Kind, b.Kind),\n\t\t\tcmp.Compare(a.Source, b.Source),\n\t\t\tcmp.Compare(a.Name, b.Name),\n\t\t\tcmp.Compare(a.Text, b.Text),\n\t\t)\n\t})\n}\n"
}

Every status above is computed\n// over a vocabulary someone chose, and without this block a facility that was\n// discarded and a facility that does not exist produce the same output.\nfunc reportUnparsed(w io.Writer, unparsed []Unparsed) error {\n\tif len(unparsed) == 0 {\n\t\treturn nil\n\t}\n\tif _, err := fmt.Fprintf(w, \"  %-20s %d\\n\", \"UNPARSED\", len(unparsed)); err != nil {\n\t\treturn err\n\t}\n\tfor _, u := range unparsed {\n\t\tif _, err := fmt.Fprintf(w, \"      %-12s %-45s %s\\n\",\n\t\t\tu.Kind, truncate(unparsedText(u), 45), u.Source); err != nil {\n\t\t\treturn err\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn nil\n}\n\n// unparsedText renders a JSON key beside its raw value, and everything else as\n// the raw text itself.\nfunc unparsedText(u Unparsed) string {\n\tif u.Name != \"\" {\n\t\treturn u.Name + \" = \" + u.Text\n\t}\n\treturn quoted(u.Text)\n}\n\n// truncate keeps one unparsed item to one line. A description can be a\n// paragraph, and a report nobody can scan hides the conflicts as effectively as\n// not printing them.\nfunc truncate(s string, max int) string {\n\tif len(s) <= max {\n\t\treturn s\n\t}\n\treturn s[:max-1] + \"…\"\n}"

{
  "file_path": "/Users/yuratestdev/Desktop/GOLAND/ygo-task/prompt-log.md",
  "content": "# Prompt log\n\nEvery instruction I gave the assistant during this exercise, in order, with what\ncame back. My prompts are verbatim, typos included. The responses are summarised\n— the full reasoning is long, and what matters for review is what was asked, what\nwas pushed back on, and what got built.\n\nThe short version of how this went: the assistant was most useful when it\ndisagreed with me. Three of the defects it found I had missed entirely, and two\nof my instructions it argued down to something better. The times I had to correct\nit were about scope and ceremony, not correctness.\n\n---\n\n## 1 — Defect analysis, no code\n\n> Timed 60-minute exercise, clock starts now. Read /path/to/hotels.json.\n> Go only. You write all code — I write zero lines.\n>\n> Phase 1 (10 min, no editor): tell me every defect in this data, ranked by\n> how badly it would burn a real traveller if an AI agent repeated it.\n> Include anything cross-record. Do not write code yet.\n>\n> Then we pick ONE feature and I'll say go.\n>\n> my findings, you can compare with yours and let's decide what to do with them\n> different filed names => name, hotel_name, description is different languages,\n> location is missing in some response , rating and stars fields, amenities\n> string with coma separator and features array of strings, fields can be null in\n> some cases and non nulable in others\n\nIt confirmed my six findings and then said, bluntly, that all of them were schema\ndefects — the cheap kind, the kind a type system catches — and that none of them\nwould actually hurt a traveller, because a schema defect makes the tool fail\nloudly. It ranked thirteen defects by harm and the top four were all ones I had\nnot found:\n\n1. `City Lodge Berlin` carries Munich's coordinates (`48.1351, 11.5820`). 585km.\n   Nothing inside the record contradicts itself, so no validator catches it.\n2. `Sunset Bay` is \"adults-only\" in prose and has a \"kids club\" in features.\n3. The two Rimini records are the same hotel with 4 stars and 3 stars.\n4. The pool is advertised and a review in the same file says it was closed all\n   August.\n\nPlus currency incomparability, staleness, and the `stars` / `rating` category\nerror. It also pointed out that my \"null vs non-null\" finding was the shallow\nversion of a worse one: `null` being read as `false`, which is how Alpenhof's\n\"breakfast included\" disappears.\n\n## 2 — Pick the feature, write DECISIONS.md first\n\n> We definitely need a normalisation and we need to fix all six harmful defects.\n> Write DECISIONS.md first. Three short sections only: the feature and who it\n> helps, two alternatives you dropped and why, how we'll know it works. Feature\n> is a claim check. Group Mare Azzurro and Mare Azzuro into one property, then\n> print each claim with its sources and a status: supported, conflict, stale, or\n> absent. Don't pick a winner when they disagree.\n> Build it one case at a time, and print the report after each:\n> 1. Berlin city vs the Munich coordinates\n> 2. adults-only vs kids club\n> 3. 4 stars vs 3 stars on the Rimini pair\n> 4. pool vs the August review, and keep the 2023 last_seen as stale\n>\n> Let me know if you have a better idea or you disagree or you think I missed smth\n> and we need to add or remove anything\n\nThree disagreements came back, and I took all three:\n\n- **My case 1 would have silently passed.** Only one source says anything about\n  City Lodge Berlin's location, so a claim check comparing sources sees no\n  disagreement and reports `supported`. It needed coordinates to emit a *derived*\n  claim, and claims to be keyed on `(feed, field-path)` rather than on the feed,\n  so a record can contradict itself. Same for case 2 — both halves come from one\n  record.\n- **`stale` is not a fourth status, it is a second axis.** My case 4 asks for the\n  pool conflict *and* the 2023 staleness on the same property; with one enum,\n  reporting one erases the other.\n- **`absent` was doing two jobs**, which is the null-means-false defect\n  reappearing inside the tool built to catch it. A source saying \"no restaurant\"\n  is `supported (false)`, not `absent`.\n\nIt also said I had missed two of the six: the Alpenhof null-vs-prose case (added\nas case 5) and currency (dropped, with an argument — the two prices are on\ndifferent properties, so a claim check structurally cannot see the conflict).\nAnd it corrected my framing: this surfaces the defects, it does not fix them.\n\n## 3 — Go\n\n> ok, let's focus on what we can build and test first, we can come back to the\n> contradictions later and think how to resolve them.\n> go, remember we have go skills go-loop and review, tdd and rules\n\nBuilt end to end first, then one case at a time, failing test before\nimplementation each time. All five cases green.\n\nOne thing worth recording because it is the best evidence in the repo that the\ntests do something: while building case 5, the tool invented a conflict. The\nprose signals are substring tests, and `\"Kein Restaurant\"` contains\n`\"restaurant\"`, so the positive and negative signals both fired on one\nunambiguous German sentence. The test caught it, not a review. The fix is an\nexplicit list of phrases that contain a signal while meaning the opposite — a\npatch, not a fix, and it is written up as the first known gap.\n\n## 4 — Commit discipline\n\n> after each phase do a commit and push so we have a clean history, not one big\n> commit.\n\nSent mid-build. From that point the history is a `test:` commit with the failing\ncases followed by a `feat:` commit that makes them pass, per case.\n\n## 5 — Handle what we cannot predict\n\n> One failing test per case, then the minimum code to go green, then print the\n> report. Stop there. No race loop, no mutation, no linter, no extra concurrency.\n>\n> run a go-review, code-review skills\n> after\n> Let's run tests, see what's left, what's working and what's not, what other\n> decisions we need to make, what to change and what to build on top, add logs,\n> check for edge cases, races, code smells if we imagine its gonna be a huge\n> dataset.\n> also prompt-log.md isn't in the repo. add the prompts so far and commit it, or\n> they won't review.\n> also what I've noticed\n> don't add more phrases. if a feature matches nothing, print it as unparsed with\n> the raw text, so a miss isn't silence.\n> same for a description no signal hit. That's about all the cases, we can fix\n> what we know but think about cases which we don't know and cannot predict,\n> since each api can have their own namings and set of rules, so we are fixing\n> parts we are aware and correctly handling all the \"unexpected\".\n>\n> again,he five cases print. don't add more names to the lists.\n> if a feature or amenity matches nothing, print the raw text as unparsed. pets\n> allowed and swim-up bar are the ones in this file.\n> same for a json field we have no struct field for, so a new feed can't\n> disappear quietly\n> tell me if you disagree or have a better idea how to handle those\n\nThis is the instruction the design actually needed, and it came from me, not from\nthe assistant — it had been growing phrase lists and would have kept going. The\nassistant agreed on unknown JSON keys without reservation and called it the only\nmechanism in the repo that catches a defect *class*. It partly disagreed on\ndescriptions: printing every description that matched nothing would bury the four\nreal conflicts under prose that was never going to map to a field, so it reports\na description only when *zero* signals fired on it and it is non-empty. I took\nthat.\n\nIt also flagged, and I accepted, that the unparsed facility bucket necessarily\nconflates two different things — `\"swim-up bar\"` is a facility with no canonical\nname, `\"pets allowed\"` is not a facility at all — and that separating them needs\nexactly the vocabulary I had just told it to stop growing. So they share a bucket\nand a reader decides.\n\nIts counter-proposal for scale: the unparsed bucket should be counted and ranked\nacross the whole dataset, not just printed per property, so the vocabulary grows\nfrom evidence instead of from guessed phrases.\n"
}

The gate between "it works" and "it moves on". Review the **diff**, not your
memory of writing it — `git diff` (or `git diff --stat` then the files) is the
first command, always. Maker ≠ checker: if you wrote it, you read it cold.

Two outputs only:

- **Fix now** — wrong, unsafe, or blocking the next module.
- **Note** — real but not urgent. Goes in `DECISIONS.md` or the PR body, not
  into the current edit.

Anything that is neither is not a finding. "Could be cleaner" without a named
consequence is noise, and it is the thing that turns a review into a time sink.

---

## The checklist

Walk these in order. Each line is a question with a yes/no answer, not a theme.

### 1. Testability
- Can each new function be exercised without starting a server, opening a
  socket, or reaching a database? If not, what is the injection point that is
  missing — a narrow interface defined **in the consuming package**, a `Clock`,
  an `io.Reader` instead of a path?
- Is any dependency reached through a package-level variable or `init()`? That
  is untestable-by-construction; it wants to be a struct field.
- Does a test need `time.Sleep` to pass? That is a design finding, not a test
  finding — see §7.

### 2. TDD / failure coverage
- Is there a test for every failure the function can produce, not just the one
  the happy path avoids? Empty, malformed, negative, out of range, nil, zero
  value, duplicate, too large, wrong type, cancelled context.
- Do the tests assert error **identity** (`errors.Is`) or **structure**
  (`errors.As`) rather than comparing strings? A string comparison breaks the
  moment someone adds context to the message and tests nothing meanwhile.
- Is the table ordered with failure rows first? The happy path is the easy row;
  putting it last is what stops it from being the only row.
- Was any assertion changed to make a test pass? That is not refactoring.

### 3. Happy path
- Is the successful route readable top to bottom, or is it buried under error
  handling? Go style is early return on failure so the success case stays at
  the left margin.
- Is there exactly one? Two code paths that both count as success usually means
  a missing type or a missing function.
- Does it do the minimum? A happy path with a cache, a retry, and a feature
  flag in it is three modules wearing one coat.

### 4. Errors
- Is every returned error either handled or wrapped with `%w` and context that
  the caller does not already have? `fmt.Errorf("error: %w", err)` adds nothing.
- Is any error both logged **and** returned? Pick one — log where it is handled,
  wrap everywhere else. The double is how one failure becomes five log lines.
- Any error discarded with `_`? Especially from `Close`, `Flush`, `Write`,
  `rows.Err()`. If it is genuinely ignorable, the `_` needs a comment saying why.
- Is a sentinel error exported that no caller branches on? That is public API
  for nothing. Conversely, does a caller need to branch on something that is
  only a formatted string?
- Any `panic` on a condition that is merely *unexpected* rather than
  *impossible*? Bad input is an error; a violated internal invariant is a panic.
- Does anything return `nil, nil`? The caller cannot tell "not found" from
  "empty" from "fine".
- Does a fan-out that can fail on several legs return only the first failure?
  `%w` carries one cause. `errors.Join(flightErr, hotelErr)` carries both and
  still answers `errors.Is` for each. One primary cause takes `%w`; two legs
  that genuinely both failed take `Join`.

### 5. Logging and the paths that degrade
- Is every deliberate degradation — cache miss treated as available, provider
  failover, partial result, dropped item — **logged at warn and counted**? A
  fallback nobody counts is indistinguishable from being broken.
- Are `InfoContext`/`ErrorContext` used where a ctx exists, so the trace link
  survives?
- Is the correlation id the middleware puts in the context actually **in a log
  line**? Grep for the field inside a logging call, not for the middleware that
  sets it. *Observed (40-service monorepo): chi's `middleware.RequestID` wired
  into the chain and the structured-logger middleware that would attach it
  commented out behind a TODO. Every request carried an id; no log line had one,
  so nothing could be joined back to a request.*
- Is the message a constant with the detail in attributes, rather than an
  interpolated string? Interpolated messages cannot be grouped or alerted on.
- Does anything log a token, header, body, prompt content, or personal data?
  Check the struct fields that get passed to `slog.Any`, not just the literals.

### 6. Edge cases in the code itself
- Integer/float choice: is money a float anywhere? Is a count an `int` that can
  go negative?
- Slice and map: nil vs empty where the difference is observable (JSON output,
  `len` checks, range over nil).
- Bounds: any slicing with an index derived from input? Any `[0]` without a
  length check?
- Time: any wall-clock arithmetic across a boundary that could cross a DST
  change or a leap second? Any timeout that is not derived from the caller's
  deadline?
- Unicode: any `len(s)` used where runes were meant?

### 7. Concurrency
For **every** goroutine in the diff, answer all five. If any answer is "I'd
have to check", that is the finding.

1. Who starts it?
2. What makes it return?
3. Who waits for it?
4. What happens to it when the caller's context is cancelled?
5. Can it block forever on a send, a receive, a mutex, or a timer?

Then:
- Is the number of goroutines bounded by something that is not the size of the
  input? One goroutine per row of an untrusted file is a resource bug even if
  every goroutine eventually exits.
- Does the producer own channel closure, and is it the only closer?
- Is every blocking send or receive inside a `select` with `ctx.Done()`? A
  worker that checks the context only *before* blocking has not been cancelled.
- Is `context.Canceled` / `DeadlineExceeded` preserved rather than flattened
  into a generic error?
- `errgroup`: is the derived context actually passed into every worker, and do
  they honour it? Is there a concurrency limit where the input is unbounded?
- Are directional channel types used in signatures (`<-chan`, `chan<-`) so
  ownership is visible without reading the body?
- Is a channel being used where a mutex would be simpler, or a mutex where the
  thing being communicated is ownership or completion?
- Is `defer` inside a loop, deferring cleanup to function exit rather than
  iteration exit?
- For a long-lived consume or poll loop: does it take a `ctx` and exit on it, or
  is its only exit an internal error field? A loop nobody can stop is not shut
  down, it is abandoned at process exit. And if a DI container owns shutdown,
  you have inherited its stop timeout as your drain budget without choosing it
  (uber-go/fx defaults to 15s). Name the budget or set it.
- Where is the offset, ack or delete committed **relative to the work**? Before
  is at-most-once, after is at-least-once, and a client-library default is
  neither a choice nor a documented guarantee. *Observed: a Kafka consumer with
  no `Commit()` call anywhere in the repo — `enable.auto.commit` left at the
  librdkafka default, so offsets advanced on a 5s timer whether or not
  processing had succeeded.*
- Is there a poison-message path — bounded retries, then a dead-letter — or does
  one bad message either loop forever or take the whole consumer down with it?

### 8. Proving it — the race gate
Concurrency findings are not settled by reading. Run:

```bash
go test ./... -race -count=1
go test ./... -race -count=10 -run <TheConcurrentTest>   # repeat flushes flakiness
go test ./... -shuffle=on -count=1
```

`-race` only reports races on code paths that **execute**. If the concurrent
path has no test, `-race` passing proves nothing — say so rather than citing it.

Where timing is the behaviour, use `testing/synctest` so the assertion is exact
instead of approximate, and `go.uber.org/goleak` in `TestMain` to make a leaked
goroutine fail the suite rather than leak silently.

### 9. Consistency with what already exists
- Same error style, logger, context handling, and test shape as the
  neighbouring packages? A second convention is worse than either convention.
- Package name earns its existence — no `utils`, `common`, `helpers`, `misc`.
- No stutter: `http.Server`, not `http.HTTPServer`. No `Get` prefix on a
  plain accessor.
- Interfaces defined where they are **consumed**, small, and actually having
  more than one implementation (a test fake counts; a speculative future
  does not).
- Accept interfaces, return structs — unless returning the concrete type would
  leak an invariant.
- `ctx context.Context` first, named `ctx`, never stored in a struct, never
  carrying business parameters.
- Exported identifier without a doc comment, where its error contract or
  ownership is not obvious from the name?

### 10. The cheap Go-specific smells
Scan for these directly; they are the ones a reviewer from another language
does not flag:

- shadowed `err` inside an `if` block that the function then returns as nil
- naked return in anything longer than ten lines
- pointer to an interface in a parameter or field
- `any`/`interface{}` where a type parameter or concrete type would hold
- unnecessary `else` after `return`; nesting deeper than two
- a comment restating the syntax instead of the reason
- a struct constructor that only assigns fields
- `sync.WaitGroup` passed by value

### 11. Running in something — config, lifecycle, blast radius
The code is correct and the process still falls over. These are cheap to check
and almost never in a diff review.

**Deadline budgeting.** A service that receives a deadline and passes it
unchanged to its own dependency has not budgeted, it has forwarded. The
downstream work then finishes at the exact instant the caller stops listening,
and a partial result arrives to nobody. Ask: does each hop reserve time for the
work that happens *after* the call returns — the next hop, the merge, the
encode? A downstream deadline must be strictly smaller than the caller's, and
the reserve should be a named constant, not arithmetic buried in a call site.
Where the budget must cross a process boundary, it is an explicit protocol
element (a `budget_ms` parameter, a header), because the callee cannot read the
caller's context. Relying on the TCP disconnect is not cancellation; it is
noticing afterwards.

*Observed:* a gateway with a 700ms global timeout propagated it verbatim to an
inventory service that produced partial results at 700ms. The partial-result
design did not work at all until a 200ms reserve was carved out and the
remainder passed explicitly.

**Name the reason the deadline fired.** `context.DeadlineExceeded` cannot tell
"our own budget ran out" from "the caller hung up" from "we are shutting down",
and a degraded response that cannot name its cause is one the caller cannot act
on. Build the budget with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, budget, ErrBudgetSpent)`
and read it back with `context.Cause(ctx)` at the boundary that reports. Both are
stdlib, and the distinction is the difference between "some inventory was slow"
and "we were restarting".

**Label your partial data.** Any response assembled from incomplete inputs —
a dropped record, a timed-out leg, a served-stale cache entry, a failover —
must say so in the payload, not only in a log. A caller that cannot distinguish
"the cheapest option is 605" from "the cheapest option I could see in time is
605" will act on the wrong one. Ask: is there a `degraded` flag, a count of what
was dropped, and a note naming why? Is the flag set on *every* path that
degrades, including the cache-hit path that inherited someone else's
degradation? Silently truncating and returning 200 is the failure mode this
catches.

**Config and 12-factor.**
- Any host, port, URL, or credential literal in the code? `localhost` in a
  service that will run in a container is a defect, not a default.
- Does a missing required variable fail loudly at startup, or produce a zero
  value that fails confusingly on the first request?
- Is config read once into a struct at boot, or `os.Getenv` scattered through
  request handlers?

**Lifecycle.**
- Is there a `server.Shutdown(ctx)` on `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` with a bounded grace
  period? A container that is killed mid-request drops it.
- Do background goroutines started outside a request — refreshers, reapers,
  pollers — stop on shutdown, or does the process hang or leak?
- Are `ReadHeaderTimeout`, `ReadTimeout`, `WriteTimeout`, `IdleTimeout` set on
  every `http.Server`? The zero value is "no timeout" and is a trivial DoS.
  One exception worth knowing before you set all four everywhere: a blanket
  `WriteTimeout` truncates streaming, SSE and long-poll responses mid-flight.
  Those endpoints need their own server or a per-handler deadline.
- Is the shutdown context derived from `context.Background()`? A shutdown path
  that derives from the request context it is trying to drain is already
  cancelled, so `Shutdown` returns immediately and drops exactly the in-flight
  work it exists to protect.
- Does the client have a timeout? The zero-value `http.Client` waits forever.
- Does the health/readiness endpoint listen on its **own port**, separate from
  the traffic port? A probe served by the same mux sits behind the same
  throttle, middleware and saturation as the traffic it is meant to report on.
- Does readiness check the **dependencies**, or only that the process's own
  listener is up? A probe that reports healthy while Redis is unreachable is an
  instruction to the orchestrator to keep sending traffic to a service that
  cannot serve it. *Observed: liveness and readiness both returning a
  package-level `var errServerFailure`, written by the server goroutine and read
  by the probe goroutine with no synchronisation — a data race in the health
  path itself.*

**Blast radius.**
- Is any unbounded collection keyed on caller-controlled input? A cache, map,
  or metric label keyed on a raw query parameter grows until the process dies.
  This is the one that reads as a memory leak and is actually a remote
  resource-exhaustion vector.
- Is the container image `scratch`/`distroless`, running non-root, with no
  compiler or shell in the final layer?
- Is there a `HEALTHCHECK`, and does orchestration actually wait on it
  (`condition: service_healthy`) rather than on process start?

**A config file is not evidence a tool runs.** Before citing any repo's tooling
— including your own CI — as coverage, check three things: that a pipeline step
invokes it, that its failure fails the build, and that it is configured for this
language. *Observed in one repo, all four at once: `go vet ./... || echo "vet
reported errors"` (advisory since the day it was written), the Sonar step
commented out with a note about server maintenance, a `qodana.yaml` pinning a
**JavaScript** linter in a pure-Go monorepo, and a test-report script whose
reporting logic was commented out. Four files present, nothing enforced.*

### 12. Model boundary
Only when the diff calls a model, turns a sentence into a query, ranks or
packages from model output, or exposes a tool. Otherwise this section is not a
finding. The catalogue is go-loop's `references/llm-boundary.md`.

- Does schema-invalid or truncated model output fail the call, rather than
  decoding into a partial struct that is then treated as success?
- Is an id checked against inventory after it type-checks, before it is
  returned or booked?
- Is a parsed filter asserted against the intent, not only against a nil error?
- Is a token or cost ceiling a named cause, distinct from the request deadline
  and from a per-request 429?
- Is a side-effecting action idempotent when called twice? The test already
  lives in the Go taxonomy; this asks whether this call site has it.
- Can one booking event move a ranking or training counter twice?
- Does the tool layer refuse an out-of-scope call regardless of the argument
  text?
- Are the tests properties or contracts against a fake provider? A golden
  completion is not coverage of the ranker.

Learning a ranker from bookings is not a finding to implement. If bookings feed
a ranker, the gap to name is a double-counted event, a click that reinforces
itself, and training examples that do not match what serving saw.

---

## Output format

```
FIX NOW
  price.go:42  Parse returns nil error for "" and a zero Cents — caller cannot
               distinguish empty from free. Add ErrEmpty, test row first.
  run.go:88    Worker blocks on results <- r with no select on ctx.Done(); a
               cancelled request leaks one goroutine per in-flight item.

NOTE
  feed.go:17   Decoder allocates per row; fine at this volume, would batch above ~10k.
  enrich.go:5  No counter on the provider-failover branch. Logged, not countable.

NOT CHECKED
  The concurrent path in run.go has no test, so -race passing says nothing
  about it. Would need TestRun_CancelMidFlight before I'd believe it.
```

That last block matters more than it looks. Naming what the gate did **not**
prove is the difference between a review and a reassurance.

---

## Depth control

A full pass costs real time. Scale it:

- **Sprint / timed build** — §3, §4, §7, and, when the diff is a gateway, a
  fan-out, or a partial result, the §11 lines on deadline reserve, named cause,
  degraded flag, and blast radius. When the diff calls a model or exposes a
  tool, §12 as well. Ten minutes, maximum. Findings go to `NOTE` unless unsafe.
  Skip a queue, a container, or CI when it is not in the repo you just built.
  Do not skip a second service when the task is that service. The deadline and
  the partial result are the finding.
- **Pre-commit** — full checklist, fix-now acted on immediately.
- **Pre-PR / pre-merge** — full checklist plus `golangci-lint run`,
  `govulncheck`, and the repeat-race run.

Never run the full checklist against a diff you have not read. The checklist is
a way of reading, not a replacement for it.

package claimcheck

import (
	"cmp"
	"log/slog"
	"slices"
	"sync/atomic"
	"time"
)

// unresolvedCoords counts coordinate pairs the lookup could not place. It is a
// process counter, not a per-run one: the rate is the thing worth alerting on.
var unresolvedCoords atomic.Int64

// UnresolvedCoords is how many records carried coordinates that matched no
// known city, and so went without a location cross-check.
func UnresolvedCoords() int64 { return unresolvedCoords.Load() }

// knownFields is the set of fields the report always speaks about. A field is
// only ever "absent" relative to a list like this one — without it, a field
// nobody claimed is indistinguishable from a field nobody thought to ask about.
var knownFields = append([]string{"city", "stars", "policy.children"}, amenityFields()...)

// lastSeenLayout is the date format the scrape feed uses.
const lastSeenLayout = "2006-01-02"

// Check groups records and reports the claim status of every known field.
func Check(recs []Record, now time.Time) []Property {
	groups := groupRecords(recs)
	props := make([]Property, 0, len(groups))
	for _, g := range groups {
		p := g.property()
		claims, unparsed := extract(g.records)
		p.Findings = findings(claims, now)
		sortUnparsed(unparsed)
		countUnparsed(unparsed)
		p.Unparsed = unparsed
		props = append(props, p)
	}
	return props
}

// extract pulls every claim each record makes, and everything it published that
// this tool could not place.
func extract(recs []Record) ([]Claim, []Unparsed) {
	var claims []Claim
	var unparsed []Unparsed
	for _, rec := range recs {
		claims = append(claims, cityClaims(rec)...)
		claims = append(claims, starClaims(rec)...)

		policy, proseUnparsed := policyClaims(rec)
		claims = append(claims, policy...)
		unparsed = append(unparsed, proseUnparsed...)

		amenities, facilityUnparsed := amenityClaims(rec)
		claims = append(claims, amenities...)
		unparsed = append(unparsed, facilityUnparsed...)

		unparsed = append(unparsed, unknownFieldUnparsed(rec)...)
	}
	return claims, unparsed
}

// cityClaims are what a record says, and what its coordinates imply, about
// which city the property is in.
//
// The coordinate claim is attributed to "derived:coords" rather than to the
// feed, so that a record contradicting itself produces two comparable claims.
// Attributing both to the feed would make the contradiction invisible: one
// source, no disagreement, reported as supported.
func cityClaims(rec Record) []Claim {
	observed := observedAt(rec)
	var out []Claim

	if rec.City != "" {
		out = append(out, Claim{
			Field: "city", Value: rec.City,
			Source: rec.Source + "/city", ObservedAt: observed,
		})
	}
	if city := locationCity(rec); city != "" {
		out = append(out, Claim{
			Field: "city", Value: city,
			Source: rec.Source + "/location", ObservedAt: observed,
		})
	}
	if rec.Coords != nil {
		// A coordinate outside the lookup asserts nothing. Naming the nearest
		// entry regardless of distance would manufacture a conflict.
		city, ok := nearestCity(*rec.Coords)
		if !ok {
			// This is the report's one silent degradation: a property whose
			// location is never cross-checked looks the same as one that was
			// checked and agreed. Counting it is how a lookup that has fallen
			// behind the feed becomes visible instead of just quiet.
			slog.Warn("coordinates matched no known city; location left unchecked",
				"source", rec.Source, "name", recordName(rec),
				"lat", rec.Coords.Lat, "lng", rec.Coords.Lng)
			unresolvedCoords.Add(1)
		} else {
			out = append(out, Claim{
				Field: "city", Value: city,
				Source: "derived:coords", ObservedAt: observed,
			})
		}
	}
	return out
}

// locationCity is the city half of a joined "City, Country" location string.
func locationCity(rec Record) string {
	if rec.City != "" || rec.Location == "" {
		return ""
	}
	return statedCity(rec)
}

// observedAt is when the feed says it saw this, or the zero time when it does
// not say. Zero is "unknown", never "now": treating an undated record as fresh
// is how three-year-old data gets presented as current.
func observedAt(rec Record) time.Time {
	if rec.LastSeen == "" {
		return time.Time{}
	}
	t, err := time.Parse(lastSeenLayout, rec.LastSeen)
	if err != nil {
		// An unparseable date is not a reason to drop the record's claims, and
		// it is not a reason to call them fresh. It is unknown, like no date.
		return time.Time{}
	}
	return t
}

// findings reports every known field, including the ones nobody claimed.
func findings(claims []Claim, now time.Time) []Finding {
	byField := map[string][]Claim{}
	for _, c := range claims {
		byField[c.Field] = append(byField[c.Field], c)
	}

	out := make([]Finding, 0, len(knownFields))
	for _, field := range knownFields {
		fieldClaims := byField[field]
		slices.SortFunc(fieldClaims, func(a, b Claim) int {
			return cmp.Or(cmp.Compare(a.Source, b.Source), cmp.Compare(a.Value, b.Value))
		})
		out = append(out, Finding{
			Field:     field,
			Status:    statusOf(fieldClaims),
			Staleness: stalenessOf(fieldClaims, now),
			Claims:    fieldClaims,
		})
	}
	return out
}

// statusOf counts distinct values, not claims: two feeds agreeing is stronger
// support, never a conflict.
func statusOf(claims []Claim) Status {
	if len(claims) == 0 {
		return Absent
	}
	values := map[string]bool{}
	for _, c := range claims {
		values[c.Value] = true
	}
	if len(values) > 1 {
		return Conflict
	}
	return Supported
}

// stalenessOf reports on the freshest observation behind the claims, and
// distinguishes "we know it is old" from "no feed told us how old it is".
func stalenessOf(claims []Claim, now time.Time) Staleness {
	var newest time.Time
	for _, c := range claims {
		if c.ObservedAt.After(newest) {
			newest = c.ObservedAt
		}
	}
	if newest.IsZero() {
		return Unknown
	}
	if now.Sub(newest) > FreshWindow {
		return Stale
	}
	return Fresh
}

Trigger: `/graphify`\nWhen the user types `/graphify`, invoke the Skill tool with `skill: \"graphify\"` before doing anything else.\n\n## graphify (per-project usage)\n\nIf the current project contains a `graphify-out/` directory with a `graph.json`, treat it as a queryable knowledge graph for that codebase.\n\nRules:\n- For codebase questions, when graphify-out/graph.json exists. **Feed it SYMBOL NAMES, not sentences** — query keyword-matches your string against node names, so a natural-language question latches onto its most generic noun and BFS-floods with noise (verified on Orbit 2026-07-28: \"how are organisation permissions resolved for a user\" returned 35 mostly-test nodes and missed `PermissionsService` entirely; `query \"PermissionsService GetOrganisationPermissions\"` returned 8 exact nodes with line numbers). So: `explain \"<Symbol>\"` first when you know the name (file:line + its members), `query \"<Symbol> <member>\"` to widen, `path \"<A>\" \"<B>\"` for relationships (hit-or-miss — silently returns \"no path\" when there isn't a direct structural edge). Fall back to Grep only when you don't have a symbol name to start from. Read GRAPH_REPORT.md only for whole-architecture questions.\n- If graphify-out/wiki/index.md exists, use it for broad navigation instead of raw source browsing.\n- Read graphify-out/GRAPH_REPORT.md only for broad architecture review or when query/path/explain do not surface enough context.\n- After modifying code, run `graphify update .` to keep the graph current (AST-only, no API cost).\n- If no `graphify-out/` exists in the project, ignore all of the above and use Grep/Read as normal.\n\n# Design / UI work — choose the design tool first\nWhen a task involves building or reworking UI (components, pages, screens, design systems), BEFORE generating code:\n1. Briefly state which design tool you'd use and why, and offer the alternative so I can choose. Don't silently pick one.\n2. The two options (use either, or combine them):\n   - **`frontend-design`** (Anthropic official skill) — best for *web* UIs where the priority is a distinctive, polished, non-generic look. Default for React / Next.js / Tailwind components and pages.\n   - **`ui-ux-pro-max`** (community plugin) — best when I need a specific style system (glassmorphism, bento, neumorphism, etc.), curated palettes / font pairings / charts, or **non-web stacks: Flutter, SwiftUI, React Native, Jetpack Compose**, or shadcn/ui component search.\n3. Rule of thumb: web polish → `frontend-design`; broad design-system menu or Flutter/mobile → `ui-ux-pro-max`; large feature → suggest `ui-ux-pro-max` for the system + `frontend-design` for final polish. Always let me confirm before proceeding.\n\n# Prose / writing — apply Stop Slop\nWhen you draft or substantially edit human-facing prose — READMEs, docs, PR/commit descriptions, Slack/announcement text, reports — apply the `stop-slop` skill before finalizing.\nDo NOT apply it to: code, code comments, terse chat replies, or tool output. Keep it scoped to prose deliverables so it adds no per-turn token overhead.\n\n# Advisor mode (how to talk to me)\nYou are not my assistant. You are my advisor who happens to be smarter than me. Calibrate hard, flatter never.\n1. Challenge when warranted: open by surfacing the flaw, the missing piece, or a question that exposes a gap. When I'm actually right, don't manufacture an objection — confirm it with a confidence tag and spend the opening on the non-obvious caveat or risk.\n2. Tag confidence before any claim: [Certain] = hard evidence, [Likely] = strong inference, [Guessing] = filling gaps. If most of the reply is guess, say so first.\n3. Banned openers — delete and rewrite if one appears: \"Great question\", \"You're absolutely right\", \"That makes a lot of sense\", \"Absolutely\", \"Definitely\".\n4. Disagree with structure: \"I disagree because [reason]. Here's what I'd do instead [alternative]. The risk in your approach is [specific downside].\"\n5. Uncomfortable truth first — first line, not buried in paragraph three.\n6. No warm-up paragraphs. Start with the most useful thing you can say.\n7. Don't fold to social pressure; DO update on better logic or evidence. \"But I really think\" is not a reason — a stronger argument is.\nScope: these rules govern how you talk to me in conversation, not the tone of artifacts you produce for others (docs, PRs, emails, reports) unless I ask.\n\n# Reframe my tasks into goal / done / loop (act, don't just chat)\nBefore acting on any **non-trivial** request, silently recast it — this is the \"write a better prompt to myself\" step:\n- **Goal** — the outcome I actually want, not the literal wording.\n- **Done when** — concrete, checkable signal(s): named tests green, build/LSP clean, a `graphify query` returns X, a screenshot shows Y, a repro stops reproducing. If you can't name at least one check, that's the smell — the task is underspecified.\n- **Loop** — iterate against those checks until they pass or you're genuinely blocked.\n\nRules:\n1. **Threshold — don't do this for everything.** Full reframe only for multi-step work, ~3+ files, refactors with a coherent end state, or anything where \"what exactly should this do?\" is the hard part. Trivial / lookup / one-line asks: just do them, no ceremony, no clarifying questions.\n2. **Show it briefly** (≤6 lines) before or as you start, so I can catch a wrong target early. Not a wall of text.\n3. **Ask only when the target is genuinely ambiguous** — i.e. you can't write a verifiable \"Done when\" without guessing. Then ask me first (AskUserQuestion). If you can infer a sensible target, state the assumption in one line and proceed.\n4. **Then plan + execute as already configured:** spec.md + plan.md for 4+ files (persist them, show the plan, wait for OK); `/delegate` the read-/edit-heavy body to cheap models; keep Opus for the spec and the review gate; verify against the Done-when with an independent checker (maker ≠ checker) before claiming done.\n5. **Cost guard.** Never loop Opus without an oracle. Berlin city vs the Munich coordinates\n> 2. adults-only vs kids club\n> 3. 4 stars vs 3 stars on the Rimini pair\n> 4. pool vs the August review, and keep the 2023 last_seen as stale\n>\n> Let me know if you have a better idea or you disagree or you think I missed smth\n> and we need to add or remove anything\n\nThree disagreements came back, and I took all three:\n\n- **My case 1 would have silently passed.** Only one source says anything about\n  City Lodge Berlin's location, so a claim check comparing sources sees no\n  disagreement and reports `supported`. It needed coordinates to emit a *derived*\n  claim, and claims to be keyed on `(feed, field-path)` rather than on the feed,\n  so a record can contradict itself. A source saying \"no restaurant\"\n  is `supported (false)`, not `absent`.\n\nIt also said I had missed two of the six: the Alpenhof null-vs-prose case (added\nas case 5) and currency (dropped, with an argument — the two prices are on\ndifferent properties, so a claim check structurally cannot see the conflict).\nAnd it corrected my framing: this surfaces the defects, it does not fix them.\n\n## 3 — Go\n\n> ok, let's focus on what we can build and test first, we can come back to the\n> contradictions later and think how to resolve them.\n> go, remember we have go skills go-loop and review, tdd and rules\n\nBuilt end to end first, then one case at a time, failing test before\nimplementation each time.
