      "path": "userSettings:hour-build",
      "content": "Base directory for this skill: /Users/yuratestdev/.claude/skills/hour-build\n\n# hour-build\n\nThe exercise is not \"write the best code you can in an hour\". It is **\"show how\nyou decide under a constraint\"**. The reader gets 15 minutes with the repo and\nthen 30 minutes with you. Almost everything that scores happens in\n`DECISIONS.md` and in the shape of the commits, not in the code's polish.\n\nThe single most common way to fail: run out of clock at 70% of an ambitious\ndesign, push something that does not run, and spend the call explaining what it\nwould have done.\n\n---\n\n## Before the clock starts (does not count as work)\n\nDo this the day before, not in the window:\n\n- Create the **empty public repo**. Name it neutrally. One commit: a `README.md`\n  stub and `.gitignore`. Nothing task-shaped — you do not know the task yet, and\n  anything that looks pre-built poisons the whole submission.\n- Confirm `git push` works to it with no auth prompt.\n- Confirm the toolchain: `go version`, `go test ./...` in a scratch module,\n  editor and terminal already open.\n- **Warm the module cache.** The test libraries the loop can ask for are not in\n  a fresh cache, and a download at T+30 on venue wifi is a dead stop:\n\n  ```bash\n  cd $(mktemp -d) && go mod init warm && go get \\\n    github.com/google/go-cmp/cmp pgregory.net/rapid go.uber.org/goleak\n  ```\n\n  This primes `~/go/pkg/mod`; your own `go.mod` is untouched. Warming is not\n  planning to use them. `go-cmp` is near-certain — `go-loop` Phase 2 mandates\n  `cmp.Diff`. `rapid` and `goleak` are conditional and each is a dependency you\n  have to defend on the call: `goleak` only if you spawn a goroutine, `rapid`\n  only if an invariant genuinely will not fit a table. A hand-rolled loop over\n  fifty constructed candidates is the same property test, reads clearer to a\n  reviewer who does not know the library, and adds nothing to `go.mod`. The\n  invariant is the deliverable, not the framework that checks it.\n- Have a `DECISIONS.md` heading skeleton in your head (below), not in the repo.\n- Decide the commit cadence: **roughly every 8–10 minutes, always green or\n  explicitly marked WIP.** This is the part that reads as an honest hour.\n\nIf a rule anywhere says \"commits after the mark are ignored by timestamp\":\npush **before** the mark, not at it. A push that starts at T+60 finishes after\nit.\n\nTwo mechanics behind that rule, because they cut in opposite directions. Git\nstamps the author date at `commit` time, not at push — so an on-time commit\npushed a few minutes late is still on time by the letter of the rule. Do not\nlet a slow push talk you out of a commit at T+57. But `git commit --amend` and\nany rebase **rewrite the committer date**, so a tidy-up amend at T+61 can\nretroactively stamp your honest hour as late. **No amends and no rebases after\nT+50.** Whatever is committed is what you push.\n\n---\n\n## The clock\n\nAnchor everything to T+0 = the moment the task email lands. Write the wall-clock\ntimes down before starting.\n\n| | Window | Output |\n|---|---|---|\n| **T+0 → T+10** | Read the data and the brief | A written list of what is in the data and what is wrong with it |\n| **T+10 → T+20** | `DECISIONS.md`, first draft | Scope, cut line, approach — committed |\n| **T+20 → T+50** | Build | 3–4 commits, tests on the one hard thing |\n| **T+50 → T+55** | Review pass + `DECISIONS.md` final | Honest gaps section |\n| **T+55 → T+60** | Push, verify the public URL loads | Link sent |\n\nSay the current phase out loud at each boundary. When a phase overruns, take the\ntime out of **build**, never out of `DECISIONS.md` or the push.\n\nThe table is a ceiling, not a quota. The hour is the latest you may push.\nQuality is the thing being graded, and padding a five-minute task out to thirty\nis the over-build failure in disguise. If the brief is small, do it properly\nand push early: data, `DECISIONS.md`, RED then green on the one hard behaviour,\nthe gate, the review, Known gaps. Do not invent a second feature so the log\nlooks long. Do not skip those steps because the task was short, either. A fast\nsolution with no failing test and no named gap is unfinished in the way that\nreads as dishonest.\n\n**When the brief suggests its own split, it will not have a review window.** A\nbrief that says \"~10 on the data, ~10 on DECISIONS.md, ~35 building, ~5 to\npush\" has handed the review's five minutes to build. Take them back. The review\npass is what produces the Known gaps section, and a silent gap is the one\nfailure mode below that reads as dishonest rather than incomplete. Five more\nminutes of code and no review is more built and worse submitted. That does not\nmean build for thirty minutes. It means do not spend the review's time on\nanother feature.\n\n### T+0 → T+10 — the data\nDo not open an editor. Look at the actual dataset:\n\n```bash\nhead -5 <file>; wc -l <file>\n# for CSV/JSON: count distinct values, find the nulls, find the duplicates\n```\n\nWrite down, in `DECISIONS.md` notes: the row count, the fields, the ones that\nare malformed or missing, the encoding or locale traps (decimal commas, dates,\nmixed currencies), and the one thing about the data that is not obvious from\nthe brief. **Finding a defect in their dataset and saying so is worth more than\na fourth feature.** They almost always plant one.\n\n### T+10 → T+20 — DECISIONS.md\nWrite it **before** the code, not after. It is the primary artifact.\n\n```markdown\n# Decisions\n\n## What I read in the data\n<3–5 bullets, including the defect you found>\n\n## What I'm building\n<one paragraph, the smallest thing that answers the brief end to end>\n\n## What I'm deliberately not building\n- <thing> — because <reason>, would take <estimate>\n- <thing> — because it does not change the answer\n\n## Choices and why\n| Choice | Took | Rejected | Because |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| ... | ... | ... | ... |\n\n## What I'd do with the next hour\n<ordered, specific>\n\n## Known gaps\n<what is untested, what would break, what I'd check first in prod>\n```\n\nCommit it immediately. A timestamped `DECISIONS.md` at T+18 proves the thinking\ncame first.\n\n### T+20 → T+50 — build\nHand off to `module-loop` and `go-loop`. This skill decides the SCOPE; the\nlanguage loop keeps its full depth (RED before green, mutation on every guard,\nthe gate) on whatever scope you hand it. Cut the number of things you build,\nnever the verification of the things you built. Constraints:\n\n- **End to end before deep.** A pipeline that reads the file, does the simplest\n  correct thing, and prints an answer — at T+35 — is the floor. Only then go\n  back and make one part good. Never leave the last stage unwritten.\n- **Test one thing properly, smoke-test the rest.** Pick the function where\n  correctness is genuinely hard — the parser, the dedupe, the aggregation —\n  and give it a failure-rows-first table test. Testing everything shallowly\n  scores lower than testing the hard thing convincingly. If a model is in the\n  path, the hard thing is the boundary in go-loop's `references/llm-boundary.md`\n  (a schema-valid result that is the wrong trip, an id not in inventory, a tool\n  call out of scope), tested as a property against a fake provider. A golden\n  completion is the smoke test.\n- **No framework, no DI container, no interface with one implementation, no\n  config system, no Dockerfile** unless the brief asks. Each one is a decision\n  you now have to defend and it bought nothing.\n- **Keep the suite under about five seconds.** You will run it twenty times,\n  and every mutation in Phase 5b runs it again. A fixture that pays a simulated\n  timeout on each iteration turns a property test into minutes of dead clock.\n  Ask what the test is actually about: if it is about a filter, an ordering or\n  an invariant, the fixture's latencies should be trivial, and the one test\n  that is about the deadline pays the deadline once. *Observed (ygo-core): a\n  50-iteration property test inherited an 800ms row from the dataset and took\n  30 seconds; the same property with 1ms fixtures took under one.*\n- **Structured logging and one counter on the degradation path** cost about two\n  minutes and are the cheapest senior signal available. `log/slog`, JSON\n  handler, warn + count where you drop or skip a row.\n- Concurrency only if the data volume actually demands it. An unnecessary\n  worker pool in a 60-minute exercise is the clearest possible signal that\n  someone optimises before measuring. If you do use one, it is bounded and it\n  honours the context — see `go-review` §7.\n- Commit at each module boundary. `git log` is read, so it is an artifact: use\n  conventional prefixes so the shape of the hour is legible at a glance.\n\n  | Prefix | For |\n  |---|---|\n  | `docs:` | `DECISIONS.md`, README, the gaps write-up |\n  | `test:` | the RED commit — failing tests, before the implementation |\n  | `feat:` | the GREEN commit and each capability after it |\n  | `fix:` | something that was wrong and now is not |\n  | `refactor:` | shape change, no behaviour change |\n  | `chore:` | module init, gitignore, tooling |\n\n  Short and specific, imperative, no trailing period, no body unless it carries\n  a decision the subject cannot. `test: failing cases for activity degradation\n  and the destination invariant` reads as an hour; `wip` and `more stuff` read\n  as a scramble. The RED-then-GREEN pair is the single most legible thing in\n  the log — do not squash it away.\n\n### T+50 → T+55 — the review pass\n`go-review` at sprint depth: §3 happy path, §4 errors, §7 concurrency. When\nthe thing you built is a gateway, a fan-out, or a partial result, also the §11\nlines on deadline reserve, named cause, degraded flag, and blast radius. When\nit calls a model or exposes a tool, §12 as well. Five minutes. Findings go\ninto `DECISIONS.md` under **Known gaps** unless something is actually broken.\n\nThe sprint profile used to skip every line that named a second service. That\ndrops §11 on the brief where §11 is the work. A second service is in scope\nwhen the brief is the integration.\n\nRun the gate and paste nothing, but check it:\n\n```bash\ngofmt -l . && go vet ./... && go test ./... -race -count=1\n```\n\nIf a test is red at T+52, either fix it in two minutes or **mark it skipped\nwith a comment saying why and put it in Known gaps.** Do not push a red suite\nwithout saying so in the README.\n\n### T+55 → T+60 — push\n```bash\ngit add -A && git commit -m \"...\" && git push\n```\nThen open the public URL and confirm it renders. A private repo is a failed\nsubmission. Send the link.\n\n---\n\n## What goes in the repo, and what does not\n\nThe submission is an engineering artifact. It carries decisions about the\nproblem, the data and the code. It carries **nothing about the tooling that\nproduced it** — no phase names, no `T+` markers, no skill or checklist names,\nno \"the mutation pass found\", no notes on how long a step took. A reader who\nopens `DECISIONS.md` should see an engineer's reasoning about bundling and\ndeadlines, not a process log. `T+0 = 16:10` at the top of the file is for the\nauthor and belongs in a scratch note, not in the commit.\n\nThe same goes for the findings themselves. \"Deleting the context case makes the\nengine return a cheaper package outside the SLA\" is an excellent line in the\nrepo — it is a fact about the code. \"Phase 5b mutation caught this\" is the same\nfact wearing a process badge, and it invites questions about the process\ninstead of the engineering.\n\nRunning commentary to the operator — which tool misbehaved, how much clock is\nleft, whether a skill fired correctly — is for the terminal, and only when\nasked. It never reaches the repo.\n\nThe exception is the call, below. **How you worked with Claude is question 3\nand they asked for it**, so it gets a real, specific, spoken answer. Spoken —\nnot a section in `DECISIONS.md`.\n\n---\n\n## What the 30-minute call actually asks\n\nPrepare these four answers while building, not after:\n\n1. **What did you pick and why?** — the table in `DECISIONS.md` is the script.\n2. **What did you reject?** — the \"not building\" list. Have a real estimate for\n   each, and know which one you would do first.\n3. **How did you work with Claude?** — the honest version. What you delegated,\n   what you checked, where it was wrong and how you caught it. The failure you\n   caught is worth more than the throughput. If a hook or a checklist blocked\n   something, say which and show it.\n4. **What would break in production?** — the Known gaps section, plus the one\n   thing you did not have time to instrument.\n\nDo not claim production experience you do not have. The build in front of them\nis the evidence; anything you assert beyond it invites a question you cannot\nanswer, and the cost of being caught overclaiming is total.\n\n---\n\n## The failure modes, ranked\n\n1. Nothing runs. Everything else is worse than this only in theory.\n2. Pushed after the mark, or pushed private.\n3. No `DECISIONS.md`, or one written after the code as a summary.\n4. Over-built: abstraction layers, interfaces, config, concurrency the problem\n   did not ask for. Reads as inability to judge scope.\n5. Silent gaps — untested, unhandled, or known-broken things not written down.\n   This is the only one that reads as dishonest rather than incomplete.\n\n\nARGUMENTS: 60-minute timed exercise: hotel data normalisation from /Users/yuratestdev/Downloads/hotels.json. Phase 1 = 10 min defect analysis, no code. Then user picks ONE feature."
    }
  ]
}

    "- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions (\"Can Claude...\", \"Does Claude...\", \"How do I...\") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)",
    "- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)",
    "- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: \"medium\" for moderate exploration, \"very thorough\" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)",
    "- feature-dev:code-architect: Designs feature architectures by analyzing existing codebase patterns and conventions, then providing comprehensive implementation blueprints with specific files to create/modify, component designs, data flows, and build sequences (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)",
    "- feature-dev:code-explorer: Deeply analyzes existing codebase features by tracing execution paths, mapping architecture layers, understanding patterns and abstractions, and documenting dependencies to inform new development (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)",
    "- feature-dev:code-reviewer: Reviews code for bugs, logic errors, security vulnerabilities, code quality issues, and adherence to project conventions, using confidence-based filtering to report only high-priority issues that truly matter (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)",
    "- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)",
    "- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)",
    "- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See \"When to invoke\" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)",
    "- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.\n\nExamples:\n\n<example>\nContext: The assistant has just implemented a new feature that adds user authentication to an API endpoint.\nuser: \"Please add authentication to the /api/users endpoint\"\nassistant: \"I've implemented the authentication for the /api/users endpoint. Here's the code:\"\n<function call omitted for brevity>\n<commentary>\nSince a logical chunk of code has been written (authentication feature), use the Task tool to launch the code-simplifier agent to improve the code's clarity and maintainability while preserving functionality.\n</commentary>\nassistant: \"Now let me use the code-simplifier agent to refine this implementation for better clarity and maintainability\"\n</example>\n\n<example>\nContext: The assistant has just fixed a bug by adding several conditional checks.\nuser: \"Fix the null pointer exception in the data processor\"\nassistant: \"I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:\"\n<function call omitted for brevity>\n<commentary>\nAfter modifying code to fix a bug, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the fix follows best practices and maintains code quality.\n</commentary>\nassistant: \"Let me refine this bug fix using the code-simplifier agent to ensure it follows our best practices\"\n</example>\n\n<example>\nContext: The assistant has just refactored a function to improve performance.\nuser: \"Optimize the data sorting algorithm for better performance\"\nassistant: \"I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:\"\n<function call omitted for brevity>\n<commentary>\nAfter completing a performance optimization task, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and maintainable.\n</commentary>\nassistant: \"Now I'll use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and follows our coding standards\"\n</example> (Tools: All tools)",
    "- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See \"When to invoke\" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)",
    "- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See \"When to invoke\" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)",
    "- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:\\n\\n<example>\\nContext: Daisy has just finished implementing a new feature that fetches data from an API with fallback behavior.\\nDaisy: \"I've added error handling to the API client. Can you review it?\"\\nAssistant: \"Let me use the silent-failure-hunter agent to thoroughly examine the error handling in your changes.\"\\n<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>\\n</example>\\n\\n<example>\\nContext: Daisy has created a PR with changes that include try-catch blocks.\\nDaisy: \"Please review PR #1234\"\\nAssistant: \"I'll use the silent-failure-hunter agent to check for any silent failures or inadequate error handling in this PR.\"\\n<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>\\n</example>\\n\\n<example>\\nContext: Daisy has just refactored error handling code.\\nDaisy: \"I've updated the error handling in the authentication module\"\\nAssistant: \"Let me proactively use the silent-failure-hunter agent to ensure the error handling changes don't introduce silent failures.\"\\n<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>\\n</example> (Tools: All tools)",
    "- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See \"When to invoke\" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)",
    "- scout: Read-only codebase explorer. Use for \"where / how / why\" questions, tracing execution paths, or locating code WITHOUT pulling files into the main thread. graphify-first; returns a tight brief with file:line pointers, plus verbatim edit-ready anchors when the caller is about to change code. Never raw file dumps. Runs on Sonnet to keep delegation cheap. (Tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob)",
    "- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)"

  "addedBlocks": [
    "## atlassian\nUse getTeamworkGraphContext when retrieving or reasoning about relationships and connections between Atlassian entities - such as work items, people, teams, goals, projects, or third-party objects. Do not use Teamwork Graph tools for basic CRUD operations. After calling getTeamworkGraphContext, call getTeamworkGraphObject on key linked entities to retrieve richer detail.",
    "## claude-in-chrome\n**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**\n\nStart a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:\n\nToolSearch with query \"select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp\"\n\nAdd task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.",
    "## firecrawl\nExecution with firecrawl_scrape alexandria uses requestId; reuse the returned ID for retries of the same payload, never a new ID to bypass a pending or uncertain 409. Firecrawl provides web search, page retrieval, site URL discovery, multi-page collection, structured page data, monitoring, and multi-source research that returns structured data. Match the requested operation to the tool boundary: firecrawl_scrape retrieves one supplied page and can return JSON matching a supplied schema, firecrawl_map enumerates URLs under a site without retrieving their content, and firecrawl_agent runs multi-source research and returns structured data when the URLs are not known or the answer spans several sites (an entity plus its fields, a list, a dataset); its result is read with firecrawl_agent_status. For biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature, the firecrawl_research_* tools search a paper index of abstracts and full text; firecrawl_search with categories: [\"research\"] is a website filter over ordinary web results and reaches different sources. For a programming question — code behaviour, a library or framework, an API contract, an error message, or a known bug — firecrawl_developer_search (or firecrawl_search with categories: [\"developer\"]) searches an index of repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and curated documentation sites. Authenticated firecrawl_search returns web results together with matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. Alexandria is Firecrawl's catalogue of data providers and workflows across companies, people, jobs, finance and filings, public records and government spending, real estate, places and restaurants, retail and prices, package registries and developer data, news, research, and more; providers return typed, sourced records through published contracts. When a provider matches, prefer it over scraping pages if the task needs the same fields across several entities, provenance, exact figures or timestamps, or a large set of records; execute it through fire… [truncated]",
    "## perplexity\nPerplexity AI server for web-grounded search, research, and reasoning, backed by the Perplexity Agent API. Use perplexity_search for finding URLs, facts, and recent news. Supports recency filters and domain restrictions. Use perplexity_ask for quick AI-answered questions with citations. Supports recency filters, domain restrictions, and search context size control. Use perplexity_research for in-depth multi-source investigation (slow, can take minutes). Use perplexity_reason for complex analysis requiring step-by-step logic. Supports recency filters, domain restrictions, and search context size control. All tools are read-only and access live web data.",
    "## plugin:context7:context7\nUse this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.\n\nDo not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts."
  ],
  "removedNames": []
}

  "content": "- analyze-video: Analyze a local video file or URL by extracting frames + transcribing audio, then reasoning over them. Use when the user shares a video path or link and wants it \"watched\" — summarized, described, or a specific moment found.\n- delegate: Offload read-heavy, search-heavy, or mechanical work to cheap (Haiku/Sonnet) subagents that return tight summaries, keeping the main Opus thread's context small and the cost down. Use when a task involves reading many files, broad codebase search, bulk mechanical edits, or any multi-file feature where the main thread would otherwise accumulate large context. Trigger: /delegate\n- estimate-tickets: Estimate unestimated Jira tickets in Fibonacci story points (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13). Use when the user asks to estimate, point, or size a backlog/sprint subset — e.g. \"estimate the Orbit tickets in To Do\", \"point the APOS backlog\", \"/estimate-tickets\". Auto-discovers the correct Story Points field per Atlassian site, calibrates against already-estimated tickets in the same scope, skips Epics/UXD/Spikes by default, flags duplicates, and always asks the user to confirm the proposed table before writing to Jira.\n- evolve: Complete context for the Evolve Cloud Platform contractor engagement (VR headset with clinical-grade biosensing, AWS platform, Sept 15 / Oct 6 releases). Use for any question about Evolve — their architecture, their product docs, the case-study exercise, Andy's answers, our proposed design, the five decisions, C1–C4 deep dives, open questions — and when preparing, checking or updating any Evolve document. Trigger on \"Evolve\", \"Andy\", \"Rupert\", \"Assessment v1\", \"the case study\", or during a live Evolve interview.\n- explainer: Write long technical explanations that read like a person teaching, not a system describing. Use for longreads, theory docs, architecture walkthroughs, onboarding guides, presentation notes, deep-dive artifacts, checkpoint write-ups, and any \"explain this in depth\" or \"give me the theory behind it\" request. Runs after stop-slop, never instead of it. Not for short messages or chat replies.\n- go-loop: The execution loop for writing, changing or reviewing Go. Enumerate the failure taxonomy, write the failing failure-mode tests first, take the minimal green, instrument every path that can go wrong, then pass a fixed verification gate. Use whenever a task touches .go files, a go.mod, a Go service, goroutines, channels, contexts, slog, table tests, go test, go vet, golangci-lint, testcontainers, or a Go take-home or pairing exercise.\n- go-review: Review Go code against a fixed checklist before moving on — testability, TDD coverage of failure modes, happy path, logging, code quality, edge cases, race safety, goroutine and channel correctness, consistency with the patterns already in the repo, and, when a model or tool is in the diff, the model boundary. Use at a module boundary, before a commit or PR, after a chunk of Go is written, or when asked to review Go, find code smells, or check whether a function does what it is supposed to. Produces findings with a fix-now / note-it split, not a wall of suggestions.\n- graphify: any input (code, docs, papers, images, videos) to knowledge graph. Use when user asks any question about a codebase, documents, or project content - especially if graphify-out/ exists, treat the question as a /graphify query.\n- hour-build: Run a hard-timed build exercise — a 60-minute interview case study, a take-home with a clock, a demo with a deadline — where an unfinished honest result beats a polished late one. Use when a task arrives with a stated time limit, a dataset plus a brief, a \"push to a public repo by X\" instruction, or when the user says they are starting a timed exercise. Fires on the words practice interview, mock interview, interview session, technical test, take-home, case study, timed exercise, or any stated duration (\"an hour\", \"60 minutes\", \"90 min\") — including when the task is also a coding task in a specific language, in which case this skill loads FIRST and decides how much to attempt, while the language loop keeps full verification depth on whatever is attempted. Owns the clock, the DECISIONS.md deliverable, the commit cadence that proves the work happened inside the window, and the list of things to deliberately not build.\n- module-loop: Build a multi-part change as a sequence of small modules with a review gate between each one. Use when a task needs planning before code — a feature spanning several files, a service from scratch, a take-home or case study, a refactor with a coherent end state, or any request that names more than one moving part. Also use when asked to \"plan this\", \"break this down\", \"build it module by module\", or when the work is large enough that finishing one piece changes what the next piece should be. Carries an explicit time budget so the loop cannot eat the whole clock.\n- stop-slop: Remove AI writing patterns from prose. Use when drafting, editing, or reviewing text to eliminate predictable AI tells.\n- suite-review: Code-review a pull request in a Blüm \"*-suite\" template repo — hom-suite (Verbo), mersey-burns-suite, apos-suite (AccentPOS), taihona-suite. These share one Lerna monorepo shape: packages/apis (Hasura metadata + SQL migrations), packages/services/webhook (Fastify/TS service Hasura calls into), packages/apps/core (CRA React + Apollo + typed-graphqlify). Trigger with /timesheet-month, optionally \"/timesheet-month last-month\" or \"/timesheet-month 2026-04\".\n- timesheet-week: Generate and submit a weekly work-hours report. Applies Confluence semantics and safe write rules.\n- twg-context-discovery: Use with root `twg` for deep context, dependency maps, related entities, project-to-repo discovery, OOO catch-ups, and \"catch me up\" requests around a concrete anchor.\n- twg-engineering-work: Use with root `twg` for code search, repositories using an API/package, implementation and reverse-dependency discovery, PR status and reviews, repo contributors, hot areas, and issue-to-PR lookups.\n- twg-jira: Use with root `twg` for Jira workitems, similar issue discovery, duplicate detection, projects, boards, sprints, fields, transitions, comments, links, and administration. Dry-run single items, lists, boards, sprints, epics, or projects by matching Jira keys/titles to merged PRs, repos, Rovo/search-code hits, and assignee activity.\n- twg-operational-health: Use with the root `twg` skill for on-call handoffs, incident response and investigation, post-incident reviews, reliability reviews, Assets refresh, capacity views, meeting summaries, and operational risk readouts.\n- twg-responsibility-routing: Use with root `twg` to route owners, subject-matter experts, maintainers, reviewers, approvers, decision authorities, Heads of Engineering, or escalation paths for a topic, area, ask, project, service, or component.\n- twg-status-rollups: Use with root `twg` for status rollups, personal work summaries, and decision-readiness or go/no-go briefs. This is a calibration layer, not a style generator: the marker count scales with message length, from near zero in a short ping to three or four in a long Slack message. Research + shortlist only — never installs.\n- checkpoint: Save a semantic, task-scoped checkpoint before /clear so the next session reloads only the relevant one.\n- spec-loop: Spec-driven loop — reframe a task into goal/done/loop, spec+plan, delegate the build to cheap models, verify against an oracle, Opus review gate. #635 ATTACHMENT · 2026-09-22T12:21:07.729Z
{
  "type": "mcp_instructions_delta",
  "addedNames": [
    "firecrawl",
    "perplexity",
    "plugin:context7:context7"
  ],
  "addedBlocks": [
    "## firecrawl\nExecution with firecrawl_scrape alexandria uses requestId; reuse the returned ID for retries of the same payload, never a new ID to bypass a pending or uncertain 409. Firecrawl provides web search, page retrieval, site URL discovery, multi-page collection, structured page data, monitoring, and multi-source research that returns structured data. Match the requested operation to the tool boundary: firecrawl_scrape retrieves one supplied page and can return JSON matching a supplied schema, firecrawl_map enumerates URLs under a site without retrieving their content, and firecrawl_agent runs multi-source research and returns structured data when the URLs are not known or the answer spans several sites (an entity plus its fields, a list, a dataset); its result is read with firecrawl_agent_status. For biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature, the firecrawl_research_* tools search a paper index of abstracts and full text; firecrawl_search with categories: [\"research\"] is a website filter over ordinary web results and reaches different sources. For a programming question — code behaviour, a library or framework, an API contract, an error message, or a known bug — firecrawl_developer_search (or firecrawl_search with categories: [\"developer\"]) searches an index of repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and curated documentation sites. Authenticated firecrawl_search returns web results together with matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. Alexandria is Firecrawl's catalogue of data providers and workflows across companies, people, jobs, finance and filings, public records and government spending, real estate, places and restaurants, retail and prices, package registries and developer data, news, research, and more; providers return typed, sourced records through published contracts. When a provider matches, prefer it over scraping pages if the task needs the same fields across several entities, provenance, exact figures or timestamps, or a large set of records; execute it through fire… [truncated]",
    "## perplexity\nPerplexity AI server for web-grounded search, research, and reasoning, backed by the Perplexity Agent API. Use perplexity_search for finding URLs, facts, and recent news. Supports recency filters and domain restrictions. Use perplexity_ask for quick AI-answered questions with citations. Supports recency filters, domain restrictions, and search context size control. Use perplexity_research for in-depth multi-source investigation (slow, can take minutes). Use perplexity_reason for complex analysis requiring step-by-step logic. Supports recency filters, domain restrictions, and search context size control. All tools are read-only and access live web data.",
    "## plugin:context7:context7\nUse this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.\n\nDo not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts."
  ],
  "removedNames": []
}

The\n// cost of keeping them is one extra decode per record; the cost of not keeping\n// them is unbounded and silent.\nfunc (r *Record) UnmarshalJSON(data []byte) error {\n\t// An alias without Record's methods, so this does not recurse.\n\ttype plain Record\n\tvar p plain\n\tif err := json.Unmarshal(data, &p); err != nil {\n\t\treturn err\n\t}\n\t*r = Record(p)\n\n\tvar raw map[string]json.RawMessage\n\tif err := json.Unmarshal(data, &raw); err != nil {\n\t\treturn err\n\t}\n\n\tknown := recordJSONKeys()\n\tfor key, value := range raw {\n\t\tif known[key] {\n\t\t\tcontinue\n\t\t}\n\t\t// Deliberately not logged here.       "content": "package claimcheck\n\nimport (\n\t\"fmt\"\n\t\"io\"\n\t\"strings\"\n\t\"unicode/utf8\"\n)\n\n// Report writes every property with every claim, its source, and what the\n// claims add up to.\n//\n// A conflict prints every competing value side by side and stops there. No feed\n// outranks another, the newest does not win, and the majority does not win:\n// nothing in this data justifies any of those rules, and a single merged value\n// would carry the authority of a schema while being a guess.\nfunc Report(w io.Writer, props []Property) error {\n\tfor i, p := range props {\n\t\tif i > 0 {\n\t\t\tif _, err := fmt.Fprintln(w); err != nil {\n\t\t\t\treturn err\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t}\n\t\tif err := reportProperty(w, p); err != nil {\n\t\t\treturn err\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn nil\n}\n\nfunc reportProperty(w io.Writer, p Property) error {\n\tif _, err := fmt.Fprintf(w, \"%s\\n  sources: %s\\n\", p.Name, strings.Join(p.Sources, \", \")); err != nil {\n\t\treturn err\n\t}\n\tfor _, f := range p.Findings {\n\t\tif _, err := fmt.Fprintf(w, \"  %-20s %-10s %s\\n\",\n\t\t\tf.Field, strings.ToUpper(string(f.Status)), f.Staleness); err != nil {\n\t\t\treturn err\n\t\t}\n\t\tfor _, c := range f.Claims {\n\t\t\tif _, err := fmt.Fprintf(w, \"      %-22s %-36s %s\\n\",\n\t\t\t\tquoted(c.Value), c.Source, observedLabel(c)); err != nil {\n\t\t\t\treturn err\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn reportUnparsed(w, p.Unparsed)\n}\n\n// reportUnparsed prints what the feed published and this tool could not place.\n//\n// It is the section that keeps the rest honest. Every status above is computed\n// over a vocabulary someone chose, and without this block a facility that was\n// discarded and a facility that does not exist produce the same output.\nfunc reportUnparsed(w io.Writer, unparsed []Unparsed) error {\n\tif len(unparsed) == 0 {\n\t\treturn nil\n\t}\n\tif _, err := fmt.Fprintf(w, \"  %-20s %d\\n\", \"UNPARSED\", len(unparsed)); err != nil {\n\t\treturn err\n\t}\n\tfor _, u := range unparsed {\n\t\tif _, err := fmt.Fprintf(w, \"      %-12s %-45s %s\\n\",\n\t\t\tu.Kind, unparsedText(u), u.Source); err != nil {\n\t\t\treturn err\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn nil\n}\n\n// unparsedText renders a JSON key beside its raw value, and everything else as\n// the raw text itself.\nfunc unparsedText(u Unparsed) string {\n\tif u.Name != \"\" {\n\t\treturn u.Name + \" = \" + truncate(u.Text, 45-len(u.Name)-3)\n\t}\n\t// Truncate inside the quotes, so a clipped line still reads as a complete\n\t// quoted string rather than one missing its closing mark.\n\treturn quoted(truncate(u.Text, 43))\n}\n\n// truncate keeps one unparsed item to one line. A description can be a\n// paragraph, and a report nobody can scan hides the conflicts as effectively as\n// not printing them.\n//\n// The limit counts runes, not bytes. These feeds carry German and Spanish prose,\n// and a byte slice lands inside a multi-byte rune often enough that the report\n// would print mojibake exactly where it is quoting text nobody parsed.\nfunc truncate(s string, max int) string {\n\tif utf8.RuneCountInString(s) <= max {\n\t\treturn s\n\t}\n\trunes := []rune(s)\n\treturn string(runes[:max-1]) + \"…\"\n}\n\n// observedLabel keeps \"the feed carried no date\" visually distinct from a date,\n// so an undated claim is never read as a current one.\nfunc observedLabel(c Claim) string {\n\tif c.ObservedAt.IsZero() {\n\t\treturn \"no date\"\n\t}\n\treturn c.ObservedAt.Format(lastSeenLayout)\n}\n\n// quoted wraps a value so an empty string is visible in the report rather than\n// printing as blank space.\nfunc quoted(s string) string { return `\"` + s + `\"` }\n",

      "filePath": "/Users/yuratestdev/Desktop/GOLAND/ygo-task/internal/claimcheck/model.go",
      "content": "// Package claimcheck groups hotel records from mixed feeds into properties and\n// reports what each feed claims about them, without resolving disagreements.\npackage claimcheck\n\nimport (\n\t\"encoding/json\"\n\t\"io\"\n\t\"time\"\n)\n\n// Status is what the set of claims for one field looks like taken together.\ntype Status string\n\nconst (\n\t// Supported means at least one source asserts a value and all agree. The\n\t// value may be \"false\": an affirmative denial is support, not absence.\n\tSupported Status = \"supported\"\n\t// Conflict means two or more sources assert incompatible values.\n\tConflict Status = \"conflict\"\n\t// Absent means no source asserts anything about the field.\n\tAbsent Status = \"absent\"\n)\n\n// Staleness is independent of Status: a field is routinely both in conflict and\n// out of date, and collapsing the two into one enum loses whichever is reported\n// second.\ntype Staleness string\n\nconst (\n\tFresh   Staleness = \"fresh\"\n\tStale   Staleness = \"stale\"\n\tUnknown Staleness = \"unknown\"\n)\n\n// FreshWindow is how old an observation may be before it is reported stale.\nconst FreshWindow = 365 * 24 * time.Hour\n\n// Claim is one source asserting one value for one field.\n//\n// Source is a feed name joined to the field path it came from, not the feed\n// alone, because the sharpest errors in this data are a single record\n// disagreeing with itself.\ntype Claim struct {\n\tField      string\n\tValue      string\n\tSource     string\n\tObservedAt time.Time // zero value means the feed carried no timestamp\n}\n\n// Finding is every claim about one field of one property, plus what they add up\n// to.\ntype Finding struct {\n\tField     string\n\tStatus    Status\n\tStaleness Staleness\n\tClaims    []Claim\n}\n\n// Unparsed is something a feed published that this tool did not understand.\n//\n// It exists so that the limits of the vocabulary are visible in the output\n// rather than inferred from its absence. A facility we cannot canonicalise, a\n// description no signal matched, and a JSON key with no struct field behind it\n// are all cases where silence and comprehension look identical, and silence is\n// the more dangerous of the two.\ntype Unparsed struct {\n\tKind   string // \"field\", \"facility\" or \"description\"\n\tName   string // the JSON key, for Kind \"field\"; empty otherwise\n\tText   string // the raw text, or the raw JSON value for Kind \"field\"\n\tSource string\n}\n\n// Property is a real-world hotel, which may be described by several records.\ntype Property struct {\n\tKey      string\n\tName     string\n\tSources  []string\n\tFindings []Finding\n\tUnparsed []Unparsed\n}\n\n// Coords is a decimal lat/lng pair as it appears in the partner feeds.\ntype Coords struct {\n\tLat float64 `json:\"lat\"`\n\tLng float64 `json:\"lng\"`\n}\n\n// Record is the union of every field shape seen across the feeds. Pointer and\n// slice fields distinguish \"the feed said null or nothing\" from \"the feed said\n// an empty value\", which is a distinction the report depends on.\ntype Record struct {\n\tSource         string   `json:\"source\"`\n\tHotelName      string   `json:\"hotel_name\"`\n\tName           string   `json:\"name\"`\n\tCity           string   `json:\"city\"`\n\tCountry        string   `json:\"country\"`\n\tLocation       string   `json:\"location\"`\n\tStars          *int     `json:\"stars\"`\n\tRating         string   `json:\"rating\"`\n\tDescription    string   `json:\"description\"`\n\tAmenities      *string  `json:\"amenities\"`\n\tFeatures       []string `json:\"features\"`\n\tReviewSnippets []string `json:\"review_snippets\"`\n\tCoords         *Coords  `json:\"coords\"`\n\tPriceFromEUR   *int     `json:\"price_from_eur\"`\n\tPriceFrom      string   `json:\"price_from\"`\n\tLastSeen       string   `json:\"last_seen\"`\n\n\t// UnknownFields holds every JSON key this struct has no home for, mapped to\n\t// its raw value. Populated by UnmarshalJSON; never decoded from the feed.\n\tUnknownFields map[string]string `json:\"-\"`\n}\n\n// LoadRecords decodes a feed dump.\nfunc LoadRecords(r io.Reader) ([]Record, error) {\n\tvar recs []Record\n\tif err := json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(&recs); err != nil {\n\t\treturn nil, err\n\t}\n\treturn recs, nil\n}\n\n// FindingFor returns the finding for a field, and whether one was reported.\nfunc (p Property) FindingFor(field string) (Finding, bool) {\n\tfor _, f := range p.Findings {\n\t\tif f.Field == field {\n\t\t\treturn f, true\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn Finding{}, false\n}\n",
      "numLines": 132,
      "startLine": 1,
      "totalLines": 132
    }
  },
  "displayPath": "internal/claimcheck/model.go"
}

      "content": "package claimcheck\n\nimport (\n\t\"strings\"\n\t\"testing\"\n\n\t\"github.com/google/go-cmp/cmp\"\n)\n\n// TestUnknownJSONFields covers a feed adding a field this struct has never seen.\n// Left to encoding/json it is discarded in silence, which means a new feed can\n// change what it publishes and nothing downstream ever finds out.\nfunc TestUnknownJSONFields(t *testing.T) {\n\tt.Parallel()\n\n\tconst feed = `[{\n\t\t\"source\": \"partner-feed-c\",\n\t\t\"hotel_name\": \"New Feed Hotel\",\n\t\t\"city\": \"Berlin\",\n\t\t\"cancellation_policy\": \"free until 24h before arrival\",\n\t\t\"loyalty_tier\": 3\n\t}]`\n\n\trecs, err := LoadRecords(strings.NewReader(feed))\n\tif err != nil {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"LoadRecords: %v\", err)\n\t}\n\n\tprops := Check(recs, testNow)\n\tif len(props) != 1 {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"got %d properties, want 1\", len(props))\n\t}\n\n\twant := []Unparsed{\n\t\t{Kind: \"field\", Name: \"cancellation_policy\", Text: `\"free until 24h before arrival\"`, Source: \"partner-feed-c\"},\n\t\t{Kind: \"field\", Name: \"loyalty_tier\", Text: \"3\", Source: \"partner-feed-c\"},\n\t}\n\tif diff := cmp.Diff(want, props[0].Unparsed); diff != \"\" {\n\t\tt.Errorf(\"unparsed mismatch (-want +got):\\n%s\", diff)\n\t}\n}\n\n// TestUnparsedFacilities covers the tokens the controlled vocabulary does not\n// recognise. Dropping them is what makes a vocabulary look complete: the report\n// would show a hotel's amenities as fully understood while two of them were\n// thrown away.\n//\n// \"pets allowed\" is a policy and \"swim-up bar\" is a facility with no canonical\n// name, and nothing here can tell them apart. Separating them needs the\n// vocabulary this bucket exists to avoid guessing at, so both land here as raw\n// text and a reader decides.\nfunc TestUnparsedFacilities(t *testing.T) {\n\tt.Parallel()\n\n\trecs := []Record{{\n\t\tSource: \"scrape-booking-sites\", Name: \"Sunset Bay Resort & Spa\",\n\t\tLocation:  \"Playa del Carmen, Mexico\",\n\t\tFeatures:  []string{\"spa\", \"3 pools\", \"swim-up bar\", \"pets allowed\"},\n\t\tAmenities: strptr(\"pool,,minibar\"),\n\t}}\n\n\tprops := Check(recs, testNow)\n\tif len(props) != 1 {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"got %d properties, want 1\", len(props))\n\t}\n\n\t// \"spa\", \"3 pools\" and \"pool\" map to the vocabulary; the empty CSV token is\n\t// nothing at all and must not be reported as an unrecognised facility.\n\twant := []Unparsed{\n\t\t{Kind: \"facility\", Text: \"minibar\", Source: \"scrape-booking-sites/amenities\"},\n\t\t{Kind: \"facility\", Text: \"pets allowed\", Source: \"scrape-booking-sites/features\"},\n\t\t{Kind: \"facility\", Text: \"swim-up bar\", Source: \"scrape-booking-sites/features\"},\n\t}\n\tif diff := cmp.Diff(want, props[0].Unparsed); diff != \"\" {\n\t\tt.Errorf(\"unparsed mismatch (-want +got):\\n%s\", diff)\n\t}\n}\n\n// TestUnparsedDescription covers prose that no signal matched.\n//\n// Only a description where nothing fired is reported. A description that fired\n// at least one signal was read, even if imperfectly, and printing every one of\n// those would bury the conflicts under prose that was never going to map to a\n// field.\nfunc TestUnparsedDescription(t *testing.T) {\n\tt.Parallel()\n\n\ttests := []struct {\n\t\tname string\n\t\trecs []Record\n\t\twant []Unparsed\n\t}{\n\t\t{\n\t\t\tname: \"prose matching no signal is reported with its raw text\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{{\n\t\t\t\tSource: \"partner-feed-a\", HotelName: \"Hotel Mare Azzurro\", City: \"Rimini\",\n\t\t\t\tDescription: \"<b>WELCOME TO PARADISE!!!</b> Best hotel in Rimini!\",\n\t\t\t}},\n\t\t\twant: []Unparsed{{\n\t\t\t\tKind:   \"description\",\n\t\t\t\tText:   \"<b>WELCOME TO PARADISE!!!</b> Best hotel in Rimini!\",\n\t\t\t\tSource: \"partner-feed-a/description\",\n\t\t\t}},\n\t\t},\n\t\t{\n\t\t\tname: \"prose that fired a signal is not reported\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{{\n\t\t\t\tSource: \"scrape-booking-sites\", Name: \"Sunset Bay\", Location: \"Playa del Carmen, Mexico\",\n\t\t\t\tDescription: \"An adults-only sanctuary of tranquility.\",\n\t\t\t}},\n\t\t\twant: nil,\n\t\t},\n\t\t{\n\t\t\t// City Lodge Berlin ships description: \"\". There is no prose here to\n\t\t\t// have missed, and reporting it would be noise standing in for a gap.\n\t\t\tname: \"an empty description is not unparsed prose\",\n\t\t\trecs: []Record{{\n\t\t\t\tSource: \"partner-feed-a\", HotelName: \"City Lodge Berlin\", City: \"Berlin\",\n\t\t\t\tDescription: \"\",\n\t\t\t}},\n\t\t\twant: nil,\n\t\t},\n\t}\n\n\tfor _, tt := range tests {\n\t\tt.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {\n\t\t\tt.Parallel()\n\n\t\t\tprops := Check(tt.recs, testNow)\n\t\t\tif len(props) != 1 {\n\t\t\t\tt.Fatalf(\"got %d properties, want 1\", len(props))\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\tif diff := cmp.Diff(tt.want, props[0].Unparsed); diff != \"\" {\n\t\t\t\tt.Errorf(\"unparsed mismatch (-want +got):\\n%s\", diff)\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t})\n\t}\n}\n",

      "content": "Base directory for this skill: /Users/yuratestdev/.claude/skills/go-review\n\n# go-review\n\nThe gate between \"it works\" and \"it moves on\". Review the **diff**, not your\nmemory of writing it — `git diff` (or `git diff --stat` then the files) is the\nfirst command, always. Maker ≠ checker: if you wrote it, you read it cold.\n\nTwo outputs only:\n\n- **Fix now** — wrong, unsafe, or blocking the next module.\n- **Note** — real but not urgent. Goes in `DECISIONS.md` or the PR body, not\n  into the current edit.\n\nAnything that is neither is not a finding. \"Could be cleaner\" without a named\nconsequence is noise, and it is the thing that turns a review into a time sink.\n\n---\n\n## The checklist\n\nWalk these in order. Each line is a question with a yes/no answer, not a theme.\n\n### 1. Testability\n- Can each new function be exercised without starting a server, opening a\n  socket, or reaching a database? If not, what is the injection point that is\n  missing — a narrow interface defined **in the consuming package**, a `Clock`,\n  an `io.Reader` instead of a path?\n- Is any dependency reached through a package-level variable or `init()`? That\n  is untestable-by-construction; it wants to be a struct field.\n- Does a test need `time.Sleep` to pass? That is a design finding, not a test\n  finding — see §7.\n\n### 2. TDD / failure coverage\n- Is there a test for every failure the function can produce, not just the one\n  the happy path avoids? Empty, malformed, negative, out of range, nil, zero\n  value, duplicate, too large, wrong type, cancelled context.\n- Do the tests assert error **identity** (`errors.Is`) or **structure**\n  (`errors.As`) rather than comparing strings? A string comparison breaks the\n  moment someone adds context to the message and tests nothing meanwhile.\n- Is the table ordered with failure rows first? The happy path is the easy row;\n  putting it last is what stops it from being the only row.\n- Was any assertion changed to make a test pass? That is not refactoring.\n\n### 3. Happy path\n- Is the successful route readable top to bottom, or is it buried under error\n  handling? Go style is early return on failure so the success case stays at\n  the left margin.\n- Is there exactly one? Two code paths that both count as success usually means\n  a missing type or a missing function.\n- Does it do the minimum? A happy path with a cache, a retry, and a feature\n  flag in it is three modules wearing one coat.\n\n### 4. Errors\n- Is every returned error either handled or wrapped with `%w` and context that\n  the caller does not already have? `fmt.Errorf(\"error: %w\", err)` adds nothing.\n- Is any error both logged **and** returned? Pick one — log where it is handled,\n  wrap everywhere else. The double is how one failure becomes five log lines.\n- Any error discarded with `_`? Especially from `Close`, `Flush`, `Write`,\n  `rows.Err()`. If it is genuinely ignorable, the `_` needs a comment saying why.\n- Is a sentinel error exported that no caller branches on? That is public API\n  for nothing. Conversely, does a caller need to branch on something that is\n  only a formatted string?\n- Any `panic` on a condition that is merely *unexpected* rather than\n  *impossible*? Bad input is an error; a violated internal invariant is a panic.\n- Does anything return `nil, nil`? The caller cannot tell \"not found\" from\n  \"empty\" from \"fine\".\n- Does a fan-out that can fail on several legs return only the first failure?\n  `%w` carries one cause. `errors.Join(flightErr, hotelErr)` carries both and\n  still answers `errors.Is` for each. One primary cause takes `%w`; two legs\n  that genuinely both failed take `Join`.\n\n### 5. Logging and the paths that degrade\n- Is every deliberate degradation — cache miss treated as available, provider\n  failover, partial result, dropped item — **logged at warn and counted**? A\n  fallback nobody counts is indistinguishable from being broken.\n- Are `InfoContext`/`ErrorContext` used where a ctx exists, so the trace link\n  survives?\n- Is the correlation id the middleware puts in the context actually **in a log\n  line**? Grep for the field inside a logging call, not for the middleware that\n  sets it. *Observed (40-service monorepo): chi's `middleware.RequestID` wired\n  into the chain and the structured-logger middleware that would attach it\n  commented out behind a TODO. Every request carried an id; no log line had one,\n  so nothing could be joined back to a request.*\n- Is the message a constant with the detail in attributes, rather than an\n  interpolated string? Interpolated messages cannot be grouped or alerted on.\n- Does anything log a token, header, body, prompt content, or personal data?\n  Check the struct fields that get passed to `slog.Any`, not just the literals.\n\n### 6. Edge cases in the code itself\n- Integer/float choice: is money a float anywhere? Is a count an `int` that can\n  go negative?\n- Slice and map: nil vs empty where the difference is observable (JSON output,\n  `len` checks, range over nil).\n- Bounds: any slicing with an index derived from input? Any `[0]` without a\n  length check?\n- Time: any wall-clock arithmetic across a boundary that could cross a DST\n  change or a leap second? Any timeout that is not derived from the caller's\n  deadline?\n- Unicode: any `len(s)` used where runes were meant?\n\n### 7. Concurrency\nFor **every** goroutine in the diff, answer all five. If any answer is \"I'd\nhave to check\", that is the finding.\n\n1. Who starts it?\n2. What makes it return?\n3. Who waits for it?\n4. What happens to it when the caller's context is cancelled?\n5. Can it block forever on a send, a receive, a mutex, or a timer?\n\nThen:\n- Is the number of goroutines bounded by something that is not the size of the\n  input? One goroutine per row of an untrusted file is a resource bug even if\n  every goroutine eventually exits.\n- Does the producer own channel closure, and is it the only closer?\n- Is every blocking send or receive inside a `select` with `ctx.Done()`? A\n  worker that checks the context only *before* blocking has not been cancelled.\n- Is `context.Canceled` / `DeadlineExceeded` preserved rather than flattened\n  into a generic error?\n- `errgroup`: is the derived context actually passed into every worker, and do\n  they honour it? Is there a concurrency limit where the input is unbounded?\n- Are directional channel types used in signatures (`<-chan`, `chan<-`) so\n  ownership is visible without reading the body?\n- Is a channel being used where a mutex would be simpler, or a mutex where the\n  thing being communicated is ownership or completion?\n- Is `defer` inside a loop, deferring cleanup to function exit rather than\n  iteration exit?\n- For a long-lived consume or poll loop: does it take a `ctx` and exit on it, or\n  is its only exit an internal error field? A loop nobody can stop is not shut\n  down, it is abandoned at process exit. And if a DI container owns shutdown,\n  you have inherited its stop timeout as your drain budget without choosing it\n  (uber-go/fx defaults to 15s). Name the budget or set it.\n- Where is the offset, ack or delete committed **relative to the work**? Before\n  is at-most-once, after is at-least-once, and a client-library default is\n  neither a choice nor a documented guarantee. *Observed: a Kafka consumer with\n  no `Commit()` call anywhere in the repo — `enable.auto.commit` left at the\n  librdkafka default, so offsets advanced on a 5s timer whether or not\n  processing had succeeded.*\n- Is there a poison-message path — bounded retries, then a dead-letter — or does\n  one bad message either loop forever or take the whole consumer down with it?\n\n### 8. Proving it — the race gate\nConcurrency findings are not settled by reading. Run:\n\n```bash\ngo test ./... -race -count=1\ngo test ./... -race -count=10 -run <TheConcurrentTest>   # repeat flushes flakiness\ngo test ./... -shuffle=on -count=1\n```\n\n`-race` only reports races on code paths that **execute**. If the concurrent\npath has no test, `-race` passing proves nothing — say so rather than citing it.\n\nWhere timing is the behaviour, use `testing/synctest` so the assertion is exact\ninstead of approximate, and `go.uber.org/goleak` in `TestMain` to make a leaked\ngoroutine fail the suite rather than leak silently.\n\n### 9. Consistency with what already exists\n- Same error style, logger, context handling, and test shape as the\n  neighbouring packages? A second convention is worse than either convention.\n- Package name earns its existence — no `utils`, `common`, `helpers`, `misc`.\n- No stutter: `http.Server`, not `http.HTTPServer`. No `Get` prefix on a\n  plain accessor.\n- Interfaces defined where they are **consumed**, small, and actually having\n  more than one implementation (a test fake counts; a speculative future\n  does not).\n- Accept interfaces, return structs — unless returning the concrete type would\n  leak an invariant.\n- `ctx context.Context` first, named `ctx`, never stored in a struct, never\n  carrying business parameters.\n- Exported identifier without a doc comment, where its error contract or\n  ownership is not obvious from the name?\n\n### 10. The cheap Go-specific smells\nScan for these directly; they are the ones a reviewer from another language\ndoes not flag:\n\n- shadowed `err` inside an `if` block that the function then returns as nil\n- naked return in anything longer than ten lines\n- pointer to an interface in a parameter or field\n- `any`/`interface{}` where a type parameter or concrete type would hold\n- unnecessary `else` after `return`; nesting deeper than two\n- a comment restating the syntax instead of the reason\n- a struct constructor that only assigns fields\n- `sync.WaitGroup` passed by value\n\n### 11. Running in something — config, lifecycle, blast radius\nThe code is correct and the process still falls over. These are cheap to check\nand almost never in a diff review.\n\n**Deadline budgeting.** A service that receives a deadline and passes it\nunchanged to its own dependency has not budgeted, it has forwarded. The\ndownstream work then finishes at the exact instant the caller stops listening,\nand a partial result arrives to nobody. Ask: does each hop reserve time for the\nwork that happens *after* the call returns — the next hop, the merge, the\nencode? A downstream deadline must be strictly smaller than the caller's, and\nthe reserve should be a named constant, not arithmetic buried in a call site.\nWhere the budget must cross a process boundary, it is an explicit protocol\nelement (a `budget_ms` parameter, a header), because the callee cannot read the\ncaller's context. Relying on the TCP disconnect is not cancellation; it is\nnoticing afterwards.\n\n*Observed:* a gateway with a 700ms global timeout propagated it verbatim to an\ninventory service that produced partial results at 700ms. The partial-result\ndesign did not work at all until a 200ms reserve was carved out and the\nremainder passed explicitly.\n\n**Name the reason the deadline fired.** `context.DeadlineExceeded` cannot tell\n\"our own budget ran out\" from \"the caller hung up\" from \"we are shutting down\",\nand a degraded response that cannot name its cause is one the caller cannot act\non. Build the budget with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, budget, ErrBudgetSpent)`\nand read it back with `context.Cause(ctx)` at the boundary that reports. Both are\nstdlib, and the distinction is the difference between \"some inventory was slow\"\nand \"we were restarting\".\n\n**Label your partial data.** Any response assembled from incomplete inputs —\na dropped record, a timed-out leg, a served-stale cache entry, a failover —\nmust say so in the payload, not only in a log. A caller that cannot distinguish\n\"the cheapest option is 605\" from \"the cheapest option I could see in time is\n605\" will act on the wrong one. Ask: is there a `degraded` flag, a count of what\nwas dropped, and a note naming why? Is the flag set on *every* path that\ndegrades, including the cache-hit path that inherited someone else's\ndegradation? Silently truncating and returning 200 is the failure mode this\ncatches.\n\n**Config and 12-factor.**\n- Any host, port, URL, or credential literal in the code? `localhost` in a\n  service that will run in a container is a defect, not a default.\n- Does a missing required variable fail loudly at startup, or produce a zero\n  value that fails confusingly on the first request?\n- Is config read once into a struct at boot, or `os.Getenv` scattered through\n  request handlers?\n\n**Lifecycle.**\n- Is there a `server.Shutdown(ctx)` on `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` with a bounded grace\n  period? A container that is killed mid-request drops it.\n- Do background goroutines started outside a request — refreshers, reapers,\n  pollers — stop on shutdown, or does the process hang or leak?\n- Are `ReadHeaderTimeout`, `ReadTimeout`, `WriteTimeout`, `IdleTimeout` set on\n  every `http.Server`? The zero value is \"no timeout\" and is a trivial DoS.\n  One exception worth knowing before you set all four everywhere: a blanket\n  `WriteTimeout` truncates streaming, SSE and long-poll responses mid-flight.\n  Those endpoints need their own server or a per-handler deadline.\n- Is the shutdown context derived from `context.Background()`? A shutdown path\n  that derives from the request context it is trying to drain is already\n  cancelled, so `Shutdown` returns immediately and drops exactly the in-flight\n  work it exists to protect.\n- Does the client have a timeout? The zero-value `http.Client` waits forever.\n- Does the health/readiness endpoint listen on its **own port**, separate from\n  the traffic port? A probe served by the same mux sits behind the same\n  throttle, middleware and saturation as the traffic it is meant to report on.\n- Does readiness check the **dependencies**, or only that the process's own\n  listener is up? A probe that reports healthy while Redis is unreachable is an\n  instruction to the orchestrator to keep sending traffic to a service that\n  cannot serve it. *Observed: liveness and readiness both returning a\n  package-level `var errServerFailure`, written by the server goroutine and read\n  by the probe goroutine with no synchronisation — a data race in the health\n  path itself.*\n\n**Blast radius.**\n- Is any unbounded collection keyed on caller-controlled input? A cache, map,\n  or metric label keyed on a raw query parameter grows until the process dies.\n  This is the one that reads as a memory leak and is actually a remote\n  resource-exhaustion vector.\n- Is the container image `scratch`/`distroless`, running non-root, with no\n  compiler or shell in the final layer?\n- Is there a `HEALTHCHECK`, and does orchestration actually wait on it\n  (`condition: service_healthy`) rather than on process start?\n\n**A config file is not evidence a tool runs.** Before citing any repo's tooling\n— including your own CI — as coverage, check three things: that a pipeline step\ninvokes it, that its failure fails the build, and that it is configured for this\nlanguage. *Observed in one repo, all four at once: `go vet ./... || echo \"vet\nreported errors\"` (advisory since the day it was written), the Sonar step\ncommented out with a note about server maintenance, a `qodana.yaml` pinning a\n**JavaScript** linter in a pure-Go monorepo, and a test-report script whose\nreporting logic was commented out. The failure cases become failing tests first\n\nWrite the table test with the failure rows first and the happy path **last**.\nA table whose rows are four failures and one success is the shape to aim for.\n\n```go\nfunc TestParsePrice(t *testing.T) {\n\ttests := []struct {\n\t\tname    string\n\t\tin      string\n\t\twant    Cents\n\t\twantErr error\n\t}{\n\t\t{\"empty\", \"\", 0, ErrEmptyPrice},\n\t\t{\"not a number\", \"abc\", 0, ErrMalformedPrice},\n\t\t{\"negative\", \"-1.00\", 0, ErrNegativePrice},\n\t\t{\"overflow\", \"99999999999999999999\", 0, ErrPriceRange},\n\t\t{\"comma decimal\", \"199,00\", 19900, nil},\n\t\t{\"plain\", \"199.00\", 19900, nil},\n\t}\n\tfor _, tt := range tests {\n\t\tt.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {\n\t\t\tt.Parallel()\n\t\t\tgot, err := ParsePrice(tt.in)\n\t\t\tif !errors.Is(err, tt.wantErr) {\n\t\t\t\tt.Fatalf(\"err = %v, want %v\", err, tt.wantErr)\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\tif got != tt.want {\n\t\t\t\tt.Errorf(\"got %d, want %d\", got, tt.want)\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t})\n\t}\n}\n```\n\nRun it and **show the failure**. If your first test run is green, you wrote the implementation first —\nwhich is the rule people break while believing they followed it, because the\ntests do eventually get written and do eventually go red. Do not retrofit the\norder. Say it plainly in Phase 6: \"tests were written after the implementation\",\nand treat every guard in the diff as unverified until Phase 5b mutates it. The `go-checks.sh` hook reports this automatically on\nevery `.go` edit, so the red state lands in the transcript without you narrating it.\n\nAssertion rules:\n- `errors.Is` / `errors.As` for error identity, never string comparison.\n- `cmp.Diff(want, got)` for structs, with the diff in the failure message.\n- One behaviour per subtest, named for the behaviour, not `case1`.\n- `t.Parallel()` only when the subtest touches no process-global state. `t.Setenv`\n  and `t.Chdir` are incompatible with it.\n\nIf a model produced the output, there is no single wanted value, and a table of\n`cmp.Diff` against one completion does not test the behaviour. If you notice something worth doing that is out of scope, note it and\nkeep going.\n\n## Phase 4 — Instrument what can go wrong\n\nEvery branch identified in Phase 1 gets one of three treatments, and you should be\nable to say which and why:\n\n| Treatment | When | Shape |\n|---|---|---|\n| Return a wrapped error | The caller can decide | `fmt.Errorf(\"enrich %s: %w\", id, err)` |\n| Log and continue | Degradation the caller must not see as failure | `slog.WarnContext(ctx, \"cache unavailable, falling through\", \"err\", err)` |\n| Count it | Silent degradation that must not stay silent | a counter plus an alert on the rate |\n\nThe third is the one people forget, and it is the one that matters in an AI or\nnetwork-facing service: a fallback nobody counts is indistinguishable from being\nbroken.\n\nRead [references/observability.md](references/observability.md) for the `log/slog`\nerror-path idioms: where to log versus where to wrap, what never goes in a log\nline, `LogValuer` for redaction, and how a span and a log line divide the work.\n\n## Phase 5 — The gate\n\nRun these in order. Paste the real output. Stop at the first failure and fix it.\n\n```bash\ngofmt -l .                                   # must print nothing\ngo vet ./...\ngo test ./... -count=1 -shuffle=on\ngo test ./... -race -count=1                 # the one people skip\ngolangci-lint run ./...                      # if the repo configures it\ngovulncheck ./...                            # on dependency changes\n```\n\n`-race` is not optional. A data race is invisible until it corrupts data in\nproduction, and the detector is the only thing that finds it. `-shuffle=on`\ncatches tests that pass only in declaration order.\n\n### Phase 5b — Mutate the guard. A green suite is not evidence yet.\n\nEvery tool above answers \"does the code pass the tests\". None answers \"would\nthe tests notice if the code were wrong\". So for each guard you wrote in\nPhase 4 — a `case <-ctx.Done()` in a select, a channel's buffer size, a mutex,\na bounds check, a deadline — **delete it, run the suite, and name the test that\ngoes red.**\n\n```bash\ncp pkg/thing.go \"$TMPDIR/thing.bak\"   # session scratch, not /tmp\n# delete exactly one guard\ngo test ./... -count=1 -run TheTestThatMustFail\ncp \"$TMPDIR/thing.bak\" pkg/thing.go   # always restore before moving on\n```\n\n**A mutation run that produced no output did not run.** It is never a pass.\nThe two states look identical through a `grep`, and the wrong reading is the\none that reassures you. Before recording any mutant as uncaught, confirm the\nsuite actually executed — a `--- FAIL` or an `ok` line, not an empty filter.\n*Observed (ygo-core, 2026-09): a mutation deleting `ctx.Done()` from a fetch\nloop was wrapped in `timeout 60 go test`. `timeout` is GNU coreutils and is not\non macOS, so the shell printed `command not found`, the grep matched nothing,\nand the mutant was one keystroke from being recorded as \"no test catches this\".\nRe-run with `go test -timeout`, it failed loudly in two places.* If a mutant\ngenuinely needs a wall-clock bound, use `go test -timeout`, which is in the\ntoolchain you already have.\n\nIf nothing fails, you have a test that cannot fail. That is worse than no test,\nbecause its green tick will be cited as evidence — by you, in the next message.\n\nAn invariant is a guard too. \"Never recommend out-of-stock inventory\", \"never\nexceed the budget\", \"never return an id that is not in the set\" — delete the\ncheck, run the suite, and name the test that goes red. That test is the\nproperty test, not one hand-picked example. A single example stays green when\nthe check is gone and the example happened to be safe. See\n[references/llm-boundary.md](references/llm-boundary.md).\n\nThis is not optional on concurrency work, and it is cheap: one edit, one run.\nObserved cost of skipping it: a goroutine-leak test that polled for two seconds\npassed with the cancellation case deleted, because an uncancelled worker still\nexits when its own timer fires. `vet`, `golangci-lint`, `govulncheck`,\n`-shuffle=on` and `-race -count=10` all passed against that hole. Only the\nmutation found it. Rebuild the test so the mutant is still misbehaving at the\nmoment you measure — a latency far longer than the test, and a short window.\n\nSay in Phase 6 which guards you mutated and which you did not.\n\nRead [references/verify.md](references/verify.md) for the full gate, the\n`golangci-lint` v2 linter set worth enabling, `testing/synctest` for deterministic\nconcurrency tests, native fuzzing, `rapid` for property tests, and testcontainers\nfor integration tests.\n\n## Phase 6 — Say what you did not do\n\nClose with the honest remainder: what is untested, what you assumed, what you\ndeliberately left out, and what would change your mind.
